sources.title: Lenny on how he built his newsletter and podcast: follow pull, stay lean, iterate
sources.originalTitle: A behind-the-scenes interview with Lenny Rachitsky on building his newsletter and podcast
sources.summary: Lenny's wife Michelle Rial interviews him on how he went from Airbnb to a 1.2M-subscriber newsletter. He covers following pull over a plan, committing weekly using the Lindy effect, sourcing advice from practitioners, staying lean with no full-time employees, and heavy iteration. Also includes a fraud lesson from an overly generous launch.

principles.text: Pursue what you enjoy and others value; that overlap is rare, so follow the pull even without a plan.
principles.quote: Which is very rare, that Venn diagram of things. Just like, how often do you enjoy something and people value it?

principles.text: Use the Lindy effect: how long you've sustained a consistent habit signals you can keep it up, so commit weekly.
principles.quote: I've been doing this every week for 9 months. Which means I could probably do this for 9 more months.

principles.text: The best content comes from practitioners doing the real thing, not people pontificating from the clouds.
principles.quote: that's the source of the best advice is from practitioners doing the thing for real.

principles.text: Stay lean: avoid full-time employees and complexity so you don't build a job you hate.
principles.quote: I also am trying very hard to never have full-time employees. I'm trying to keep things really simple

principles.text: Quality comes from relentless iteration; he rewrites each newsletter post around 50 times before editors touch it.
principles.quote: when I write a newsletter post, I go through it probably, let's say 50 times making it better.

principles.text: An offer that's too generous attracts fraudsters; stress-test your free perks and APIs for abuse before launch.
principles.quote: that was way too good an offer. People came for it. Bad people.

sources.title: How to kickstart and scale a marketplace: playbook from 17 marketplaces
sources.originalTitle: How to kickstart and scale a marketplace business by Lenny Rachitsky
sources.summary: Lenny distills interviews with founders and early growth leads at 17 major marketplaces into a four-step playbook for cracking the chicken-and-egg problem, then covers scaling, quality control, and regrets. Key finding: constrain by geography or category, focus on supply first, and use direct sales and word of mouth early.

principles.text: Start with the smallest viable marketplace: constrain by geography if service is physical, otherwise by category.
principles.quote: if the service requires physical interaction if you have to like pick up food or get in a car or stay at home that's it you can constraint it geographically

principles.text: Most marketplaces should focus on supply first; 80% of those studied did.
principles.quote: eighty percent of companies focused on supply so I take away there is most likely you're gonna want to focus on supply initially when you're building a marketplace

principles.text: Early supply growth is mostly unscalable direct sales, not SEO, viral loops or paid ads.
principles.quote: Dirk sales was the biggest lever by far across all these companies which surprised me I thought I was gonna be like forints marketing or SEO or viral loops and it turned out it's just sales

principles.text: Pick the few growth levers that work and double down; companies used only about two and a half levers on average.
principles.quote: even though there are many ways to grow supply probably there's going to be just a few that work for you and so learning there is don't try to do them all just pick the ones that seem to be working and double down on those

principles.text: Demand growth is led by word of mouth, which signals product-market fit; supply can also drive demand.
principles.quote: where to mouth is by far the biggest driver of growth for all of these companies which is really amazing and to me that just reaffirms how important product market fit is

principles.text: Don't expand into new business lines early; deepen the core and add new layers later once growth plateaus.
principles.quote: in the general case you don't want to do that because it's very hard to get any kind of business operating

sources.title: How Lenny Rachitsky grew his newsletter to 531,000 subscribers with quality and jobs to be done
sources.originalTitle: How Lenny Rachitsky Got 531,000 Substack Subscribers | How I Write Podcast
sources.summary: Lenny explains how he built a top Substack newsletter on product management. He spends heavy time on each post, defines the job each post does for readers, and grows through word of mouth rather than ads. He also covers his research and interview process, answer-first writing, and protecting his creative time.

principles.text: Define the job your content does for the reader, then do it better than anything else.
principles.quote: people buy your product people listen to your podcast people read your newsletter because they have a job they want you to do for them

principles.text: Beat the noise by investing far more time per piece and keeping quality high consistently.
principles.quote: I spend about 10 hours per post something like that some post take like a 100 hours some more

principles.text: Word of mouth from useful content outgrows every paid or promotional channel.
principles.quote: I've tried Twitter ads I've tried Facebook ads LinkedIn ads uh cross promotion all the things nothing nothing's done anything like it's all a blip compared to just the the growth that comes from Word of Mouth

principles.text: Lead with the answer, keep intros short, and save the supporting detail for after.
principles.quote: just tell them right away here's the answer and then if you want to learn more here's how here's how I got to this and here's a bunch more detail

principles.text: Build deep posts by asking top operators the questions your audience has, then synthesizing patterns into a framework.
principles.quote: I basically come at it from here's all the questions people that are building a Marketplace are going to have and I just ask them all those questions

principles.text: As you succeed, guard the time for the core work by saying no to talks, events and interviews.
principles.quote: as you become successful you just have less time to do that thing that made you successful and there's all these distractions that try to pull you away

sources.title: How Lenny grew a paid newsletter to 3,000+ subscribers: quality content, guest posts, and staying simple
sources.originalTitle: Lenny Rachitsky - The Dark Side of Paid Newsletters Nobody Talks About - The Nathan Barry Show 022
sources.summary: Lenny explains how he went from leaving Airbnb with no plan to a six-figure paid newsletter. He covers early growth via Twitter and high-quality guest posts, pricing, free-to-paid conversion, a sustainable writing process, and why he deliberately keeps the business small and simple.

principles.text: Anything not spent creating high-quality content barely moves newsletter growth; value drives word of mouth.
principles.quote: i find there's any time not spent creating high quality content is not time well spent and i just keep finding it over and over

principles.text: Guest post early, putting your best work where the audience already is, to jump-start your first thousand subscribers.
principles.quote: you just want to go to where your audience is and if you can write something that in a place somebody already has that whole audience and show how awesome you are they're gonna come follow you wherever you are

principles.text: Price higher than you think you should (he settled on $15/month), then discount occasionally with holiday deals.
principles.quote: priced higher than you think you should everybody always wants to start at five bucks a month because that's the lowest you can go and no one ever thinks their stuff is worth it

principles.text: Share drafts with supporters and peers before launching so they give feedback and then promote it.
principles.quote: i ran it by folks like andrew chan and and a bunch of other people with a large twitter following like generally to get their feedback on how to frame the announcement because they were supporters along the way and then also it led to them tweeting about it

principles.text: Write mostly what you're curious about (about 80%) with 20% for what readers want, or you'll burn out.
principles.quote: i try to do like a 80 what do i actually care about this week and i'm excited to write about with a 20 of like well people care about it this week

principles.text: Keep the business simple instead of scaling headcount and business units, to avoid becoming a workaholic again.
principles.quote: i feel like i could make more just keeping it my own thing not hiring anyone full-time not trying to you know add more business units to it

sources.title: How Lenny grew his newsletter to 30K subscribers and six figures by writing in public
sources.originalTitle: Writing in Public: Lenny Rachitsky & David Perell
sources.summary: Lenny walks through how he went from a Medium post to a paid newsletter with about 30,000 free and 1,400 paid subscribers. He covers how he picks topics, runs research posts, and distributes through a Twitter and newsletter flywheel. The core idea: deliver consistent, practical value and give the good stuff away.

principles.text: Growth comes from consistent value; there is no distribution hack beyond delivering it.
principles.quote: the secrets any newsletter success slash maybe anything that's successful is just deliver consistent value to people

principles.text: Test every post: is it actionable, close to what you know, and does it add something new?
principles.quote: is it actually actionable and valuable and practical or is it just like fluffy high level sounds good kind of talk

principles.text: Find topics by noticing questions with no good answer online, then do primary research to fill the gap.
principles.quote: someone asked me a question i try to look it up and there's no answer and so that tells me there's an opportunity to do primary research

principles.text: Time invested is a durable advantage because most people won't spend the hours to research a topic deeply.
principles.quote: the more time you put into a thing for example a post or a newsletter the better it's going to be than anything else out there

principles.text: Give away the best of each post on Twitter instead of teasing it; this drives subscriptions and feeds a two-way flywheel.
principles.quote: give away all the goods on twitter even if it's like even if it's a paid post give away like as much as i can with the post on twitter because then people end up subscribing

principles.text: Prefer examples that are concrete and actionable, grouping many companies' shared approach over deep dives on one company.
principles.quote: what they're really looking for is what it would work for a lot of companies slash what worked best for my type of company

sources.title: Lenny Rachitsky: the race car growth framework (engines, boosts, lubricants, fuel) and early users
sources.originalTitle: Lenny Rachitsky: how to grow a startup
sources.summary: Lenny lays out his race car framework for long-term growth: pick one of four self-sustaining engines (performance marketing, virality, content, sales), then layer turbo boosts and lubricants. He also covers getting the first users, retention benchmarks, and how he built his newsletter to 55k free and 5k paid subscribers.

principles.text: Only four engines drive long-term growth: performance marketing, virality, content, sales. Become best in the world at one.
principles.quote: it turns out there's essentially four engines you can choose from as a company and uh and these engines are self-sustaining loops that keep your business growing

principles.text: Spreading effort across many channels rarely works. Concentrate on one engine, add a second only when the first plateaus.
principles.quote: you have to become really really good at one to any chance and often people kind of spread their resources too thin

principles.text: Anticipate the S-curve plateau and plant the next engine early, building a layer cake of growth.
principles.quote: you want to anticipate this plateau approaching at some near future and start to plant seeds for another engine

principles.text: Performance marketing fits only if users pay you immediately and nobody is searching for your product. Otherwise avoid building on it.
principles.quote: you need to be generating revenue from your users immediately so that you can feed that right back into the ads and then two is your product is not something people are naturally looking for

principles.text: Measure virality by the share of new users arriving via friends or referral; well over half signals a real viral engine.
principles.quote: look at the percentage of your new users who came in through a referral or a word of mouth

principles.text: Early on, do non-scalable turbo boosts to ignite the engine: reach out to your 'customers who care' and find them directly.
principles.quote: early on most of your work is should be these boosts which kind of ignite the engine a little bit like reaching out to strangers to get them to try your thing

sources.title: Lenny Rachitsky: How to know you have product-market fit, benchmark retention, and plan growth for a Series A
sources.originalTitle: Product & Marketing by Lenny Rachitsky at Growth Week 2021
sources.summary: Lenny draws on research into successful companies to explain three signs of product-market fit, retention benchmarks by business type, and a four-engine growth framework. He also covers 10 ways startups found their first thousand users, all aimed at a Series A raise.

principles.text: Product-market fit means a real market exists; look for sudden pull, gradual compounding pull, or flattening cohort retention curves.
principles.quote: you look for a sudden and significant pull from the market or gradual but compounding pull from the market or and or actually uh your cohort retention curves flatten

principles.text: Retention is the ultimate PMF measure: if the cohort curve flattens above zero, a segment wants your product.
principles.quote: if that curve flattens out and doesn't drop to zero you have product market fit with some segment of the market

principles.text: Track retention by cohort, not blended monthly churn, so you can see whether product changes actually helped.
principles.quote: the other approach blends together new users and existing users and you can tell if changes to your product are having an impact because you don't know what percentage of those are new

principles.text: Good retention benchmarks vary by business type, scaling with acquisition cost and customer stickiness.
principles.quote: the cost to acquire users scale basically linearly through this list so with the consumer social spectrum it's very cheap to acquire snapchat user and instagram user very expensive to acquire an enterprise

principles.text: Your growth is driven by one of four engines (paid, content, sales, virality); pick the best fit and master it.
principles.quote: there's only one of these four engines is going to be responsible for the majority of your growth so it's really important that you figure out which of these engines is most likely to drive your growth

principles.text: Don't mistake one-off turbo boosts like PR for a self-sustaining engine; invest in the engine itself.
principles.quote: mistake a lot of founders make is they rely on these things again and again and again thinking it's going to drive their growth ongoing without investing in their engine

sources.title: How Lenny Rachitsky built a $500K+/year newsletter: quality, time and primary research
sources.originalTitle: How Lenny Rachitsky Makes +$500,000/Year With A Newsletter (#96)
sources.summary: Lenny explains how he grew his newsletter and podcast with no hacks: consistent high-quality content, lots of time, and primary research rooted in real audience problems. He also covers early growth sources, Substack recommendations, ruthless editing, and the downsides of the creator treadmill.

principles.text: Sustainable content growth comes from consistency and quality, not hacks; referrals and paid ads barely moved the trend line.
principles.quote: nothing helps it grow other than just consistency and quality of content.

principles.text: Root content in a real problem someone has. Starting as an advice column kept the work grounded in actual needs.
principles.quote: that content is rooted in a real problem somebody actually has, not just me pontificating on something that may be a thing.

principles.text: Pick the job your content does for the reader, then do that job better than anyone else.
principles.quote: figure out what's the job you're doing for someone, and then just do that better than anyone else that's doing it out there.

principles.text: Do primary research on behalf of your audience (talk to the companies directly); it delivers expensive-to-get value cheaply.
principles.quote: I'm just doing primary research on behalf of people, and it's like very low cost for them.

principles.text: Time invested drives quality. Going full-time and spending many more hours per piece is the edge.
principles.quote: I find a really direct correlation between the amount of time I put into something and the success of that piece.

principles.text: Build the newsletter first, then launch a podcast. Sharing each episode with an existing audience makes podcast growth easier.
principles.quote: build an awesome newsletter and then launch a podcast. It's harder, I think, the other way around.

sources.title: How Lenny Rachitsky used high-quality writing and word of mouth to build a top newsletter
sources.originalTitle: Lenny Rachitsky: How To Use Writing To Scale Your Expertise
sources.summary: Lenny explains how he went from a post-Airbnb Medium essay to a paid Substack newsletter that grows ~90% through word of mouth. He covers choosing topics by energy and curiosity, investing heavily in quality and research, using Twitter for distribution, and going paid and building a community.

principles.text: Follow the work that gives you energy and treat early content traction as a signal worth pursuing.
principles.quote: you should actually be spending more time on things that give you energy and less time on things that sap your energy

principles.text: Write what you are genuinely curious about, with audience input as a secondary signal; otherwise you rebuild a job you dislike.
principles.quote: the more interested i am in a thing i'm working on the better it gets and so i try to stay close to like just writing things i'm really interested in

principles.text: Quality wins in a sea of free content: time invested in a post correlates directly with how it performs.
principles.quote: the only way you stand out is you're better than all of those other ones like not just a little bit better but it's like oh wow this is so good

principles.text: Spend almost no time on distribution; great content spreads via word of mouth, and Twitter nuggets bootstrap the audience.
principles.quote: i think 90 of my growth is just word of mouth people sharing it with each other

principles.text: Build an audience by adding value in public (e.g. Twitter) first, then point it at your newsletter at launch.
principles.quote: find places to add value to people's lives and then you'll build the audience there over time

principles.text: Give away the best parts upfront in tweets and posts instead of building to a reveal.
principles.quote: the more you just give away all the good stuff quickly the better it does

sources.title: Lenny Rachitsky: 7 ways to increase your influence as a PM, taught through Frodo
sources.originalTitle: Lenny Rachitsky on How to Increase Your Influence at Lean Product Meetup
sources.summary: Lenny walks through seven influence tactics for people without formal authority, using Lord of the Rings and Airbnb stories: align goals, build trust, share your reasoning, show success, bring evidence, borrow authority, and be likable. Practical for PMs and anyone who must get others to commit resources.

principles.text: Connect your ask to the other person's goals; this one skill alone makes you a strong influencer.
principles.quote: anytime you're asking someone for favor just like spend like 10 seconds it's like it's very little time just like what what are they trying to do what are their goals and then and then how do I connect what I'm trying to do to their goal

principles.text: Trust is a battery you charge over time, so build it with key people before you need to make the big ask.
principles.quote: trust is a battery trust isn't this like binary I trust you I don't trust you there's this like battery that charges indeed and depletes as you build trust with someone and lose trust with someone

principles.text: Help people see what you see: loop them in early and explain the why. Rushing buy-in just gets reversed later.
principles.quote: with people in general slow as fast and Fast is slow which essentially refers to when you try to like rush through something with people they may pretend like they are on board but they're often not

principles.text: Keep showing success; consistent wins and visible progress earn you continued resources and trust, even on scary projects.
principles.quote: the reason we continue to make progress or to continue to have resources to work on this thing is we continue to show success we kept moving the metric we promised

principles.text: Evidence persuades most when it is quantifiable; when data is missing, walk people through what convinced you or cite comparable examples.
principles.quote: quantifiable numbers is by far the most powerful maybe below that is user research like really good research

principles.text: Push back by prioritizing and communicating: place the ask in your priority list and show your manager the trade-offs.
principles.quote: you look at your to-do's take their ask you put it where you think it belongs and then you tell your manager here's where I put it in my party list what do you think

sources.title: Lenny's "Grand Unifying Theory of Growth": four steps from first users to growth engines
sources.originalTitle: Brainstorming the "Grand Unifying Theory of Growth" | Lenny Rachitsky | Highlighter
sources.summary: Lenny brainstorms a zero-to-scale growth playbook: pick a wedge early adopter, craft a remarkable value prop, find them through concentric circles of channels, then commit to one of four growth engines. He backs it with many company examples and open discussion on the messy middle and on humane growth.

principles.text: Start with a narrow early-adopter wedge into a bigger market, then a value prop that resonates with them.
principles.quote: step one is identify your early adopter users who are kind of a wedge into a broader market step two is identify a value prop that resonates with these specific users

principles.text: Aim for a value prop that is genuinely remarkable, so people want to talk about it.
principles.quote: remarkable just means it's worth remarking about and so what you want to figure out is a value prop that is remarkable to the people you're pitching to

principles.text: Early users come from concentric circles around the founder; friends and colleagues bootstrap trust, especially in B2B.
principles.quote: it's more that if there's a reason to believe that it's worth trying so just bootstrapping trust

principles.text: Early tactics spike but don't last; you need a sustainable growth engine, and there are only four: paid, virality, content/SEO, sales.
principles.quote: everything that we've talked about so far is not sustainable and it's not going to last it's going to be like a spike of growth

principles.text: Be the best in the world at one engine in your market; competitors then win through other engines.
principles.quote: you need to be the best in the world at one of these engines in your market

principles.text: Once you know which engine will drive growth, commit to it instead of poking at it on the side.
principles.quote: if you know that's where you're gonna drive growth from you should just commit to it and and focus on and move as fast as you can

sources.title: How to launch and scale a marketplace: Lenny's research on 17 founders' playbooks
sources.originalTitle: How to Build & Scale Marketplace Business | Lenny Rachitsky | The Product Folks
sources.summary: Lenny presents research from about 24 interviews with founders of 17 marketplaces (Airbnb, Uber, DoorDash, OpenTable, Etsy and others). The pattern: solve chicken-and-egg by narrowing, building supply first, using a few growth levers, then broadening levers and policing quality at scale.

principles.text: Product-market fit comes first; marketplace tactics only matter once people actually want what you offer.
principles.quote: কিন্তু আমি বলব একটি মার্কেটপ্লেস ব্যবসার সাফল্যের ৯০ শতাংশই নির্ভর করে এই প্রশ্নের উপর যে, এটি কি এমন কিছু যা মানুষ চায়?

principles.text: Start tiny: constrain the marketplace, pick one side, build supply first, then demand.
principles.quote: আপনার মার্কেটপ্লেসকে সীমাবদ্ধ করুন, এক বা অন্য দিকে মনোযোগ দিন, সরবরাহ তৈরি করুন, তারপর চাহিদা তৈরি করুন।

principles.text: Most marketplaces focus on supply first; go demand-first only when supply is effortless to attract.
principles.quote: আমি যে মার্কেটপ্লেসগুলোর সাথে কথা বলেছি তার ৮০%প্রথমে সরবরাহের উপর মনোযোগ দিয়েছে।

principles.text: Seed early supply with unscalable direct sales (door-to-door, calls, email), not SEO or paid ads.
principles.quote: নিঃসন্দেহে এক নম্বরে ছিল, যদি আপনারা দেখতে পান, প্রাথমিক সরবরাহ বাড়ানোর জন্য এটিই ছিল সবচেয়ে সাধারণ উপায়।

principles.text: Pick the two or three growth levers that work for you rather than trying all of them.
principles.quote: এখানে আমার একটি শিক্ষা হলো যে সবগুলো করার চেষ্টা করবেন না। মূলত এমন কয়েকটিই থাকবে যা আপনার জন্য সত্যিই কাজ করবে।

principles.text: At scale there is no silver bullet; growth comes from stacking levers, and quality means removing bad suppliers.
principles.quote: কোনো জাদুকরী সমাধান নেই। এমন কোনো একটি চালিকাশক্তি থাকবে না যা শেষ পর্যন্ত আপনার জন্য সবকিছু করে দেবে।

sources.title: How Lenny Rachitsky grew a newsletter from Medium posts to a six-figure paid Substack
sources.originalTitle: How To Start and Grow a Newsletter with Lenny Rachitsky and Nadia Eghbal
sources.summary: Lenny explains how he went from ex-Airbnb PM with no writing history to a full-time paid newsletter. He covers content ideation, consistency, distribution via guest posts and Twitter, when to go paid, and pricing. Nadia Eghbal adds Substack's view on audience ownership and bundles.

principles.text: Newsletter success comes from consistently providing real value: entertain, make money, make smarter, inform, or create belonging.
principles.quote: there's kind of five jobs to be done in newsletter and I don't know if this is completely right but the way I think about it it's either entertain me make me money make me smarter keep me informed or help me feel like I'm part of something bigger

principles.text: Quality and depth win; most content is low-effort because people lack time to research deeply, so invest the time.
principles.quote: if you have time and you put in the and you put in the time into writing I think you'll lead it'll lead to really high quality stuff that people end up valuing

principles.text: Use guest posts on adjacent audiences to get your first subscribers.
principles.quote: you kind of find the audience that you think is going to become your newsletter audience and then go write something awesome within their newsletter or blog

principles.text: Run a Twitter-newsletter flywheel, and give away the best content on Twitter rather than teasing it.
principles.quote: you just need to give away the best stuff on Twitter and not kind of like entice people to go read the post because no one's going to read it

principles.text: Grow a big free list before going paid; only go paid if it's your main income, otherwise use the newsletter as a funnel.
principles.quote: you should only go paid is if you want that to be your main source of income otherwise you should use a newsletter to drive something else you're doing

principles.text: Create accountability and write about what genuinely interests you to sustain a publishing cadence.
principles.quote: if you stay close to things you're curious about you're innately interested in exploring it and writing about it so so that's again really important to build that Cadence

sources.title: How to know if you've got product-market fit: a curated set of definitions and signals
sources.originalTitle: How to know if you've got product-market fit
sources.summary: Lenny curates the most actionable definitions of product-market fit from founders and investors, split into pre-product and post-product signals. Key tests: retention curves that flatten, the 40% "very disappointed" survey, organic growth, and LTV exceeding CAC. He closes with Ben Horowitz's point that PMF is not a single moment.

principles.text: Most people have only a vague grasp of PMF, and few pursue it systematically. Collect concrete definitions and measure against them.
principles.quote: I’ve noticed that most people (including myself) have only a vague grasp on what product-market fit actually is. And even fewer people are going after it in a systematic way.

principles.text: Before you have a product, test PMF by trying to get people to pay now, even via an invoice for early access.
principles.quote: Nothing will be a better signal of interest and PMF if you can get people to put down money before you have a product.

principles.text: Retention is a core post-product PMF test: if cohort retention curves flatten, a group of customers is finding lasting value.
principles.quote: If it flattens off at some point, you have probably found product/market fit for some market or audience.

principles.text: Survey users on how they'd feel if the product disappeared; more than 40% answering 'very disappointed' signals PMF.
principles.quote: If that percentage is over 40%, you have PMF.

principles.text: Organic, word-of-mouth growth is a key PMF indicator: users who love a product spontaneously tell others.
principles.quote: Organic growth is the key indicator of product/market fit.

principles.text: PMF is not a one-time, discrete point in time; competitors and markets keep evolving, so keep checking.
principles.quote: Product/market fit isn’t a one-time, discrete point in time that announces itself with trumpet fanfares.

sources.title: What PMF feels like: lessons from 25 iconic founders (Netflix, Airbnb, Superhuman, Stripe and more)
sources.originalTitle: What it feels like when you've found product-market fit
sources.summary: Lenny asked founders of 25 iconic companies when they first knew they had product-market fit. Pull comes in many forms, about half found PMF right after launch while half took months or years, and pull intensity depends on both product fit and initial market size. PMF is only the first of three requirements for a real business.

principles.text: Market pull takes many forms: organic growth inflection, customers asking to pay, complaints when you're down.
principles.quote: Customers asking to pay for the product before you ask

principles.text: Roughly half of companies find PMF right after launch; the other half iterate for months or years, but once there it's obvious.
principles.quote: About half of these companies found PMF immediately after launch, but half spent months or years iterating to get there

principles.text: Pull intensity depends on both fit (how well you solve the problem) and initial market size (niche vs broad).
principles.quote: The intensity of the pull is a factor of the fit (how good your product is at solving the user’s problem) AND initial market size (is it niche or broad).

principles.text: A 10x better product in a narrow market gives steady, compounding pull rather than a sudden explosion.
principles.quote: Instacart, Superhuman, and Substack were 10x better products but for a narrow set of initial customers —> steady and compounding pull.

principles.text: A feeling of PMF alone doesn't make a business; you also need to profit at scale and sustainably find and keep customers.
principles.quote: getting to a feeling of PMF does not mean you’ll automatically be able to build a successful business.

principles.text: The biggest killer is the first requirement: not building something people want.
principles.quote: Of these three milestones though, the most likely to kill your business is the first: not building something people want.

sources.title: What is good retention? Benchmarks for user and net revenue retention by business type
sources.originalTitle: What is good retention?
sources.summary: Lenny and Casey Winters polled 20 growth experts to set GOOD and GREAT benchmarks for 6-month user retention and 12-month net revenue retention across consumer, SMB and enterprise models. It also explains when lower retention is acceptable and why retention is the most telling metric for a business.

principles.text: Retention is the scalable way to grow and the best signal of product-market fit; no metric predicts thrive-or-die better.
principles.quote: No other metric is as singularly telling of whether your business will thrive or die.

principles.text: Benchmark user retention by business type: consumer social ~25% good/45% great; enterprise SaaS ~70% good/90% great at 6 months.
principles.quote: Consumer social: ~25% is GOOD, ~45% is GREAT

principles.text: Benchmark net revenue retention: bottom-up SaaS ~100% good, ~120% great; enterprise ~110% good, ~130% great.
principles.quote: Bottom-up SaaS: ~100% is GOOD, ~120% is GREAT

principles.text: Low retention can be OK if CAC and marginal costs are low, since cheap acquisition lets you afford to lose users.
principles.quote: If you can acquire new users cheaply (e.g. SEO, word of mouth, or virality), you can afford to lose more users.

principles.text: Growth is a balance of CAC, retention and unit economics; retention doesn't live in a vacuum.
principles.quote: Growth is a balancing act between CAC, retention, and unit economics.

principles.text: Not every business needs venture-scale retention; a flat retention curve enabling scalable acquisition can sustain a business.
principles.quote: a flat retention curve that drives a scalable acquisition strategy is enough to keep your business alive.

sources.title: How the fastest growing B2B companies found their first ten customers: three sourcing strategies
sources.originalTitle: How today's fastest growing B2B businesses found their first ten customers
sources.summary: Lenny researched 20+ hyper-growth B2B companies (Figma, Stripe, Slack, Shopify, Airtable, Salesforce and more) and found every one sourced early customers through just three routes: tapping personal networks, going where customers already gather, and press. Most combine the first two, and personal network matters most when you have to sell rather than grow bottom-up.

principles.text: Only three strategies source nearly every B2B company's first customers: personal network, finding customers where they are, and press.
principles.quote: Only three sourcing strategies account for every B2B company's very early growth (unlike the seven strategies for consumer apps). Thus, your choices are easy, yet limited.

principles.text: Do both: hit your network and go where prospects spend time. The real question is how far your network takes you before you move on.
principles.quote: almost every B2B business BOTH hits up their personal network AND heads to the places their potential customers were spending time.

principles.text: A strong personal network is a big B2B advantage, and you can build one via a connector investor or an incubator like YC.
principles.quote: It's a huge advantage to have a strong personal network in B2B, which you can also build by bringing on a connector investor or joining an incubator such as YC.

principles.text: Network matters even more when you must sell the product (not bottom-up), since early customers need a reason to trust you.
principles.quote: Tapping your personal network is even more important if you need to "sell" your product (i.e. not going bottom-up), likely because early customers need to have a reason to trust you.

principles.text: Press is rarely how B2B companies get started.
principles.quote: Getting press is rarely the way to get started

principles.text: Ask yourself who in your network could buy, where your target customers spend time, and what untold story you could pitch press.
principles.quote: Who in your network could be a potential customer? How could you quickly build a network?

sources.title: How to find and win your first 10 B2B customers: a seven-step sequence from trust outward
sources.originalTitle: How to find and win your first 10 B2B customers
sources.summary: Part four of Lenny's B2B series distills how dozens of top startups (Figma, Gong, Retool, Vanta, Canva, Ramp) landed their first 10 customers. The core pattern is concentric circles of trust: start with your network, then creative cold outbound, investor networks, communities, content, press, and launch. None of it scales, which is why it works.

principles.text: Early-customer tactics don't scale, and that is why they work. B2B starts with hand-to-hand combat.
principles.quote: None of these seven strategies scale. That’s why they work. In B2B, it always starts with hand-to-hand combat.

principles.text: Start with your own network and your early employees' networks; they carry the most innate trust and least skepticism.
principles.quote: This group will have the most innate trust (and the lowest amount of skepticism) about your idea.

principles.text: Cold outbound works early if you are creative and targeted; if responses are poor, get more specific.
principles.quote: One of the recurring themes (and biggest surprises) across my interviews is the value, and effectiveness, of going cold outbound in the early stages

principles.text: Use investors' networks by digging in and cold-emailing yourself, not just asking for intros, and ask those founders for further intros.
principles.quote: But not by asking for introductions—instead, by doing the hard work of digging into the investors’ own networks (including batch-mates within YC) and cold-emailing them.

principles.text: In communities, add value first; nobody wants to pay attention to someone who only shows up to pitch.
principles.quote: When joining communities, focus first on adding value to the community. No one wants to pay attention to you if you’re there just to pitch your product.

principles.text: Trust is the secret weapon: start with the highest-trust channels and work outward.
principles.quote: Start with the channels that have the most innate levels of trust, and work your way outward.

sources.title: How the most successful B2B startups found their original idea: past pain, ponder and probe, present pull
sources.originalTitle: How the most successful B2B startups came up with their original idea
sources.summary: Lenny synthesizes interviews with two dozen B2B founders (Gong, Notion, Figma, Retool, Slack, etc.) into a framework for finding a startup idea. A great idea is important, underserved, and something you're excited about. Founders found it through three paths, always chasing "pain" and "pull".

principles.text: A great B2B idea is important, underserved, and something you're excited to spend years on.
principles.quote: Find an idea that solves a problem that is important, underserved, and that you’re excited about.

principles.text: Venture-scale needs a big market: most startups fail because the market is too small, not the idea.
principles.quote: Most startups fail not because the idea isn’t good but because the market for the solution is just too small.

principles.text: Your solution must beat the existing one by 4 points out of 10 (Delta-4); a 6+ incumbent is very hard to replace.
principles.quote: Your solution needs to be +4 better for anyone to care about your product.

principles.text: Three reliable paths to an idea: past pain, ponder and probe, present pull.
principles.quote: Across all of the interviews I did, I found three reliable paths for discovering a great idea:

principles.text: Whatever the path, look for both pain (important problem) and pull (you're actually solving it).
principles.quote: Pain tells you there’s an opportunity to solve a problem, and that it’s important. Pull tells you that you’re actually solving the problem.

principles.text: Whiteboarding works only if you pick a space and talk to customers quickly; otherwise ideas stay abstract.
principles.quote: There’s a wrong way of whiteboarding and a right way (i.e. ideating and building in a silo versus quickly talking to potential users to validate your idea).

sources.title: How to come up with a consumer startup idea: 5 strategies from 50 winning companies
sources.originalTitle: How to kickstart and scale a consumer business
sources.summary: Lenny studied how 50+ top consumer companies (Airbnb, Uber, Instagram, Coinbase and more) found their ideas. Nearly all came from paying attention: to your own problems, your curiosity, what's already working, paradigm shifts, or brainstorming with friends. He also lists traits of good ideas and what to do first once you have one.

principles.text: Winning consumer ideas come from paying attention, and the largest share come from solving your own problem.
principles.quote: there are only five common strategies for coming up with a great startup idea—**all rooted in paying attention**

principles.text: Don't rely on forced ideation; most big consumer ideas emerged organically rather than from sitting down to brainstorm.
principles.quote: Less than a third of founders were actively ideating** a startup idea when they came up with their big idea. In other words, most startup ideas emerged organically.

principles.text: Launch what excites you now; if one element unexpectedly works, double down on it because it may be the bigger idea.
principles.quote: it should motivate you to launch whatever it is you’re currently most excited about—because even if the idea doesn’t work, it may lead you to the bigger idea.

principles.text: Good ideas come from founders' unique insight and gut instinct, not early user research, and often sound trivial or crazy at first.
principles.quote: rarely is user research a big factor in the early ideating. Most ideas emerged out of the founders’ experience, vision, and gut instincts.

principles.text: A strong idea combines founder obsession, a quick prototype with the skills to build it, unique insight, and simplicity.
principles.quote: Every product we’ve looked at can be explained in a sentence or two.

principles.text: Once you have an idea, prototype it cheaply and quickly to validate it, then talk to potential customers to refine it.
principles.quote: Prototype it cheaply and quickly to validate the idea

sources.title: How to find your first 1,000 users: the seven early-growth strategies from 100+ consumer startups
sources.originalTitle: How to kickstart and scale a consumer business: find your early adopters
sources.summary: Lenny reviewed the early growth of 100+ consumer companies and found only seven reliable ways to get the first 1,000 users: friends, targeted strangers, where your audience hangs out, influencers, press, viral content, and physical placement. Pick two or three, focus, and start with the easy inner circle before moving outward.

principles.text: Only seven channels reliably get your first 1,000 users; pick two or three, try them, and focus rather than doing everything.
principles.quote: Like with a menu, your job is to peruse this list, pick two or three items that seem appetizing, and try them. If something works, chow down. If not, try something else.

principles.text: Most startups get nearly all early growth from one or two channels, so focus instead of ordering everything on the menu.
principles.quote: almost every startup finds the vast majority of their early growth from just one or two channels.

principles.text: Start with the easy stuff near the founder (friends, colleagues) and migrate outward only if it isn't working.
principles.quote: So in your decision of where to start, start with the easy stuff and migrate outward if nothing is working.

principles.text: The highest-ROI early channel is going where your super-specific audience already gathers and giving real value, not spam.
principles.quote: The single most popular (over 50%!), effective, and highest-ROI strategy for finding your first 1,000 users is to find an existing gathering spot for your super-specific who

principles.text: Marketplaces should manually recruit targeted strangers on the supply side, because each supplier is valuable enough to justify heavy cold outreach.
principles.quote: this tactic was almost exclusively used by marketplace startups to bootstrap the supply side and rarely used by non-marketplaces. I imagine this is because one unit of supply is worth a lot to a new marketplace

principles.text: Friends are the fastest early source, but only useful if they resemble your super-specific who; don't get discouraged if they aren't.
principles.quote: just don't get discouraged if it doesn't bear fruit, as your friends may not be anything like your super-specific who.

sources.title: How to kickstart a marketplace: constrain by geography or category first, from 17 marketplaces
sources.originalTitle: How to kickstart and scale a marketplace business
sources.summary: Lenny shares research from interviews with founders and early employees at 17 major marketplaces. The first step to cracking the chicken-and-egg problem is to constrain the marketplace by geography or category, since the best way to get big is to start small. He also warns against over-relying on any single company's story.

principles.text: A marketplace connects demand and supply and leads to a financial transaction, without owning supply itself.
principles.quote: A marketplace business is one that **(1) connects demand** (i.e. people who want a thing) with **(2) supply** (i.e. people who have that thing), and **(3) leads to a financial transaction**.

principles.text: Starting a marketplace is hard because one side must commit before the other exists (chicken-and-egg).
principles.quote: it’s challenging to get the flywheel going. You must convince one side of the marketplace to commit before the other side.

principles.text: Constrain your initial marketplace; going small first is the fastest way to get big.
principles.quote: every single marketplace that I interviewed constrained their initial marketplace** to more quickly get to critical mass.

principles.text: Constrain by geography when supply and demand must meet physically; otherwise constrain by category.
principles.quote: If the offering requires supply and demand to be in the same physical location, the constraint is always geographical (e.g. a limited set of markets). Otherwise, it’s category-based (e.g. handmade goods).

principles.text: Don't over-index on one company's story; focus on the ways of thinking behind tactics, since past tactics often stop working.
principles.quote: focus more on ways of thinking and the cleverness behind the ideas –– not only the specific tactics. Many of the most successful growth levers of the past no longer work, or are significantly less effective.

principles.text: Many marketplaces succeeded primarily through product/market fit; growth levers accelerated and controlled growth rather than creating it.
principles.quote: For many of these companies, the primary reason they became successful was not because of some amazing growth insights – it was primarily because of great product/market fit

sources.title: What seven years at Airbnb taught Lenny about building a business: culture, focus, ambitious goals
sources.originalTitle: What seven years at Airbnb taught me about building a business
sources.summary: Lenny distills seven years at Airbnb into lessons on culture, problem statements, wildly ambitious goals, working backward from the ideal experience, org design, a high bar, and team focus. Practical, with concrete Airbnb examples like Instant Book and Snow White.

principles.text: A well-crafted, aligned problem statement is the single most important step in solving any problem.
principles.quote: Crafting and aligning on a problem statement is the single most important step in solving any problem.

principles.text: Set uncomfortable goals and give each one a single accountable owner by name.
principles.quote: If a number doesn’t have a person’s name next to it, it’s not going to happen.

principles.text: Start from the ideal user experience and work backward instead of micro-optimizing the funnel.
principles.quote: Instead of spending months or years micro-optimizing individual parts of the funnel, we stepped back and explored what the ideal booking experience would look like.

principles.text: Treat org design as a product: dedicated cross-functional teams with a clear mandate, few dependencies.
principles.quote: Optimize for dedicated cross-functional teams with a clear mandate.

principles.text: Good goals are few, fast-feedback, tied to top-line growth, easy to understand, and uncomfortable.
principles.quote: Goals should 1) be limited in number — ideally just one or two, 2) have quick feedback loops that allow you to see impact immediately, 3) be directly connected to top-line business growth, 4) be easily understood, and 5) be uncomfortable.

principles.text: Hire only people you feel strongly about; a maybe is a no.
principles.quote: My advice is to only hire people you feel “hell yes” about. If it’s a maybe, it’s a no.

sources.title: Content-driven growth: five strategies and lessons from HubSpot, Ahrefs, Intercom, Slidebean, Webflow
sources.originalTitle: Content-driven growth
sources.summary: Lenny maps content-driven growth on a 2x2 (SEO vs. virality, user- vs. employee-generated), giving five strategies, then zooms into editorially generated SEO content. He collects how HubSpot, Ahrefs, Intercom, Slidebean and Webflow started, staffed and operationalized content. Takeaways: start small, set a clear goal, be patient, dedicate a team.

principles.text: Content-driven growth splits into five strategies, defined by SEO vs. virality and users vs. employees as creators.
principles.quote: Where you sit on this 2x2 is based on what you’re optimizing for (SEO vs. virality) and who’s generating the content (users vs. employees).

principles.text: Start scrappy and experiment with platform, topic, and style until something works.
principles.quote: Start small: Start scrappy and play around with platform, topic, and style until you find something that works.

principles.text: Be explicit about whether content is for SEO traffic, virality, brand, or sales enablement.
principles.quote: Align on a clear goal: Is your goal to bring SEO traffic, to drive virality, to build your brand, or to enable sales? Make sure you’re clear on this.

principles.text: Find topics where searchers are underserved and deliver differentiated value.
principles.quote: Hunt for opportunity: Research topics where searchers are underserved, and create content that delivers compelling, valuable, and differentiated value to those searchers.

principles.text: Give content to someone who truly cares: founders or a passionate full-time employee.
principles.quote: The best content will be produced by people who truly care about the product/business/topic—normally, the founders or a passionate full-time employee.

principles.text: Content pays off slowly; expect years and a dedicated team of at least five.
principles.quote: Be patient: It took years for each company chronicled below to see significant payoff.

sources.title: How Lenny grew his newsletter to 500,000 subscribers: ten lessons on quality, consistency, and focus
sources.summary: Lenny reflects on hitting 500,000 subscribers and distills ten lessons. Growth comes from consistently publishing high-quality, original, shareable work, not from design, branding, or growth strategy. He covers picking a topic by energy, spending more time per post, cutting words, and sustaining a cadence.

principles.text: Growth comes from quality and consistency; design, title, strategy and growth plans mostly don't matter.
principles.quote: There’s no trick to making something like this grow. Growth comes from publishing something valuable, that people want to share with their friends and colleagues, over and over and over.

principles.text: Define the concrete job you do for a specific audience, and do it better than anyone.
principles.quote: Who exactly is your audience? Think of a specific person—what would they find extremely interesting or useful?

principles.text: Pick a topic by following your energy and real-life experience; avoid niches so narrow you get bored.
principles.quote: Follow your energy. What topics give you energy to think about, write about, and talk about? What saps you of energy? Spend more on the former and less on the latter.

principles.text: Time invested in content itself beats time on branding, website or strategy; most content is mediocre so better wins.
principles.quote: If you can spend almost zero time working on anything that isn’t creating the content itself, you’ll have an advantage.

principles.text: Cut 30-50% of your words: shorten intros and get to the meat fast.
principles.quote: Cut every word that isn’t ~absolutely~ necessary. Make your intro 50% shorter. Get into the meat of your post as quickly as possible.

principles.text: Contribute something new via primary research, and choose a sustainable cadence you can keep for years.
principles.quote: Remember, quality + consistency = you win, and people don’t want more emails. They want better emails.

sources.title: How Lenny built a top-10 tech podcast to 10M downloads: lessons, guests, stack, workflow
sources.originalTitle: My podcast tech stack, workflows, and lessons
sources.summary: Lenny reflects on two years of podcasting (10M downloads, 3M YouTube views). He covers niching down to 100 superfans, interviewing craft, landing dream guests via cold outreach, his tool and hardware stack, outsourcing production, and why YouTube drives most discovery.

principles.text: Aim to be 100 people's favorite thing, not something many people mildly like; expand once you have that foothold.
principles.quote: Instead of trying to make something a lot of people like, create something that 100 people _love_.

principles.text: Don't wait for A+ to start. Lower the pressure, start at B+, and improve from there.
principles.quote: My advice is to aim for B+ to start, then work up from there.

principles.text: Don't pre-produce too much before launch. You learn what resonates only after launching, and early batches can't be improved.
principles.quote: I'd recommend recording only three to five ahead of time, just so you aren't immediately behind schedule.

principles.text: Build a wishlist of dream guests and work backward. Most people say yes to a simple cold DM or email, and persistence pays off.
principles.quote: It's surprisingly easy to convince people to be a guest on a podcast.

principles.text: Inbound requests are the least useful source of great guests; prioritize your own wishlist and say no to most.
principles.quote: Some of these inbound requests have turned into great episodes, but I find this channel to be the least helpful for finding great guests.

principles.text: YouTube is the best discovery channel for a podcast; start earlier, since most new-listener growth comes from its algorithm.
principles.quote: There's no better way for new people to discover your podcast than through YouTube's algorithms.

sources.title: PM career path: why reaching senior IC PM is the biggest lever
sources.originalTitle: Becoming a senior product manager
sources.summary: Lenny's framing intro to Jackie Bavaro's guest post on becoming a senior PM. He lays out the three career milestones (senior IC, manager of PMs, director) and argues the first takes longest, so speeding it up matters most. The detailed strategy, autonomy and nuance framework is Jackie's, not Lenny's.

principles.text: The PM career has three milestones: senior IC, manager of PMs, then manager of PM managers.
principles.quote: The PM career is unnecessarily shrouded in mystery.

principles.text: Going from entry-level to senior PM is the slowest milestone in the PM career.
principles.quote: In my experience, of these three milestones, it takes the longest to progress through the first milestone, going from an entry-level PM to a senior PM.

principles.text: Rough timeline: about 3 years to senior PM, 1-2 to PM manager, 2-3 more to Director.
principles.quote: I’d guess that the median amount of time is 3 years, followed by 1-2 years to become a manager of PMs, and another 2-3 to become a Director.

principles.text: Accelerating the senior PM step has the largest effect on your whole career trajectory.
principles.quote: Thus, if you can accelerate getting to Senior PM, you’ll have the most impact on accelerating your overall PM career.

sources.title: How to get into product management: paths, fit, and the seven core skills
sources.originalTitle: How to get into product management
sources.summary: Lenny explains how to tell if PM is right for you, the four common routes into a first PM role, and the seven skills to build, in order of importance. Advice is drawn from his Airbnb transition from engineering to product and from helping others make the move.

principles.text: Check your motivations before becoming a PM: it's thankless and all-consuming, so you must enjoy solving problems, deciding, and leading.
principles.quote: It’s often a thankless, nerve-racking, and all-consuming. But, when it works, you feel like you were born to do it.

principles.text: For an internal PM transfer, you need a transfer process, a chance to show skills, and an internal PM champion; make the missing one happen.
principles.quote: If two of three exist, find a way to make the third happen. Otherwise, pursue one of the other paths.

principles.text: Joining a startup as PM depends on founder connections, hustle, and a strong growth mindset since you learn on the fly.
principles.quote: Having a very strong growth mindset is key since you’ll have to learn how to do this job on the fly.

principles.text: Execution is the most valuable PM baseline; a PM who can't execute makes the team worse off, so practice it immediately.
principles.quote: A PM that is good at nothing else but execution is valuable to a team, while a team with a PM that can’t execute is better off without that PM.

principles.text: Communication is the PM's job: everything runs through writing, speaking and meetings, and you can hardly over-communicate.
principles.quote: You can never be too good at this, and it’s very difficult to over-communicate.

principles.text: Build an 'I got this' aura through preparation, detail orientation, and a higher bar than those around you.
principles.quote: The key to building this aura is to become increasingly detail oriented, to be more prepared than anyone else, and to have a higher bar than those around you.

sources.title: How people discover new products: Lenny's seven channels and how to pick yours
sources.originalTitle: How people discover new products
sources.summary: Lenny lays out seven ways people become aware of a new product, from friend referrals to outbound sales, with examples and the conditions under which each channel works. He closes with a five-step process for picking where to invest based on your early adopters.

principles.text: Friend-to-friend word of mouth is the cheapest, best growth channel, but only if the product is naturally suited to it.
principles.quote: This is by far the cheapest and best way to grow if you can pull it off.

principles.text: Invest in word of mouth only if the product is better with others, fun to share, or remarkable. You can't layer it on later.
principles.quote: Most products do not grow this way (and it’s nearly impossible to layer on if the product isn’t naturally suited for this), so don’t be sad if you can’t make this work.

principles.text: Organic discovery online works when your product is remarkable, people already search for it, or your company makes a good story.
principles.quote: Your product or company makes for a good story—one that reporters would want to cover, for example

principles.text: Paid online promotion fits products people don't search for, where new users generate revenue that funds more ads.
principles.quote: You generate revenue directly from new users (e.g., purchasing a product, subscribing to a service), which you can then use to fund more ads

principles.text: Outbound sales suits high AOV/LTV products, ones needing hand-holding, and early companies hunting their first customers.
principles.quote: That are just getting started and looking for their initial customers

principles.text: Pick channels by finding early adopters, where they spend time, then the quickest and cheapest way to reach them and what makes you stand out.
principles.quote: What’s the _cheapest_ way you can get in front of this group?

sources.title: What is a good growth rate: investor benchmarks by stage (Lenny's survey of two dozen VCs)
sources.originalTitle: What is a good growth rate
sources.summary: Lenny surveyed about two dozen top investors on what counts as good and great growth by stage. Early on, investors ignore small-base MoM percentages and watch time to $1M ARR, retention, and efficiency. For consumer, engagement and retention beat revenue. Most of the quotes are from the investors, not Lenny.

principles.text: Early-stage MoM growth percentages mean little because the base is tiny; investors want to see accelerating momentum instead.
principles.quote: In the early stages, investors don’t care about month-over-month growth

principles.text: If you need a sub-$1M ARR MoM benchmark, investors typically cited 15%-25% month over month.
principles.quote: if you’re looking for a month-over-month benchmark below $1m ARR, answers typically fell in the 15%-25% range.

principles.text: For early B2B, speed to $1M ARR after launch is the key metric: within 12 months is good, within 9 months is great.
principles.quote: getting to $1m ARR within a year of launch is GOOD, and getting there in three quarters (9 months) is GREAT.

principles.text: Launch strategically: weak traction after launch is worse than being pre-launch, since it signals a weak market or value prop.
principles.quote: For this reason, you want to be strategic about when you launch

principles.text: Without fast ARR growth, show that people want the product via high retention and efficiency.
principles.quote: Without fast ARR growth, you’ll need to show strong signals that people really want your product—through high retention and efficiency

principles.text: For early consumer products, engagement, virality and retention matter more than revenue.
principles.quote: for early-stage _consumer_ businesses, it’s all about intensity of engagement, virality, and retention—not revenue

sources.title: How Lenny Rachitsky built a paid newsletter business by following energy and optimizing for curiosity
sources.originalTitle: Interview with Lenny Rachitsky, writer of Lenny's Newsletter
sources.summary: Lenny explains how he stumbled into full-time writing after leaving Airbnb by tracking what energized him, and how he runs his newsletter: topic selection, a dense-advice writing style, Substack's discovery value, and niche opportunities. He also covers his angel investing and personal finance approach.

principles.text: Follow energy: do more of what energizes you and less of what drains you, then lean into the pull.
principles.quote: my philosophy was to do more of what gave me energy, and do less of what sapped me of energy. After every call, every project, every meeting, I paid attention to whether I was more energized or less energized.

principles.text: Optimize for your own curiosity over what the audience says it wants; it produces better work and keeps you sane.
principles.quote: I optimize for my own curiosity vs. what people want because it ends up being better that way, and I stay sane

principles.text: Win on density: high-quality, easy-to-understand advice, no long intros or pontification. Cut relentlessly.
principles.quote: Get to the point, synthesize it clearly, and get out of your own way.

principles.text: Frame content as a concrete, simple, direct question from a reader to anchor each post.
principles.quote: I always frame my posts as a question, since it’s an advice column, the post always starts with a concrete, simple, direct question from a reader.

principles.text: Time invested in a piece correlates strongly with performance, though some quick pieces and guest posts also win big.
principles.quote: there’s a very strong correlation between the time I put into a post and how well it does (e.g. all the posts that took 100+ hours are in the top 10)

principles.text: Stay on a platform that drives discovery and removes admin; time spent off great content is wasted, and leaving to save fees can slow growth.
principles.quote: I find that time spent on anything that isn’t making great content is wasted time, and time spent -> quality

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Lenny's wife Michelle Rial interviews him on how he went from Airbnb to a 1.2M-subscriber newsletter. He covers following pull over a plan, committing weekly using the Lindy effect, sourcing advice from practitioners, staying lean with no full-time employees, and heavy iteration. Also includes a fraud lesson from an overly generous launch.

chunks.heading: Starting the newsletter: following the pull
chunks.text:
- Lenny left Airbnb after 7 years with several plans: start a company, join a startup as first PM, join a big company as PM, or consult. Writing a newsletter was nowhere on the list.
- He kept writing on the side while exploring startup ideas. His first post, on what he learned at Airbnb, did very well. Medium featured it and Brian Chesky shared it with the whole company.
- A friend (Lee Jacobs, now a VC) pointed out that "you seem to be enjoying it" and people valued it, a rare overlap worth doubling down on.
- Lenny says he would otherwise have been "on the struggle bus of startup life" and, once that failed, joined a company as a PM.
- He had never written online before and describes himself as an introvert who liked staying behind the scenes. The newsletter began during COVID, so he could just type and publish from home.

chunks.heading: The 9-month weekly commitment and the Lindy effect
chunks.text:
- He moved to Substack and committed to a weekly newsletter, announcing it as an experiment.
- After 9 months of weekly posts, he reasoned that if he'd kept going that long, he could probably do it another 9 months. He cites the Lindy effect: something that has lasted a given time will most likely last at least that long again.
- He had many more ideas to write about, so he kept going.
- That was the point he added a paywall. COVID had hit Airbnb's stock, so he needed income from the newsletter.
- The paywall worked: he made "meaningful dollars" about a month in.
- He now has 1.2 million subscribers, and his podcast is regularly in the top 10 of tech podcasts.

chunks.heading: Enjoying it, and the treadmill downside
chunks.text:
- His test for a path worth pursuing is the overlap of three things: it's good, people like it, and he enjoys it.
- He can't imagine doing anything more fulfilling: writing about interesting things, sharing other people's insights, interviewing people and extracting wisdom, all in his own business.
- He cites the artist Finch's post on becoming an artist: once it's a thing you have to do, it changes it.
- A post and a podcast episode every week is a treadmill. His image is "the Indiana Jones boulder is chasing me constantly": once a post ships, the question is immediately what comes next week.
- Some weeks he loves it, some weeks he'd like to skip. He says you can't survive in this life without doing something consistently and making it good every week.
- He has no answer for where this goes long term, since there's no obvious end state for a Substack writer and podcaster.

chunks.heading: Keeping the business small and avoiding a job he'd hate
chunks.text:
- He misses having someone next to him working on the same thing, now that he works from home. He has a team, but not coworkers in the room.
- He's trying hard to never have full-time employees and to keep things simple.
- His warning: it's easy to build this into something complicated, or to create a job you hate by doing what people want or by chasing things that "feel big."
- He is careful about what he commits to.

chunks.heading: Business crisis: the product pass fraud attack
chunks.text:
- Subscribers get a bundle of about 23 products (he names Linear, Mobbin, Lovable, Replit, Gamma). He used to read every one at the end of his podcast, but there are now too many.
- About a year before this recording, he launched a perk giving a free year of Cursor, Lovable, Bolt, Replit and V0. He says it was "way too good an offer."
- It attracted fraud rings, mostly in China, which built attacks to exploit the free goodies, found exploits in the API his team built, and spread the offer virally through student networks.
- He worked with Stripe and Substack to shut the attacks down. His engineer Este barely slept for a week patching holes.
- The stress was real: he feared the whole thing could unravel if people stopped trusting him, and he slept badly.

chunks.heading: Managing stress and happiness
chunks.text:
- He thinks he's more stressed than he looks (he gets headaches) but less than the average person, and credits maybe 70% genetics plus deliberate work on how he thinks.
- During his wife's complicated delivery, when a emergency happened and he was left without information in a hospital hallway, he kept telling himself "it's going to be okay" and trusting that the doctors knew what they were doing. He calls it probably the scariest moment of his life.
- A University of Pennsylvania online course on the psychology of happiness had a big impact on him. Its key idea: everyone has a baseline level of happiness, good and bad events move you away from it temporarily, and the main lever is raising the baseline.
- The practical tools he took from it: think more optimistically and don't let your mind spiral into "it's going to be terrible." He says his baseline has gone up.
- On exercise, the research he remembers (from around 15 years earlier, possibly outdated) is that it doesn't make you happier but lifts you out of the negative, from below zero to zero.
- He has also done a 10-day silent meditation and breathing work.
- A psychedelic experience in Joshua Tree around the time he started the newsletter, where the phrase "I have wisdom to share" came through repeatedly over about 3 hours, gave him confidence that he had things to share.

chunks.heading: Why the best content comes from real experience
chunks.text:
- He says the best stuff comes from doing the thing for real, then sharing the advice, not from "floating in the clouds pontificating."
- That's why most of his posts are now guest posts where someone shares the best thing they've learned in their career, and he focuses on practitioners on the ground.
- He agrees with the idea that to write, you read, but adds that lived experience is the source of the best material.
- His quality bar: he knows a piece is ready when it feels really interesting and good to him, without waiting for others' approval.
- His process is heavy iteration. He reads through and improves a newsletter post about 50 times, then it goes to his editor, a copy editor and a designer.
- Sitting on work and coming back to it often reveals what will make it better.
- He compares this to how David Sedaris says yes to everything to collect stories: you can't just sit and generate ideas, you have to try things and live.

chunks.heading: Product management, in his words
chunks.text:
- His definition: a PM's job is "to deliver business impact by prioritizing and solving the most impactful business problems."
- He still believes a PM is a mini CEO: the PM should think the way the CEO would about what helps the product and business succeed.
- The five words he first reached for: impact, collaboration, judgment, alignment, coordination.
- What carried over from PM work to his current job: being organized, a very high bar for quality, and communicating points succinctly so people grasp them.
- He is not an intuition person; he asks what the smartest people have already figured out about a problem (for example, shortening bedtime) and applies it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Lenny distills interviews with founders and early growth leads at 17 major marketplaces into a four-step playbook for cracking the chicken-and-egg problem, then covers scaling, quality control, and regrets. Key finding: constrain by geography or category, focus on supply first, and use direct sales and word of mouth early.

chunks.heading: Constrain the marketplace first (geography or category)
chunks.text:
Lenny's step one for cracking the chicken-and-egg problem is to build the smallest viable marketplace so a flywheel can form.
- Constrain by geography if the service needs physical interaction (pick up food, ride in a car, stay in a home). Constrain by category if it doesn't.
- Of the 17 marketplaces he interviewed, about 70% started with a geographic constraint and the rest with a category constraint.
- Geography examples: Airbnb started in New York. Rover started in Seattle (Amazon is a big employer, very dog friendly). Instacart picked markets with high expected demand, such as Chicago in winter. OpenTable found it needed 50 to 100 restaurants in a concentrated area for a market to work, then moved city by city.
- Category examples: Etsy started with handcrafted goods, Eventbrite with tech events and mixers, TaskRabbit with handyman tasks, housecleaning and moving help.
- TaskRabbit later felt it was still too broad and would have focused further (it eventually narrowed to IKEA furniture assembly).
- Thumbtack is the exception. It went wide on both category and geography (nationwide, all services) and brute-forced it, taking four or five years to crack. Lenny thinks it would likely have done better starting with a geographic constraint.

chunks.heading: Pick one side to focus on, usually supply
chunks.text:
Step two is deciding whether supply or demand is the initial constraint. Every company he studied picked one.
- About 80% focused on supply first, so supply is the likely default.
- Lyft knew supply growth was the unlock from the start. DoorDash studied Uber-style models, saw they start with restaurants, and saw that supply drives demand.
- Thumbtack compared Amazon, eBay and Craigslist and noticed that all three had all the supply and none cared much about brand or product. So it focused on getting all the supply and came back to product later.
- Only three companies found demand was the constraint. Rover had no supply problem, and its value prop was compelling: "$50 to have a dog over for one night." Zillow bootstrapped its supply from existing home data, so it never had to convince anyone to sign up.
- Patreon realized it wasn't really a marketplace. Creators loved it, but demand-side users didn't want to hunt for creators to pay. It removed the demand side from the roadmap and became a SaaS tool for creators, which was a huge win.
- Lenny's takeaway: you may not have a demand problem to solve, and you may not actually be a marketplace.

chunks.heading: Levers for kickstarting supply
chunks.text:
Step three is driving supply. He found 12 common levers, and the top ones were not what most people guess.
- Direct sales was by far the biggest. About 60% of companies (10 of 17) used it as their primary early lever. Airbnb was heavily direct-sales driven early on, and OpenTable staff walked restaurant to restaurant pitching and setting up the service themselves.
- Piggybacking on an existing network was next, almost always Craigslist. Uber went to Craigslist for drivers. Airbnb allegedly solicited people renting homes on Craigslist and got them to switch (before Lenny's time, unconfirmed).
- Referrals were third. Lyft got double digits of supply from referrals, Uber a third of trips, and Lenny worked on referrals at Airbnb.
- Word of mouth was fourth. OpenTable restaurants talk to each other. Eventbrite got 36% of supply from word of mouth. On Patreon, creators follow creators.
- Subsidizing supply: Lyft and Uber paid drivers a salary at first.
- Single player mode: build a tool that is useful to one side before the other side exists. OpenTable built an excellent reservation system for restaurants that worked with no demand. The pitch was about 90% reservation system and 10% "we'll drive you demand," then slowly flipped toward demand.
- Performance marketing and SEO were low on the supply side early on (only Lyft/Breather-type cases and Eventbrite for SEO).
- Companies used only about 2.5 supply levers on average (median 2). His advice is not to try all twelve. Pick the few that work and double down.

chunks.heading: Levers for kickstarting demand
chunks.text:
The demand-side ranking looks different from supply.
- Word of mouth was by far the top driver, which Lenny reads as proof of how much product-market fit matters. At Airbnb, a 2014 measurement showed about 50% of growth came from word of mouth (70% on the host side). Lyft's pink mustache drove word of mouth.
- Supply driving demand: your own suppliers bring buyers. DoorDash restaurants promote "download DoorDash to order," Etsy sellers and Eventbrite organizers share their pages. This worked for 7 companies and is a strong lever because "they do all the work for you."
- SEO is big on the demand side (7 of 17). Thumbtack's founder sat next to an SEO expert at a bar, who then joined the board, and SEO became 80 to 90% of growth. GrubHub got 30% of new users from SEO as its top lever.
- Performance marketing: Breather's founder Julien ran Twitter ads as himself ("we're launching in New York, message me"), got thousands of DMs, and hand-onboarded people through a seven-step funnel. Twitter called him in because the ad converted so well, at about a penny per click.
- PR was the fifth most common lever. TaskRabbit and Zillow relied on it as their number one channel.
- Loops: supply drives demand drives supply. GrubHub built menu pages that convert traffic into bookings, then tells restaurants "we're sending you traffic, sign up," which brings more supply and more demand.

chunks.heading: Know whether you are supply or demand constrained at scale
chunks.text:
- Constrained means which side, if you added more of it, would unlock growth. Adding an already-sufficient side does nothing.
