- About 40% of companies were always supply constrained (DoorDash, Uber, Lyft). About 20% were always demand constrained (OpenTable, and TaskRabbit, which had a waitlist of would-be taskers and started charging them a fee). The rest changed by market or category, so they built a model or heuristic.
- GrubHub sorted markets by the percentage of restaurants online and orders per restaurant.
- Thumbtack found NPS rose significantly once a search returned at least three results, so "at least three results per search" became the goal.
- Airbnb first used occupancy (e.g. 70% occupancy means supply constrained), then looked at where conversion drops (in some markets above 50% occupancy), then built a sophisticated revenue model.
- Uber's surge pricing started when a Boston GM emailed drivers promising double pay for 3 a.m. Friday rides. It worked, other cities copied it, and it became a product feature.

chunks.heading: What works at scale, and keeping quality up
chunks.text:
Fewer levers scale than work early, since early tactics don't scale. A combined supply and demand view looks like this:
- Performance marketing became number one (roughly 50% of growth at one company, and Zillow added it later with big results).
- Geographic expansion was second (a top-two-or-three lever for Instacart).
- Conversion/funnel optimization was third, though less of a huge lever than he expected.
- SEO often arrived late (OpenTable) but worked once adopted. Referrals were the sixth most common, 10 to 15% of growth at Airbnb.
- You can hold levers in your back pocket and add them later. Quote from Caviar's Gokul: there's no single silver bullet, "a lot of light bullets" that add up.
- Quality tactics: set a standard and remove or warn people below it (Rover removes hosts under a star rating); onboard early supply (Airbnb used a 12-point checklist on photos, pricing and descriptions, and DoorDash and Caviar still walk restaurants through onboarding); use search ranking to demote low quality and promote high quality.
- Find early quality signals: TaskRabbit gave a mini Myers-Briggs test and correlated personality with success. Rover found the question "where does the dog sleep at night?" predicts great sitters, since "in my bed" is a good sign.
- DoorDash noted that keeping french fries and buffalo wings hot and crispy is the white whale of delivery.

chunks.heading: Regrets, funding, and early-stage advice
chunks.text:
Asked what they'd do differently, the interviewed founders mostly said:
- Focus more. Breather tried to be a big consumer brand and a lot of things, but was really on-demand meeting rooms.
- Be more aggressive. GrubHub said it should have spent more.
- Think longer term. OpenTable only showed restaurants on its own network, and Yelp won demand because it listed everything.
- Use data sooner. Etsy had most of its team on a part of the product driving about 700 bookings a day while few worked on the part driving about 100,000.
- Add the adjacent product earlier. Rover waited on dog walking, and Wag got there first, even though it served the same customers and had better frequency economics than boarding.
- Advice from the Q&A:
  - Don't hire a "growth person" early, since everyone is growth. Hire people who build (engineers, designers, sometimes data scientists) rather than strategists.
  - Wait a long time before adding a new business line. Airbnb's founders resisted pressure for "Airbnb for dogs" and boats, and hired a Pixar storyboard artist to draw the guest and host journeys, which showed years of travel work left.
  - Marketplaces need product-market fit on both sides, which is "crazy." If you have it on only one side, cutting off the other side (Patreon) is probably the best bet.
  - Investors look at fill rate, frequency of use and dollar amount per use. High frequency, even at a low dollar amount, is often a good opportunity.
  - Airbnb's early growth was flat for about three years, driven by a combination of things rather than one spark: hosts in New York, meetups, host photography, PR (the cereal box story), cheap travel and word of mouth. After a trashed-apartment incident, liability insurance went from a planned $10,000 to $100,000 (after Marc Andreessen said to "add a zero") and later $1 million.
  - Trust is a huge part of marketplaces that this talk doesn't cover.
  - A moat comes from being the marketplace people already use, and from aggregating supply first.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Lenny explains how he built a top Substack newsletter on product management. He spends heavy time on each post, defines the job each post does for readers, and grows through word of mouth rather than ads. He also covers his research and interview process, answer-first writing, and protecting his creative time.

chunks.heading: Writing as solving a "job to be done," not as self-expression
chunks.text:
- Lenny frames all content through jobs to be done. People buy a product, listen to a podcast, or read a newsletter "because they have a job they want you to do for them" (learn a skill, make money, advance a career, be entertained, stay informed).
- His own job for readers: help them get better at building product, grow their product, and accelerate their career. Readers are mostly founders, product managers and product teams.
- He treats the newsletter like a product. He imagines a "puzzle board" of every question founders and product teams have, and his job is to fill in each piece. Popular tactical posts include how to get your first thousand users, what good retention is, and how to kick-start and scale a B2B business.
- Milky Way vs Snickers example: Snickers is bought to feel full fast, Milky Way for comfort. They look like competitors but do different jobs.
- Newsletters that fail tend to just "pontificate" on ideas. The "be smarter at dinner parties" job exists, but the bar is very high (competing with Tyler Cowen, Noah Smith, Ben Thompson).
- Check that enough people have the job. He found about 800,000 product managers in the US and 2 million worldwide, and he also writes for founders, designers and engineers.
- A niche can be enough. At 1,000 paid subscribers he was making $100,000 a year, which he ties to Kevin Kelly's "1,000 true fans".
- He wants to be what people think of when they have that problem, like Amplitude or Mixpanel for analytics. His niche is specific enough that someone can recommend it by word of mouth ("he writes really well about startups, growth and product management").
- He rejects a single narrow topic. He lets himself roam across growth, product, career and starting a company, because boredom would kill consistency.
- Pick topics you are curious about. Writing only what you think will grow an account creates "a terrible job for yourself." Aim for the overlap of what you love and what people value.

chunks.heading: The research process for his 100-hour posts
chunks.text:
- Lenny spends about 10 hours on a typical post and sometimes 100 or more. He says time is the main edge, because most people don't have much of it. Doing it full-time creates a flywheel: more time, better posts, faster growth, more income.
- His first big series came from leaving Airbnb and being asked how Airbnb grew supply, judged home quality and fixed booking conversion. He didn't trust that Airbnb's path was the right answer, so he interviewed founders of the biggest marketplaces.
- He interviewed 17 founders or early employees (including Etsy and AngelList). He found a four-step pattern: constrain to a focused problem and geography, then focus on supply, then focus on demand.
- His six steps:
  1. Pick a topic people are curious about.
  2. List the dream target companies.
  3. Find warm intros through his network or LinkedIn connections, or cold DM/email.
  4. Ask every interviewee the same questions and paste all the answers into a Google Doc.
  5. Stare at it and look for patterns.
  6. Turn the patterns into a story or framework, then look for a chart or a great quote.
- For targets, he starts with the wish list. He skips the very top (no Elon Musk at the start) and goes to a founder, early employee or someone who was there. Each round of interviews grows his network.
- For the B2B series, he interviewed companies like Amplitude, GitHub and Slack for about an hour each. He also jots down the questions builders will have: how to get the idea, first customers, product-market fit, first hires.
- Example pattern: for product-market fit, "get one company to love you." Figma's early customer story was that they drove back to a customer's office when the product "broke," and the actual problem was the customer's Wi-Fi.
- He pushes on interview claims using his product background (e.g. "How long did it really take?"), because founders' stories can be too tidy.
- He admits he keeps wanting "one more" interview and has to say "I'm just going to ship this."
- People are surprisingly open about early-days details. He says it's good marketing for them, and there's more to a big business than one tactic.

chunks.heading: Writing style: high signal to noise, answer first
chunks.text:
- He has no writing training and had never written online before starting. The less he thinks about "the beauty of the writing," the better things go. He doesn't call himself a writer and says "I write a newsletter."
- His formula is "high signal to noise, actionable, succinct, useful information."
- Put the answer first. Introductions are "way too long." Lead with the answer, then give detail. For the product-market-fit post he opens with a chart of how long it took each company, then four steps, then quotes and stories below.
- He edits by reading from the top again and again (10, 20, even 30 times), looking for what to cut, simplify or move, until he sees nothing else to fix.
- Editing guests: cut introductions by about 50% and cut anything that isn't interesting or goes off track.
- For friction, he tests like a smoothie through a straw: where does the reader get stuck? He follows "kill your darlings" and saves cut ideas for later posts.
- Intro checklist at the top of his template: What's surprising? What's a good story to open with? What's unexpected?
- Titles: "What 7 years at Airbnb taught me about building a business" worked because it had a time investment (credibility), a brand, and a clear promise. A friend told him it would go viral.
- Pop culture metaphors: he's bad at them, so he asks ChatGPT. He describes the point, asks for fictional-narrative references, and narrows over 7-8 rounds (e.g. Rocky IV, Ocean's 11 for mission/vision/strategy/goals).
- Quality bar: he credits Airbnb's culture of asking "how do we 10x this?" (designer asked to build something the internet had never seen days before launch).
- Quality and consistency: "just be high quality and do it again and again and again and good things are going to happen." Aim to be one of the best in the world on a focused topic.
- Not every post lands. A hiring post didn't do well because it wasn't surprising and its four points weren't unique, and the quotes weren't strong. He aims for "mostly doubles and triples" with a home run every month or two. He does let himself off the hook sometimes.
- The quick-win post: a templates roundup (strategy, vision, PRD, one-pager, roadmap) is a top-10 post. It reused work he'd already collected.
- A rule of thumb: a post's views correlate strongly with the time put in, though templates are an exception.

chunks.heading: How he grew to 531,000 subscribers (distribution)
chunks.text:
- About 99% of growth is word of mouth. Newsletters spread because they're easy to forward. He tried Twitter ads, Facebook ads, LinkedIn ads and cross-promotion, and says they're "a blip" next to word of mouth.
- Origins: he started on Medium with his Airbnb post, which got retweets from Andrew Chen and some VCs. Medium featured it on its homepage and it got lots of claps. That helped build his Twitter following.
- Move to an email list as soon as possible, since Medium doesn't give you your readers' emails.
- Guest posts on Andrew Chen's blog and First Round Review helped. Those came from serendipity: chatting with First Round's editor and being brave with Chen as he left Airbnb.
- He had the advantage of an Airbnb brand but says great work needs to be put in front of people.
- Substack Recommendations: about 9,000 other newsletters recommend his, and growth had a huge inflection the day the feature launched. He thinks it worked especially well because he was a known quantity when it launched, though anyone with a successful newsletter benefits.
- Early growth was slow: the first nine months were slow, and about a year to reach 10,000 subscribers. He notes newsletters grow faster now.
- Promotion channels: Twitter/X, LinkedIn and the newsletter. LinkedIn is "shockingly powerful," driving more traffic than X for his content because it's business-oriented. He starts short on Twitter and adds more on LinkedIn.
- He doesn't track email conversion. He watches views per post and asks why a post underperformed.
- He doesn't spend time on growth strategy: "see what's working, follow that pull, double down."
- Don't over-optimize setup. People who spend time on hosting, naming and design, or hop platforms, see growth slow. "Anytime you spend on that is just waste of time you could be spending on writing awesome stuff."
- Growth is linear and flattens when he's away: during about three months of paternity leave growth was flat, even though he had a backlog of posts, because he didn't promote them.

chunks.heading: Business model, goals and saying no
chunks.text:
- Goals were small milestones, not a master plan. First: $100,000 a year from the paid newsletter ("avoid getting a real job"). Next: about $300,000, roughly his Airbnb salary and stock. He has no vision for an "empire" and deliberately avoids building a media company.
- He had a list of things he'd never do (podcast, course, book). The podcast came after Harry Stebbings encouraged him to try it. It generates more revenue than the newsletter and grew faster than the newsletter. He also made a course, and a book is the one thing not done yet.
- Annual plans mean he owes readers a year of weekly quality, which he describes as pressure like the Indiana Jones boulder.
- He publishes every Tuesday and aims to be done over the weekend. He never pulls all-nighters. If he's behind he takes a week off, using a self-invented PTO policy (for example, four weeks a year).
- Make writing less work with guest posts, which are a growing share. He picks the smartest person on a topic and heavily edits. He also keeps "easy" posts (like a library of essential PM books) in his back pocket.
- A copy editor costs about $100 per post and catches roughly 100 things every time. He says writers are blind to their own text right after writing it, and last-minute tweaks after the copy edit always introduce errors.
- Guard creative time: no meetings until 3 p.m. He quotes Naval: as you become successful you have less time to do the thing that made you successful. He avoids talks, events and interviews via policies, and uses excuses like a new baby ("can we chat in six months?"). Simply not replying is another tactic.
- Advice for people writing at work: write to remember what you're learning in the moment, because it fades after you leave. Tweets are enough as a start.
- Writing prompts for ideas: what do I want to learn, what do I want to remember, what's interesting to me now, what did someone ask me that I couldn't answer well, what resonated on Twitter. The last one produced his newsletter, because people asked marketplace questions he couldn't answer.

chunks.heading: Tools and workflow
chunks.text:
- Coda is home base: a page per future post, a content calendar, about 50 idea stubs, about 5 in progress, plus a doc of writing advice to himself.
- He moves drafts to Substack once fleshed out, to see headings and formatting.
- Guest posts: Google Docs for comments and edits, then a copy editor.
- Focus: brain.fm (binaural beats), headphones, Wi-Fi, a comfy chair, sparkling water, coffee, and Magic Mind. He works in different rooms and cafes, and admits he checks Twitter and LinkedIn about 30 times while writing. He deleted the Twitter app and uses mobile web.
- Handling criticism: he mostly looks for what he did wrong. Example: Hindi subtitles on his podcast (India is his second biggest YouTube market) drew pushback that Indian tech audiences speak English. He also had to correct dates on a product-market-fit timeline of about 30 companies after companies pinged him. He avoids errors because corrections hurt credibility at a scale of 500,000+ readers.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Lenny explains how he went from leaving Airbnb with no plan to a six-figure paid newsletter. He covers early growth via Twitter and high-quality guest posts, pricing, free-to-paid conversion, a sustainable writing process, and why he deliberately keeps the business small and simple.

chunks.heading: Why Lenny says high-quality content beats every other growth tactic for a newsletter
chunks.text:
- Lenny says that anything he does besides creating high-quality content does very little for his newsletter's success. He says, "any time not spent creating high quality content is not time well spent."
- He tried Twitter ads, a referral program and cross-promotion with other newsletters. None of them did much.
- He says that over the long run, "if you provide value to people they're gonna want it and they're gonna subscribe and follow and pay."
- If a newsletter isn't growing, he would ask how to provide more value to readers "again and again and again." He says it won't happen overnight.
- He says there are no growth hacks. The hack is to "show up consistently" with consistent quality.
- He notes that a referral program worked well for Morning Brew, so non-content tactics can help in some cases.
- His growth is now almost entirely word of mouth.
- Early signals that the newsletter was working were qualitative. He got messages about how valuable the posts were, many from smart, respected people. Growth also continued when he wasn't doing anything, and people didn't unsubscribe.
- His quality test: "If I'm a founder reading this, is this actually useful to me, or is this a bunch of fluffy stuff?" He keeps it concretely actionable and immediately valuable. He cuts anything that isn't.

chunks.heading: How Lenny got his first 1,000 subscribers
chunks.text:
- He wrote Medium posts about what he learned at Airbnb. The first was featured by Medium, and Airbnb's CEO sent it to the whole company. That drove views and a Twitter following.
- He tweeted small nuggets from the posts, or ideas that didn't fit in a post. He had a few thousand followers at first, then about 10,000.
- He moved to Substack for the usual reasons: owning the audience and not giving the benefits to Medium.
- He launched by tweeting "I'm launching a Substack newsletter, you should subscribe. I don't know what it's going to be yet but don't miss it." That got his first few hundred subscribers.
- Two guest posts, one on Andrew Chen's blog and one in First Round Review, plus Twitter, got him to the first 1,000. By then he had about 20 valuable posts.
- He had no plan to start a newsletter. He wrote to collect his thoughts and crystallize what he'd learned, and the newsletter grew from there.

chunks.heading: Guest posting: how to do it, and how Lenny handles guest posts now
chunks.text:
**Writing guest posts early**
- He recommends guest posting early because you go where the audience already is. Show how good you are on someone else's audience and they'll follow you.
- Pick the right blogs and newsletters, and do a great job.
- Put your best work in, not leftovers.
- His Andrew Chen piece was "28 ways to grow supply in a marketplace." He worked on it for months, with many examples and quotes, and it was the best thing he'd written to that point.
- He showed Andrew the piece because they had gotten to know each other on Twitter. Andrew asked to republish it, and they did a 24-hour exclusive.
- First Round doesn't allow republishing. He had an outline and many of the posts done when he showed it to them, and that got them excited.
- Guest posts did little directly later on. He says "all these things add up."

**Running guest posts in his own paid newsletter**
- A paid newsletter means writing every week forever, so great content he doesn't have to write himself helps.
- He recruits the best person in each field to write a definitive answer on a topic readers keep asking about.
- He reaches out to them himself. He says the people he wants are often the ones not interested in guest posting, and so far no inbound pitch has met his bar.
- Rule of thumb: "If someone reaches out to me to try to do a guest post, that automatically means they're not going to do a guest post."
- His advice for pitching him is to send the entire article pre-written. A draft shows where it will land, and it's hard to turn someone down after starting with them.
- Even with top people, he pushes them through back-and-forth to make the piece more concrete, actionable and tactical.

chunks.heading: Getting supporters to amplify your launches
chunks.text:
- He recommends an advisor-style group, an idea he got from the Groove blog. The writer sent drafts to about 20 smart people for feedback, then emailed them when the piece went live. Those people then tweeted and shared it because they had a stake in his success.
- Lenny did this for his paid-plan announcement. He ran it by Andrew Chen and others with big Twitter followings to get feedback on framing.
- They were supporters along the way, and they tweeted about it. He says that helped a lot.

chunks.heading: The downsides of going paid, and when Lenny decided to do it
chunks.text:
- He says going paid has downsides he didn't think about beforehand.
- First, you're stuck writing every week, in theory forever, because people pay annual plans. Stopping would mean refunding everyone, which is psychologically hard. Be ready to commit for a few years.
- It took him nine months from the free newsletter to paid. Much of that was building confidence that he'd have a topic every week that he was excited about.
- Second, the same work now sits behind a paywall. Early on it feels like it "goes into a black hole" with few paying subscribers. He reminds himself that people are paying for it.
- He went paid about a year after leaving Airbnb, around the start of COVID, when he had no income and his stock was down.
- His goal was to earn more than he did at Airbnb and then stop worrying about growth.

chunks.heading: Lenny's weekly writing process
chunks.text:
- He compares it to "a boulder is always chasing me." It was stressful at first. After about a year and a half, he's confident he'll find something great each week.
- He keeps a Coda doc with about three months of topics, each on its own page with a headline. Near-term posts get bullet points. The next month or so is fleshed out in more depth.
- The format is an advice column, so readers send real questions from founders, PMs and growth people. That gives him a large backlog, and he can also revisit old topics and do better.
- He aims to be a few weeks ahead but never quite gets there. The next post is usually about 80% done a week ahead. The following ones are 10-20% done, and the rest are just headlines.
- He blocks his mornings and takes no meetings until 3 p.m. He says that's hard to do with a day job, and he doesn't know how people write a good newsletter while working full time.
- He sends on Tuesdays so he isn't in the Monday morning inbox or at the end of the week.
- He balances content types (product, growth, people) so one audience segment doesn't leave. He thinks unsubscribes happen when people feel "not what I thought it was going to be," but that's anecdotal.
- He suggests asking readers for their biggest frustrations, which gives topic prompts.
- Rule: roughly "80% what do I actually care about this week" and 20% "is this top of mind for anyone." Otherwise you've "created a job for yourself you don't like." He rearranges his topic list constantly based on what he's drawn to, to avoid burnout.

chunks.heading: Pricing, conversion and numbers
chunks.text:
**Numbers at the time**
- About 45,000 free subscribers and just over 3,000 paid, plus comps, so the real total is higher.
- Revenue is over six figures, more than he made at Airbnb.
- His first target was 1,000 paid subscribers, which roughly equated to $100K after fees and discounts. He calls it a "livable wage in San Francisco," borderline.
- Free-to-paid conversion is under 10%. At launch it was about 2%, with about 10,000 free subscribers and 200-300 paid.

**What he did on conversion**
- Paid subscribers get the email weekly. Free subscribers get one email a month, which "has to be really good because that's your sell."
- Sometimes he sends a peek at that week's paid post. Free posts also include "here's the three things you missed," and Twitter shares what's happening in the paid posts.

**Pricing**
- His advice: "priced higher than you think you should." People default to $5 a month and don't think their work is worth more.
- He looked at the Substack leaderboard. Analysis and "make me better at what I do" newsletters charged $10-20 a month, so he picked the middle.
- He started with a big launch discount at $10 a month for a year. Then he moved to $12 a month or $120 a year, and later to $15 a month or $150 a year. He says he still doesn't know if that's right.
- A 25% cyber-monday/holiday discount drove his biggest single day of subscribers. His takeaway is to price a bit higher and discount on occasion.
- He gives students a 50% discount and occasional steep discounts to people who value it but can't afford it.
- He gives free subscriptions to groups like Women in Product, a Black product managers group and Latinx VC.
- About 20% of subscribers expense it, he guesses. Proactive B2B sales did little. Companies and VCs come to him asking for discounts, and VCs sometimes offer it as a portfolio perk.

chunks.heading: Adding a community and a course, and staying simple
chunks.text:
- To justify $15 a month, he offered a private community for paid members. He calls it maybe the best thing he did that year. About 2,500 people are in it, helping each other all day.
- He turned the best conversations into their own weekly newsletter. For some people the community is the reason they subscribe.
- He's building a product management course for the next year. He cites Hunter Walk's idea of starting with one SKU, the newsletter, and adding more later.
- He tries not to pile on more work like a podcast, a book or a course. He wants to stay a solo operator and not become a workaholic again.
- He has contractors: a designer, a part-time PM who helps curate, and a friend who runs community events.
- His philosophy: "just keep it really simple," and you end up making more and being happier.
- Platform choice matters less than creating value consistently and enjoying it. He says reaching 1,000 subscribers is a meaningful bar, and below that the platform doesn't matter. He credits Substack for making it effortless to go from a post to a newsletter to paid.
- Substack's fees at scale are "very painful." He's loyal to them for now.
- Spin-offs from the audience: asking questions on Twitter gets great answers, and about 80% of founders he meets as an angel investor know the newsletter, which helps him get into deals.
- He suggests topics that help people make money, aimed at people who have money, such as product management and growth for founders and PMs.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Lenny walks through how he went from a Medium post to a paid newsletter with about 30,000 free and 1,400 paid subscribers. He covers how he picks topics, runs research posts, and distributes through a Twitter and newsletter flywheel. The core idea: deliver consistent, practical value and give the good stuff away.

chunks.heading: How Lenny went from a Medium post to a paid newsletter
chunks.text:
- Lenny left Airbnb about a year before this talk (October 2020). He wanted to write down what he had learned there so he would not have to relearn it at his next company.
- He started with Evernote bullets, which became a Medium post. It did far better than expected, landing in roughly the top 300 most-clapped Medium posts. Brian Chesky sent it to all of Airbnb, and Medium featured it and paid him.
- That gave him confidence there was something to share and maybe money to make. He wrote more Medium posts, then moved to Substack on friends' advice. He first used it only as a blog, with no newsletter plan.
- He also tweeted small nuggets on product, growth and people management. Those grew his Twitter following, which later became central to newsletter growth.
- He then experimented with writing weekly, announced it on Twitter, and got his first ~500 subscribers that first week.
- By October 2020 the newsletter had about 30,000 free subscribers and about 1,400 paid. It launched in June 2019 and went paid in April 2020. It is a six-figure income.
- He named it "Lenny's Newsletter" because he expected to rename it later, and the name stuck.
- He says plainly that "I don't actually know what I'm doing, I'm just kind of figuring this out as I go."

chunks.heading: Subscriber growth milestones and what drove them
chunks.text:
- Twitter announcement of the weekly newsletter: ~500 subscribers in week one.
- Guest post on Andrew Chen's blog, whose readers match his core audience: another ~500.
- Switching to an advice-column format, inspired by Julie Zhuo's similar column for designers: ~1,000 more, mostly from Twitter and word of mouth.
- A guest post for First Round: roughly 1,500 more. Guest posts are very valuable early on.
- An eight-part series on building marketplaces took over 100 hours of research. It roughly doubled his subscribers.
- At one point half of his growth came from two big posts: the marketplace series and "how to get your first 1,000 customers" for consumer businesses. The other half came from all his other posts.
- His lesson is to mix smaller, less time-intensive posts with occasional epic ones. Hard work on something substantial pays off.
- Most growth is word of mouth (Twitter, Facebook, LinkedIn), with a little SEO. Valuable content gets talked about, and there is no growth hack beyond that.
- He started with three questions a week, found that unsustainable, and found readers don't consume that much. One question done well is enough.
- He watches the unsubscribe rate. If growth slows, he wonders whether he is doing something wrong.
- He gives discounts or free subscriptions to people who can't afford a paid one. He says he is not very strategic about it and focuses on content.

chunks.heading: What "value" means: five jobs and three writing rules
chunks.text:
Lenny's core claim is that the secret to newsletter success, and probably to anything successful, is delivering consistent value. He sees five jobs a newsletter can do:

- Entertain
- Make people smarter
- Help them make money
- Keep them informed
- Help them feel part of something bigger

Every successful newsletter does at least one extremely well, especially a paid one. Before publishing, he checks three things:

- **Actionable:** Can someone actually use this in their job, or is it fluffy and high-level?
- **Close to what he knows:** He stays close to topics he knows. If he doesn't know one, he finds someone who does, which is where guest posts come from.
- **Adds something new:** He tries to add something to the conversation rather than rehash it.

chunks.heading: Finding topics that are new, and why time is an edge
chunks.text:
- Things that seem obvious to him are often valuable to others. You don't need to know everything to create value, and sharing what you've done is often enough. The key is to articulate it clearly and make it easy and engaging to read.
- His method for finding gaps: when someone asks him a question, he looks for an answer. If none exists, that signals an opportunity for primary research.
- Example: no one had written how the biggest B2B businesses got their first 10 customers, which surprised him.
- Many newsletters don't do primary research, meaning reaching out to people to find answers themselves.
- Time is a major advantage: "the more time you put into a thing... the better it's going to be than anything else out there." Most people don't have time to research how companies started. Just spending the time puts you ahead, even without a big network.
- He thinks he could only do this after leaving his full-time job.
- Many of his questions come from advising companies and from Twitter.
- The marketplace series started from a selfish motive. People kept asking how Airbnb succeeded, and he wanted better answers. The research simply grew into a multi-part series.

chunks.heading: The advice-column workflow
chunks.text:
- The format is a Dear Abby-style column. Readers submit questions through a form linked in each issue, and the answers land in a spreadsheet.
- Periodically he moves questions into a Coda doc as a topic list, sorted by what he most wants to write about and thinks will be useful.
- Over time he adds notes and thoughts under each topic, then fleshes it into a draft with the question and the full story.
- He moves the draft to Substack and scans it about ten times to simplify, cut words and make it punchier. He sends it to his phone to review, because he spots things there that he misses on his computer.
- He has three post types:
  - **Answering the question himself:** about half of posts, such as career advice drawing on his own path.
  - **Guest posts:** when he has no good answer, he finds an expert. For an SEO question he got a world-class SEO friend to write the post, then helped edit it.
  - **Research posts:** like the marketplace series.
- Guest posts on his own newsletter give writers a chance to build an audience and give him a week off.
- Tools: Coda for post outlines, Mem for personal notes, Grammarly, and the Centered app for focus. He keeps mornings meeting-free until 2pm to write.
- He sometimes gets distracted wanting "one more company" to interview. That is easier and more fun than solving the puzzle of the post itself.
- Charging for the newsletter helps: a post is due every week because people are paying.

chunks.heading: How he runs a research post
chunks.text:
- Make a wish list of companies and people he wants to talk to, ideally the best possible group.
- Find warm intros through LinkedIn and friends, or cold DM or email founders. A VC friend intro'd him to Thumbtack's co-founder, and they talked for half an hour.
- Throw interview notes raw into a messy Google Doc, organized by company. Keep a checklist tracking who has answered.
- Stare at the answers to see what emerges. The marketplace series became a four-step framework for starting a marketplace business, backed by stories and quotes from each company.
- Clean up each quote and run it by the person for approval.
- Getting many perspectives matters. Existing writing on solving the chicken-and-egg problem is usually one company's story (OpenTable, Uber, Airbnb). He looked for the common approach across all of them.
- He was working on a similar post on going from a B2B company's first 10 customers to its first 100.
- On examples: he asks whether it is something the reader can do, whether it is interesting or surprising, and whether it is concrete and actionable. If many companies did the same thing, he groups them together.
- He has not done a post going deep on a single company. Readers want to know what to do at their company, and one company's exact playbook rarely transfers. A group of similar companies doing the same thing is more useful.

chunks.heading: Distribution: the Twitter and newsletter flywheel
chunks.text:
- His distribution rests on one belief: a good, high-quality, valuable newsletter does well, and there is no hack.
- The flywheel runs in both directions.
  - **Newsletter to Twitter:** he extracts the "juice" of a post and puts it on Twitter, giving away the good stuff instead of teasing it. He does this even for paid posts, because people ignore tweets with nothing interesting. He did a thread on a B2B post and summarized a long retention post in one tweet that got a lot of love. People then subscribe to read more.
  - **Twitter to newsletter:** sometimes a tweet he thinks is interesting does well, and he then writes a post about it.
- His publishing steps: send the newsletter, tweet a summary that gives away the goods, copy it to LinkedIn, and encourage sharing via buttons in the post.
- He squeezes as much value as he can from each post. While writing the B2B first-customers post, he tweeted screenshots of companies at launch just for fun, and they were widely shared.
- After publishing, he tweeted out individual founder stories from the long post. One post led to five or six tweets. He did this because he didn't want people to miss the interesting parts, not to maximize likes.
- Distribution tips:
  - Because most content is paywalled, he runs one free post a month. That post has to be really good, since it is what grows the newsletter.
  - Repurpose content.
  - Do guest posts.
- Guest posts: Andrew Chen asked to distribute a post he'd written for his own newsletter. The trade-off is giving content away versus the subscribers it drives. He now puts most energy into his own newsletter, which drives more traffic directly. He still does them occasionally, such as a new First Round post.

chunks.heading: Which posts worked and how he picks topics
chunks.text:
- His most popular posts were, in order: how the biggest consumer products got their first 1,000 customers, how B2B companies got their first customers, then the marketplace posts.
- His takeaway is that people want practical answers to problems in their company. Founders especially ask "what should I actually do," not "what's the future of tech." He asks whether someone can use the post tomorrow to start something, brainstorm, or talk to their manager.
- He avoids chasing what readers want at the expense of what he enjoys writing. He looks for a balance of topics he finds interesting and that people will value, so he doesn't create a job he dislikes.

chunks.heading: Structuring and editing posts
chunks.text:
- His usability rule of thumb as a product manager: "imagine all your users are drunk and don't know what they're doing, just fumbling around clicking buttons." He applies it to writing.
- He makes posts very easy to scan:
  - a simple summary image at the top and bottom
  - big bold headings
  - visuals
  - breaking up or cutting any large block of text
- He asks what the natural flow of the reader's thoughts is.
- He keeps *On Writing Well* next to him, which teaches him to cut everything he can. His posts are still very long, but he cuts anything that adds no value.

chunks.heading: Why Airbnb's design mattered
chunks.text:
- Two of Airbnb's three founders are designers, so design value was in the company from the start.
- Airbnb competed with Craigslist, HomeAway, VRBO and later Booking.com. Lenny says there are only a few ways to differentiate: be cheaper, or be a much better experience that people feel good using and find easier.
- Every product launch had to be reviewed by Brian Chesky in a weekly meeting. The bar stayed very high, which doesn't scale but helped keep quality up.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Lenny lays out his race car framework for long-term growth: pick one of four self-sustaining engines (performance marketing, virality, content, sales), then layer turbo boosts and lubricants. He also covers getting the first users, retention benchmarks, and how he built his newsletter to 55k free and 5k paid subscribers.

chunks.heading: Growth engines: the four ways a startup grows long term
chunks.text:
Lenny describes the "race car" growth framework, built with Dan Hockenmaier. A company is a race car with four parts:
- **Engine:** the most important part. It is a self-sustaining loop that keeps growth going.
- **Turbo boosts:** one-off hero moments that give a burst and then fade.
- **Lubricants:** things that make the engine run more efficiently.
- **Fuel:** the input that powers the car.

He says there are only four engines to choose from:
- **Performance marketing:** spend on ads, ads bring customers, customers bring revenue, revenue funds more ads.
- **Virality:** users bring in new users, who bring in their friends.
- **Content:** SEO, viral content and user-generated content.
- **Sales:** hire salespeople, they close customers, revenue funds more salespeople.

Other options are partnerships and physical space (retail placement, as Casper did). He treats them as outside the core four, and says a partnership only counts as an engine if it keeps driving traffic rather than being a one-off.

His central point is that a company has to become one of the best in the world at one engine in its market to have a real chance. Airbnb won travel through virality, Booking.com through performance marketing and TripAdvisor through content. He says the common mistake is spreading effort thinly across many channels, which "is unlikely to work".

chunks.heading: Choosing an engine and layering a second one
chunks.text:
- Most companies' growth is explained by one engine at first. Later they layer on a second, and maybe a third.
- Lenny frames it as an S-curve. An engine ramps up, then plateaus, so you should anticipate the plateau and plant seeds for the next engine before it arrives. He cites Jeff Jordan's "layer cake" of growth curves.
- He reads "first-time founders focus on product, second-time founders focus on distribution" as a mental model. Work backwards from an engine you can be unusually good at, then build a product that suits it.
- Sales gets added eventually by almost every bottoms-up business. The question for enterprise B2B is when, not whether. His example is Dropbox waiting too long to build sales while Box moved early.
- Brand work, PR, events and a Super Bowl ad are turbo boosts. They give a spike that goes away.

chunks.heading: Performance marketing and sales: when each fits
chunks.text:
Performance marketing:
- Anyone can try it in a couple of weeks with a Facebook or AdWords account.
- He advises avoiding building the business on it if you can, because it is brutally competitive and a sliver of success invites competitors. Booking.com reportedly spent over a billion dollars a year on Google search ads.
- Two rules of thumb for when it fits: you earn revenue from users immediately, so it can feed back into ads, and people aren't already searching for your product. His example is a Slanket, which no one searches for.
- Winners go very deep. Wish had a founder who came from Google search ranking. Credit Karma and Casper are other examples.
- Paid ads are one of the worst ways to get retention, because those users have the lowest intent.

Sales:
- It fits when average order value and lifetime value are high and customers need hand-holding, education and onboarding.

chunks.heading: Virality: types, fit and how to measure it
chunks.text:
Lenny lists several kinds of virality:
- Word of mouth because the product is remarkable (Airbnb).
- Inviting friends to do it together (Snapchat).
- Passive exposure through shared links (Dropbox).
- Incentivized referrals (Dropbox's extra storage).
- Collaboration invites (Slack, Figma, Airtable, Coda).

Rules of thumb for fit:
- The product is better with friends or colleagues using it.
- It is innately fun or remarkable to share.
- He likes the word "remarkable" from Seth Godin: worth remarking about.

Measurement:
- K-factor (above 1 means viral) is hard to use in practice, since many invites happen offline.
- He prefers asking new users how they heard about you and measuring the share that came via friends, family or invites.
- He says you want over half from word of mouth, and closer to 70% means virality is truly your engine.

Bottoms-up B2B pairs cheap consumer-style viral growth with enterprise contract sizes, which is why those companies grow fastest.

FOMO works when you have both parts: great people or a great value prop inside, and a velvet rope outside. Clubhouse had people like Naval and Marc Andreessen inside. Robinhood offered free trades.

chunks.heading: Content as an engine
chunks.text:
Lenny maps content-driven growth on two axes: user-generated versus company-written, and SEO versus viral.
- User-generated and SEO is the best case: Quora, Reddit, Glassdoor.
- Editorial and SEO: Ahrefs' SEO blog posts.
- Data-driven or machine-generated SEO: Thumbtack's "best plumber in [city]" pages, and Zapier's pages for every app-to-app connection. This works if you have unique data nobody else has.

Rules for company content:
- Decide up front whether you are optimizing for SEO or for viral sharing. It is one or the other.
- Viral one-offs work for creators like MrBeast, and Superhuman's early blog posts built traction.
- Most companies should focus on SEO, since that loop keeps giving.
- Pick one primary KPI per piece of content and treat the rest as secondary.

chunks.heading: Lubricants, activation and retention
chunks.text:
Lubricants are conversion, activation and retention. They matter, but founders over-invest in micro-optimizing them before they have an engine.
- **Conversion:** anything that increases someone completing the next step, including sending an invite.
- **Activation:** the moment a user understands and feels the product's value. For Airbnb hosts it was getting their first booking.
- **Retention:** he calls it "the most important metric to watch" because it is the ultimate test of product-market fit.

To improve retention, change who you target:
- Target "customers who care", a phrase he credits to April Dunford.
- Retention is largely an audience-fit problem.
- On his own newsletter, Hacker News traffic converts to paid far worse than other sources.

Benchmarks:
- He surveyed about 20 growth leaders and investors to set thresholds, and it ranges from roughly 25% to 90%.
- Consumer social is 25% okay and 45% great.
- Consumer subscription is 40% okay and 70% great.
- Enterprise SaaS is 70% okay and 90% great.
- The spread follows acquisition cost. Expensive sales-led customers must stick around, while cheap consumer users can churn more.

chunks.heading: Getting the first users: turbo boosts and customers who care
chunks.text:
Early on, the work is mostly turbo boosts that ignite the engine, not designing loops. This is "do things that don't scale": reaching out to strangers, getting some PR, infiltrating online communities. Building the perfect engine from day one is a pitfall.

Step one is defining customers who care, the narrow early-adopter wedge:
- TikTok: bottom-tier Instagram influencers.
- Cameo: C-list celebrities.
- Netflix: DVD fanatics.
- WhatsApp: Russian immigrants in San Jose.
- Substack: writers already doing well online.
- Tinder: attractive, party-loving college students in LA.

For his own newsletter, about 99% of growth is word of mouth. His first thousand subscribers came from a couple of guest posts, a few retweets from influencers and Twitter. Ads, a referral program, cross-promotion and B2B offers did nothing meaningful. He says writing consistently valuable content is the only thing that moves growth. When he taught a course for three weeks and wrote less, growth slowed noticeably.

chunks.heading: Building a newsletter: the numbers, topics and value
chunks.text:
Numbers (as of this conversation):
- About 55,000 free subscribers and about 5,000 paid.
- He launched about two years earlier and started charging about one year earlier.
- He says he makes roughly twice his Airbnb tech salary.

Choosing what to write:
- He rejected "pick one niche". He writes across product, growth and startup challenges because he wants to stay excited.
- He modeled it as an advice column after Julie Zhuo's newsletter, so reader questions give him an endless queue of topics.
- A creator's pick should sit in a Venn diagram of what interests you and what creates real value for others.

He asks of each post whether it will help someone with their work. He sees five jobs content can do: make you better at your job, entertain you, help you make money, help you feel part of a cause, and others. The Browser and Pomp are his examples of value that isn't purely work help.

On platform and strategy:
- He stays on Substack despite paying an "obscene" amount, because it lets him just write and he can switch later.
- He tries to do less. He avoids a podcast or book and focuses on what is working, such as a job board and a private subscriber community.
- He treats a subscription as a promise to deliver every week.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Lenny draws on research into successful companies to explain three signs of product-market fit, retention benchmarks by business type, and a four-engine growth framework. He also covers 10 ways startups found their first thousand users, all aimed at a Series A raise.

chunks.heading: Series A criteria and what founders can influence
chunks.text:
- Lenny says investors focus on six things at the Series A: product market fit, revenue, growth rate, how amazing the founders are, market size, and why now is the right time for this kind of company.
- Only three of these can change between the seed round and the Series A: signals of product market fit, revenue, and growth rate.
- He calls the Series A "the product market fit round". It is where a startup moves from searching to raising money, "pouring fuel in the fire", and scaling.
- His advice is based on research into "basically every successful company" he could get hold of. He interviewed founders and early growth employees. He also draws on about 70 angel investments over five years, and on his seven years at Airbnb (supply growth, conversion, Superhost, reviews).

chunks.heading: How to tell if you have product market fit
chunks.text:
- He defines product market fit simply as whether there is a market for the product you are building.
- From his founder interviews, he sees three main signs: a sudden and significant pull, a gradual but compounding pull, and cohort retention curves that flatten.
- **Sudden pull** is the most common story and is hard to miss.
  - Dropbox: after launching on Digg and Hacker News, Drew Houston felt pulled back in his seat as the car raced away.
  - Netflix, Uber (uncontrollable word of mouth) and Segment (analytics.js, its third iteration) had the same experience.
  - GitHub: people asked to pay for it before it charged, because they didn't want it to go away.
- **Gradual, compounding pull** is easier to miss.
  - Substack: the founder was obsessed with measuring product market fit, then got too busy with growth to keep checking.
  - Instacart: it started with a thin market of people who don't care which store their food comes from, then expanded.
  - Superhuman: it found a sliver of the market (founders, managers, executives) and expanded to more personas.
  - Datadog: there was no explosion, but sign-ups never stopped.
- **Timing:** it takes longer than founders expect.
  - The shortest period he found was about a year and a half.
  - Segment took three tries.
  - Amplitude took four years of iterating.
- **Three early signals** to use before the main signs appear:
  - The Sean Ellis survey: over 40% of users say they would be "very disappointed" if the product went away. He says it is not necessarily true, but it is a good signal and a useful stat for a deck.
  - Steve Blank's test: people's pupils dilate and they get visibly excited. This suits idea and prototype stages.
  - People keep using the product even when it is broken or down, and are sad when it is down.

chunks.heading: Measuring retention by cohort
chunks.text:
- Retention is, for him, "the ultimate measure" of whether you are building something people want.
- There are two ways to measure it.
  - Monthly churn: the percentage of active users lost each month.
  - Cohort retention: track users who joined in the same period and watch them over time.
- He prefers cohorts. Blended churn mixes new and existing users, so you can't tell whether a new onboarding flow or landing page had an effect.
- Example table: of about 168 users who joined in one week, 14 were still around at 10 weeks and eventually only 6%. He calls that "not great".
- Plot each cohort as a line chart by day, week or month.
  - If the curve flattens and doesn't hit zero, you have product market fit with some segment of the market. The flat level shows what share of the market finds value.
  - If it goes to zero, you don't have product market fit, even if you are growing fast.
  - Cohorts stacking higher on each other means retention is improving.

chunks.heading: Good vs great retention benchmarks at six months
chunks.text:
He surveyed many top growth, product and investing people and triangulated their answers. Good / great at six months:

| Product type | Examples | Good | Great |
|---|---|---|---|
| Consumer social (ad-supported) | Twitter, Snapchat, Instagram | 25% | 45% |
| Transactional consumer | Airbnb, Lyft, Chirp, Tax | about 30% | about 50% |
| Consumer subscription | Netflix, Spotify, Hulu | about 40% | over 70% |
| Mid-market subscription (100-1,000 employees) | | about 60% | above 80% |
| Enterprise software | | 70% | 90% |

- **Why they differ:**
  - Acquisition cost rises roughly linearly down the list. Costly customers must be retained or the unit economics fail.
  - Small companies fail and switch products more often. Enterprises sign year-long contracts and train everyone, so enterprise churn means something is badly wrong.
- **Three reasons it's okay to fall below the benchmarks:**
  - You are early and haven't built the core yet. He warns it is not a long-lived excuse, because retention usually jumps once the core of the product is in.
  - Acquisition and marginal costs are near zero, as with Twitter and Shopify.
  - You aren't building a venture-scale business. He notes that Series A founders likely aren't in this group.

chunks.heading: The growth engine framework (race car)
chunks.text:
- He frames a startup as a race car with four parts: engine, turbo boosts, lubricants and fuel.
- **Engine:** a self-sustaining growth loop that drives most long-term growth. He says only four exist, and one will drive the majority of growth, so pick it and get really good at it.
  - **Performance marketing:** spend on ads, ads bring customers, customers bring revenue, revenue funds more ads. It fits when you earn revenue immediately, or when people aren't searching for you (e.g. a mattress in a box).
  - **Content:** users create content (reviews, answers), SEO brings visitors, who create more content. It fits when content is generated by the product or you have unique data for millions of pages (Thumbtack, Yelp). He also names editorial content, where employees write SEO blog posts. User-generated is best because it feeds itself.
  - **Sales:** hire salespeople, they bring customers, revenue funds more salespeople. It is like performance marketing but suits higher revenue per sale or products that need training. It is the usual B2B model for non-bottom-up businesses.
  - **Virality:** users invite friends, who invite friends. It fits products that are innately better with friends or fun to share. It also works for bottom-up B2B SaaS, which combines a cheap viral engine with enterprise contract size. He says you can't just bolt it on.
- **Examples:** Airbnb grew via virality, then performance marketing. Thumbtack grew via SEO, then added performance marketing. Booking.com started with SEO and shifted almost entirely to performance marketing.
- **Turbo boosts:** one-off lifts like PR, events and brand marketing. They are useful early. His warning is that a common founder mistake is repeating them without investing in an engine.
- **Lubricants:** improvements to conversion, activation and retention. They make everything run better but won't make or break the business alone. Retention is special once you have product market fit.
- **Fuel:** what feeds the engine: money, content or users.

chunks.heading: Getting your first thousand users: three steps
chunks.text:
He calls this a new, still-developing framework. The steps are: identify customers who care, build a remarkable value prop, then find where those customers are.

- **Step 1: Customers who care** (a narrow wedge of early adopters).
  - TikTok: bottom-tier influencers.
  - Netflix: online DVD fanatics.
  - Tinder: attractive, party-loving college students in LA.
  - Uber: tech employees in San Francisco.
  - Ask who feels the most pain without it, who would benefit significantly, and who would pay.
- **Step 2: Remarkable value prop.** "Remarkable" means people remark on it.
  - Robinhood: zero-percent trading commissions.
  - Dropbox: "throw away your USB drive".
  - Netflix: rent as many movies as you want, no late fees.
  - DoorDash to restaurants: make more money, no risk.
  - Ask what the alternatives are, what is unique, and what superpower it unlocks for the user. Most companies don't get it right at first.
- **Step 3: Find them.** He says almost every company found its first thousand customers through one or two of 10 channels:
  - Friends and colleagues, then targeted strangers.
  - Infiltrating offline communities, then online communities.
  - Building your own community.
  - Influencers, PR, partnerships, and physical placement.
  - The list is concentric circles out from the founder. The further down it, the more friction, so use the earlier ones when you can.
- **Examples:**
  - Friends and colleagues: Yelp, LinkedIn, Substack (writer Bill Bishop, a colleague of a founder), Salesforce (Marc Benioff's former colleague).
  - Targeted strangers: Cameo hired interns at $10 an hour to DM celebrities. DoorDash went door to door to restaurants. TikTok DMed influencers. Udemy pitched Ruby experts.
  - Offline: Etsy at craft fairs. Lyft handed out balloons and cupcakes at startups. Tinder threw parties at USC. Pinterest's Ben loaded the site on Apple Store laptops.
  - Own community: Product Hunt (Ryan Hoover's email list), Stack Overflow (podcast and blog), Patreon (musician friends), TikTok (influencer community).
  - PR: Instacart used it as a primary lever (a PR event with each new city or big feature). Udemy, Spotify and Airbnb (Obama O's/McCain's cereal story) also used it.
  - Physical placement: DoorDash flyers on campus and in delivery bags. Instacart put its logo on bags.
- **FOMO as a layer:** you need cool insiders sharing how great it is and a "velvet rope" such as a waitlist. One without the other doesn't work.
- **Takeaways:**
  - Consumer startups usually got their first 10,000+ users from one strategy, and usually by going to users directly.
  - For B2B, only four work most: friends and family, targeted strangers, infiltrating communities, and PR.
  - A big network is a large B2B advantage, which is part of why YC is valuable. Trust matters, e.g. "Mark Benioff, he's great, he's not going to screw me".

chunks.heading: Experiments, patience, prototypes and positioning
chunks.text:
- **Growth hacks:** as an investor he wants organic growth and market pull. "The less hacks you need the better." Hacks suit one-off turbo boosts, and Twitter is a good lever for a spike.
- **Low traffic:** startups can't run valid A/B tests for long. Experiments on little data are "complete nonsense". Talk to people qualitatively instead.
  - Paid ads can give traffic but at low intent. If low-intent users get excited, that is an even better sign.
  - For sample sizes, use the Optimizely experiment sample size calculator.
- **How long to persist:** he has no great answer. His heuristic is to give it double the time your instinct says, then consider a pivot. Pivoting sooner is often better than running out of money. Airbnb had about two years of nothing before it took off.
- **Positioning:** Amplitude thought it was building a tool for marketers testing copy. Once it pitched product teams, a product manager at a conference said it was the first product built for what he needed. The product barely changed; the positioning did.
- **Prototypes in B2B:** pitching a prototype is "super realistic". B2B customers are clear about their problems, you can look for the pupil-dilation reaction, and you can ask them to pay now for first access. Many companies raise with just Figma files or decks.
- **PM teams:** he favors companies where product teams are empowered and cross-functional, with a say over vision, strategy and priorities, rather than feature teams told what to build.
- **No-code:** he says tools like Webflow and Coda work well and will widen who can build software.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Lenny explains how he grew his newsletter and podcast with no hacks: consistent high-quality content, lots of time, and primary research rooted in real audience problems. He also covers early growth sources, Substack recommendations, ruthless editing, and the downsides of the creator treadmill.

chunks.heading: Growth for a newsletter and podcast comes from consistency and quality, not hacks
chunks.text:
- Lenny led supply growth at Airbnb, then the team that optimized the booking experience, so he spent years on conversion and growth. He says very few of those skills transferred to growing a newsletter or podcast.
- His view: "nothing helps it grow other than just consistency and quality of content."
- He tried referrals, paid ads and guest posts. Some helped early on, but "if you just look at the trend line of growth, nothing makes a dent other than just keeping at it and keeping the quality bar high."
- Referral programs ("send this to all your friends, get a hat, get stickers") don't work for his kind of newsletter. He thinks they suit a different personality of newsletter, such as Morning Brew.
- There is no real moat. Others are copying his welcome emails, advice-column format and intros. He doesn't think about defensibility much. If you keep providing valuable stuff, people keep wanting it.

chunks.heading: Subscriber growth timeline for Lenny's Newsletter
chunks.text:
- Goal at launch: He called it "Project Avoid Getting a Real Job". The first target was $100K a year, later raised to $300K, and he says it has gone far beyond that.
- First ~100 subscribers: A popular Medium post brought Medium followers. These turned into Twitter followers, and he tweeted nuggets from the post.
- Next ~1,000 subscribers: Guest posts on newsletters and blogs with the same audience, namely the First Round Review and Andrew Chen's blog. They worked because he had interesting things to say and they wanted to share it.
- Next ~10,000: Writing every week for nine months. The growth chart was linear over that period.
- Paid plan: He launched it about 8-9 months after starting, at roughly 10,000 subscribers. Covid hit, he was making no money, and Airbnb stock looked doubtful. Another year or two of weekly writing kept growth going past $300K.
- Latest inflection: Substack's recommendations feature. About 1,000 newsletters now recommend his, and new signups see 10 newsletters he picked himself. He says he is likely in the onboarding flow as the top business newsletter, and the result was a "hockey stick of growth".
- Those recommenders get no affiliate commission. They recommend organically.
- He says "there's never been an easier time to grow large newsletter" if you write awesome stuff and people recommend you.

chunks.heading: How Lenny picks topics and decides what to write
chunks.text:
- He started the newsletter as an advice column ("Dear Abby" style). Readers sent questions and he answered them. This rooted the content in real problems people have, not in his pontificating.
- He frames content as a job to be done: you need to nail one job better than anyone else. Newsletter jobs he lists: entertain me, help me make money, help me be better in life, help me be better at work. His is helping people build and grow product, one niche within the "better at work" job.
- He admits this framing came in hindsight. Getting there was "90% stumbling".
- His rule after leaving Airbnb was to notice what gave him energy and do more of it. Writing gave him energy. Startup work and advising calls drained it, so he cut them.
- A friend told him that doing something people value and keep reading is rare, and not to take it for granted. That pushed him to double down.
- His first post was what seven years at Airbnb taught him about building a company. He wrote it to remember what he learned.
- He says writing is thinking: "I don't know what I think until I've written it down." He doesn't start with the answer. He dumps thoughts into a doc, gathers quotes and talks to people, and the conclusion forms during writing.

chunks.heading: Research process: primary research and mini case studies
chunks.text:
- The model came from his first big series. After leaving Airbnb, people asked how to build a marketplace. He didn't know if Airbnb's approach was the way or worked "in spite of ourselves". So he talked to the biggest marketplace companies to find patterns. This became a five-part series on kickstarting and scaling a marketplace business, and it did very well.
- His takeaway: he does primary research on behalf of readers at very low cost to them. He is spending tens of hours answering a question for them.
- Steps for a post like the growth inflections piece:
  1. Pose the question (for example, what causes an inflection in growth?).
  2. List the companies he'd most love stories from.
  3. Email people he knows at those companies with the question and ask what they can share.
  4. Collect the responses and see what conclusions emerge.
- A flywheel: the more of this he does, the more connections he builds and the more companies he's close with. He tries not to bug people too much, and often they are excited to contribute.
- He is "doing a lot of work for people that would cost a lot of money". Paid readers feel like insiders.

chunks.heading: Quality bar: time, ruthless editing, and knowing when to stop
chunks.text:
- Direct correlation: the time he puts into a piece correlates with its success. Being full-time on this gives him far more time than people with jobs.
- Time per piece: the newsletter takes 10 hours minimum per post, some 20, some 100. A podcast episode takes about 3-4 hours of prep and recording, with a producer who edits.
- Most of his writing is editing. He starts with content and bullet points, shapes it, and reviews it up to a hundred times. He emails it to himself and reads it on his phone.
- The test is whether there is nothing he can cut and nothing that consistently confuses him.
- Influence: On Writing Well. Its conclusion is "cut, cut, cut". He tightens, simplifies, and uses bullets, charts and tables.
- He tries to open with a surprise, an interesting point or a story. His advice is to skip long intros and get right to it.
- Knowing when to stop: when he looks again and finds nothing to tweak. He may come back later in the day, maybe tweak the title, and when nothing changes it's ready. It won't be perfect forever, with weekly publishing and a $150-a-year subscription.

chunks.heading: Podcast: launching it, running interviews, and sequencing with the newsletter
chunks.text:
- He long resisted a podcast, a book and a course. Harry Stebbings told him after a 20VC recording that he should do one, and that got him over the hump.
- He finds the podcast easier than the newsletter. In the newsletter he must produce unique insights and craft them. In the podcast he extracts them from someone else's brain.
- He also says the podcast is more lucrative and more energizing.
- Sequencing: every episode is shared with his large newsletter audience, which makes the podcast easier to grow. His advice: "build an awesome newsletter and then launch a podcast". Doing it the other way is harder.
- Interview technique:
  - Keep following up when an answer is vague, to get concrete.
  - Don't react to every answer with "awesome, great, that was so interesting". Move on to the next question.
  - Watch your own interviews to find what is annoying.
- Guest vetting: He relies more on referrals from past great guests and on watching their other talks and videos. He admits you never know until you talk. He hasn't yet cut an interview.

chunks.heading: Creator-life tradeoffs and advice for starting
chunks.text:
- Upsides: easier angel investing, since founders want him involved. He also gets access to founders and companies, regular notes about how his work helped people, and a large network. He controls his own calendar.
- Downsides: no PTO, no 401K match, no health insurance, no disability coverage. It is also lonely, and it's an endless treadmill. A viral hit fades within days, and you must keep publishing.
- Exit: paid annual plans are bought every day, so stopping means losing income. He doesn't see an exit path for a creator business named after himself.
- His advice: work on something you're genuinely curious about and care about, or you create a job for yourself that sucks.
- The name doesn't matter. He called it Lenny's Newsletter because it was Substack's default suggestion when he signed up with no plan. People waste months on names. Find something you like, have a process and grind it out.
- On starting: "just do it. Stop thinking about it." Write one thing on Substack, which is free. Write what you want to get out of your head or remember, and see whether you enjoy it and whether people value it. Writing is easier than video.
- He hasn't written a book. He sees it as a year of intense work with little money, and says a collection of newsletters won't be easy. He may do it someday.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Lenny explains how he went from a post-Airbnb Medium essay to a paid Substack newsletter that grows ~90% through word of mouth. He covers choosing topics by energy and curiosity, investing heavily in quality and research, using Twitter for distribution, and going paid and building a community.

chunks.heading: How Lenny decides what to write about
chunks.text:
- Lenny never planned to be a writer. After leaving Airbnb in March 2019 (about seven years there, company sold to Airbnb in 2012), his plans A through D were: start a company, consult or advise, join an early-stage startup, or join a big company as a PM. A newsletter was not on the list.
- He started by writing down what he learned at Airbnb, turned it into a Medium post that did well, then moved to Substack and tried a weekly cadence.
- Two pieces of advice from friends shaped the pivot: spend more time on what gives you energy and less on what saps it, and don't take for granted a thing that is working for people. Writing gave him energy and startup exploration did not.
- He draws topics from four sources:
  - things he wants to get out of his head
  - reader questions (an advice-column format "gives me a huge backlog," since each question is a problem at least one person has)
  - his own curiosity ("a good excuse to learn it")
  - what resonates on Twitter (a tweet thread on performance reviews got more attention than expected, so he wrote a deeper dive)
- He warns against writing only what others ask for, because "then you just end up with a job that you don't like again." The more interested he is, the better the piece gets.
- He deliberately keeps a broad scope instead of the classic advice to pick one niche. Because the audience is a mix, he rotates growth, product, startup/business and leadership topics. If a reader sees nothing useful for about three weeks, "you just turn."
- His test for a niche is Brian Armstrong's point about Coinbase: few people combine engineering, economics and cryptography. Find the combination of things you are good at that few others share, as long as enough people care.
- A flop on a personal-interest topic is fine. His Buddhism-and-product-management post did not resonate, but there was no wave of unsubscribes. He says people give you "two or three chances in a row," and he looks for a consistent problem, not a one-off.

chunks.heading: Why quality is the whole strategy
chunks.text:
- Lenny argues there is a huge amount of free content, so you only stand out by being much better, not a little better: "oh wow, this is so good." Otherwise "you'll just get ignored."
- He is continually surprised that basic topics are poorly covered. Examples are how to start a consumer app, get your first customers, launch a B2B business, get into PM, and PM templates. His explanation is that most people have little time to write, so "if you have time to write, you're going to stand out."
- Time invested correlates directly with how well a post does. His 8-part marketplace series took at least 100 hours over a few months. It was his most popular post and an early source of growth.
- His bar is "is this actually going to be useful for somebody?" A PM should be able to read it and use it on their team. He avoids pontificating and fuzzy high-level ideas, and favors concrete, actionable steps and examples.
- Formats that do well: pieces that answer questions he hears repeatedly, and visual frameworks (for example, how B2B companies kickstart).
- He wants honesty over sounding smart. He asks whether he has seen this work in practice, and pushes founders on whether something actually had impact or just sounds like a PR pitch. For a retention post he was after "concrete stats and numbers and real things that worked."

chunks.heading: Research process for deep-dive posts
chunks.text:
1. Start with a single question to answer (for example, how do you start a marketplace business). It came from people asking how Airbnb did it, when one company's experience may not generalize.
2. List the companies he'd like to include, then find a person at each and get a warm introduction.
3. Ask them all the same question by email. He skips Zoom to keep the time he asks for small.
4. Paste every answer into one big doc and stare at it until a pattern emerges: steps one, two, three, or a few distinct approaches. A story and framework take shape from that.
5. Visualize it and write it so readers aren't overwhelmed. Keep it structured, simple and focused.
6. Keep pushing for access. He says people are more open than expected, as long as they can review their section before publishing.
- He says roughly 80% of his writing is him learning the topic, and the deep-dive posts teach him the most.

chunks.heading: Editing and finishing a piece
chunks.text:
- He reads each piece 10 to 20 times, on both his computer and his phone. A different device "tricks your brain into seeing things again for the first time," and he is always surprised how many typos he missed.
- He knows it's ready when each pass produces only a couple of changes and he stops finding typos or reasons to move things around.
- He keeps a book on writing well next to his chair and opens it at random as a reminder to cut: remove words, adjectives and adverbs, make it shorter.
- He keeps a short list of high-level rules, such as: is it interesting, is there a story to add, is there something to cut.
- He has no editor or review group, and wishes he had a group to run posts by. After publishing, reader comments often lead him to add a point or cover it in a follow-up.

chunks.heading: Distribution: word of mouth, Twitter and repurposing
chunks.text:
- He spends very little time on distribution. About 90% of growth has been word of mouth, because better writing spreads. He suggests that if you are spending a lot of time on growth, "something's off about the content" or you lack any distribution channel.
- Twitter is his main channel. He built a following by posting nuggets of value, either from his Medium posts or things he didn't turn into posts. When he launched the newsletter he tweeted it, and that brought his first 500 subscribers. His lesson: find places to add value, build an audience there, then direct it to your newsletter.
- At launch he also seeded it by telling people with large, respected followings the day he'd launch and asking them to share it if they liked it. He says this worked well, and the sharing came because they found it valuable, not because he pushed.
- On cold outreach, messaging people to read your work is fine, but be wary of writing only what you think people want.
- He starts with the long post, then tweets it with an independent nugget (a story, an image, a short thread). Only about 10% of the time does a tweet become a post. Twitter's constraint forces a simple, consumable thought, and threads give people a reason to share and save.
- Give away the best material up front, especially on Twitter. Don't build to a reveal, because "nobody's going to read it." Post the most useful parts in the tweet, and readers then click through and subscribe.
- He has experimented with Twitter ads and with discounts for groups, but they are minor.

chunks.heading: Paid newsletter, expensing and community
chunks.text:
- He ran a free weekly newsletter for nine months before going paid. That gave him confidence he had plenty to write about, and a big free base at launch. He says there is no shortcut to that confidence.
- The paid launch price was $15 a month. Because that felt like a lot for writing alone, he added an invite to a private community as an extra reason to subscribe.
- He moved paid mainly because COVID hit and he needed income. In hindsight he thinks he waited longer than he should have, but also that launching with a large free base was valuable, so not too early either.
- His emails encourage readers to expense the subscription, but he straddles the line so people who can't expense it don't feel worse about subscribing. He doesn't pitch team or bulk plans, and notes Ben Thompson has the same pattern where one person subscribes and shares internally.
- Community: he picked Slack and invited 10 to 20 people at first. It grew to about 600. His philosophy is to bring awesome people together and hope good things happen. He spends little time moderating and it is largely self-sufficient.

chunks.heading: Cadence, sustainability and platform choice
chunks.text:
- For anyone nervous about committing to a list, he suggests framing it as an experiment: "I'm going to try a weekly newsletter, we'll see how it goes," and run it for about three months. Nobody remembers when your last email arrived. The pressure gets real once people pay for yearly plans.
- Early on he answered three reader questions per week to pack in value, but he learned it isn't sustainable. He now sticks to one topic per post and saves the rest for later.
- He doubts daily newsletters, noting he can barely do a really good weekly one, and says people "don't really want more email," so weekly is often a good cadence.
- On Substack, he values that he doesn't have to think about anything but writing. His custom domain means he could move with the same URLs and keep SEO. Substack takes 10%, which at scale is a lot of money, so the question is whether the services it adds justify it. He says he wouldn't be where he is without it, and he'd consider alternatives like ConvertKit mainly if selling courses or books.
- He advises that if you're not worried about SEO, staying on Substack to build an email list is easy and worthwhile.

chunks.heading: Summary
