- **Segment:** It launched on Hacker News, and engineers tried it on side projects and then told the founders what they needed to bring it into their companies. The advice: "launch, launch, launch."
- **Stytch:** A non-friend developer put it into production eight hours after a 20-minute call and API keys, before the public beta existed. Later, publishing the seed raise on the company blog and a retweet from Benchmark's Chetan Puttagunta drove demo sign-ups. About 40% to 50% converted to demos, and roughly 20% of those onboarded.
- **Loom:** A Product Hunt launch brought thousands of extension downloads by the end of the day.

Lenny says Canva did all of the above. Its two-year wait list reached about 10,000 people, and it lined up embargoed press with TechCrunch and ZDNet. Launch night was anticlimactic, with users dripping in. Converting press into users is hard, because articles often don't link to the product. The first week brought a couple thousand sign-ups and the next about 5,000. Growth then compounded from many small channels (Cameron Adams: "never one silver bullet"). Talkative early users, such as social media managers and bloggers, drove the first 6 to 12 months.

chunks.heading: Trust is the secret weapon: start close and move outward
chunks.text:
Lenny sees the seven channels as concentric circles of decreasing trust and increasing distance from the founder. His takeaway is to start with the highest-trust channels and work outward.

Supporting points from founders:
- **Figma:** A recommendation from someone you trust beats a marketing team's. Figma deliberately mapped who designers listen to, using Twitter connections.
- **Ramp:** Early customers took a chance because of a close trust relationship, and the founders promised to obsess over saving them money. The scale was small enough, and they had backups, that the risk was acceptable.
- **Census:** Knowing the founders from YC meant skipping the "niceties of doing customer discovery."
- **Salesforce:** Marc Benioff found it hardest to convince the first prospect, since most people don't want to be first. Salesforce targeted pioneers who wanted to take part in something new. The first was Blue Martini Software, a company he had invested in.
- **Persona:** For security products, big mature companies won't trust a tiny startup with a PII system. That limit forced the founders to keep asking "Why would this person buy us?"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Lenny synthesizes interviews with two dozen B2B founders (Gong, Notion, Figma, Retool, Slack, etc.) into a framework for finding a startup idea. A great idea is important, underserved, and something you're excited about. Founders found it through three paths, always chasing "pain" and "pull".

chunks.heading: Idea sources: past pain, ponder and probe, present pull
chunks.text:
Lenny's research on how two dozen of the biggest B2B companies found their original idea (based on dozens of 1:1 founder interviews) found three reliable paths: past pain, ponder and probe, and present pull. In all three, founders look for two signals: pain (an important problem exists) and pull (people actually want your solution). Several of his findings are counterintuitive:
- The majority of founders had no special skill or background in the problem space.
- Only about 40% of ideas came from past pain at a previous job, which he did not expect.
- Every prosumer product (Notion, Figma, Airtable, Miro, Slack, Coda) took two to four years of wandering before something worked.
- Founders spoke to a median of 30 potential customers before committing.
- About 40% of startups pivoted at least once before landing on the winning idea, often more than once.
- About 20% were solo founders.
- Cold outbound was the second most common way to get early customers.

chunks.heading: The three ingredients of a great B2B idea
chunks.text:
Lenny says a great idea combines three things:
1. **The problem is important.** Many people must be willing to spend a lot to solve it. Most startups fail because the market is too small, not because the idea is bad. His rule of thumb for venture scale: a clear path to $100M a year in revenue and eventually $1B a year. Example signal: Robinhood agreed to a large contract with Sprig before it was built and installed the first version as it was being made. He points to Hunter Walk's LUV framework and Sequoia's market-curve guide for sizing.
2. **The market is underserved.** He cites Kunal Shah's (CRED) Delta-4 test: ask customers to rate the existing solution 1 to 10, then rate yours. Your solution must be at least 4 points better for anyone to care. If the incumbent scores 6 or higher (e.g. Excel), it is very hard to replace. Strong signal from Gusto: when asked about their payroll provider, over half of people "started cursing, unprompted."
3. **You are excited about it.** You may spend years on it. He endorses Dylan Field's view that many good ideas exist, so pick one you care about, because even if it fails you will have learned from it. He also quotes Paul Graham: "When in doubt, optimize for interestingness."

chunks.heading: Path 1: Past pain (about 40% of great ideas)
chunks.text:
Identify a large pain you experienced at a previous company, then build the solution. Examples he gives:
- **Gong:** co-founder Amit ran Sisense and found that why deals were lost lived in salespeople's heads; the CRM only showed outcomes, not reasons.
- **Retool:** David Hsu kept rebuilding internal tools at each company and realized they share the same building blocks.
- **Linear:** founders at Coinbase, Airbnb and Uber felt "a nagging feeling of disappointment" when their companies defaulted to Jira.
- **Persona:** Rick Song worked on identity at Square, where the team joked someone would build this well in 10 years. He saw vendors assume one technique would work, while every business needs a multi-modal approach.
- **Hex:** Barry McCardel started as a buyer, asked around for a tool, heard "No, but if you do, let us know," and eventually concluded no one else would build it.

Reflection questions he poses:
- What did you or others build at past jobs that proved very valuable to teammates?
- What tool did you wish you had and would have paid a lot for?
- What internal product have you built again and again?

Appendix examples include Snyk (security shifting left with DevOps), Canva, Stytch (a "Stripe for authentication" after Auth0 and Cognito pain at Plaid), Snowflake, and Ramp.

chunks.heading: Path 2: Ponder and probe
chunks.text:
Pick a space you are interested in, whiteboard and tinker, and talk to many potential customers looking for pain and pull. Lenny notes a wrong and right way to whiteboard: ideating in a silo is wrong; quickly validating with potential users is right. Focus on a space that is important, underserved, and exciting, ideally rooted in your experience (though that is not required).

Examples:
- **Figma:** after the Thiel Fellowship ($100,000 over two years), Dylan Field tested drones, then computational photography, then settled on design with WebGL. Field's "why now?" lens: a societal, regulatory or technological change that opens new possibilities.
- **Vanta:** Christina Cacioppo picked two spaces (team collaboration and security), banned herself from shiny objects, and learned the whiteboard trap: "if you can do it on a whiteboard, someone has probably done it. There's no $20 bills on the sidewalk." Startups she asked said they knew they should do security but didn't until customers asked, so she did it for them manually, which became Vanta.
- **Notion:** began as a no-code website builder that "didn't go anywhere for years." Four years in (early 2017) it launched Notion 1.0 focused on docs and wikis, with templates users could click into, which became the wedge.
- **Zip:** the sixth or seventh idea (earlier ones included fractional US equities for India and an accounting staffing platform that made $200k). Their YC partner advised looking for a large market with entrenched, mediocre incumbents, which led to procurement (valued over $1B).
- **Databricks:** Berkeley researchers saw Silicon Valley companies using what became Apache Spark for AI on data; open-sourcing it did not get enterprise uptake, so around 2012 they started a company.
- Others in the appendix: Coda (a 20-year-old idea revived with a friend), Gusto (whiteboarding small-business problems, then payroll), and Census.

Census's Boris Jabes learned that sitting in a room generating startup ideas "is really bad" because the ideas were not tied to a specific user pain; writing code forced them to talk to people.

Reflection questions: What emerging trend is underserved? What new technology is underused? How many customers have you spoken to? Rate problem importance 1 to 10, and how underserved the market is 1 to 10, looking for a delta of at least 4.

chunks.heading: Path 3: Present pull
chunks.text:
Keep building, but watch for a feature or side project users pull on strongly, then pivot fully to it. Examples:
- **Amplitude:** built an internal analytics tool for a voice-texting app (Sonalight), and other founders at Y Combinator wanted it.
- **Sprig:** Ryan Glasgow built a small SDK on an Airtable backend rotating three survey questions. Founders he shared it with said they'd be his first customer, and he quickly pivoted to surveys.
- **Loom:** two failed products (an expert-feedback marketplace, four months; an embeddable user-test tool, three months). Then a client recorded a video summarizing the user tests, a Product Hunt launch a month later drew thousands of extension downloads by day's end.
- **Segment:** about 15 months of failed analytics products. A growth-hack library, Analytics.js, got attention; with about six months of runway left, they built it for a week and launched on Hacker News, where it hit the top.
- **Slack:** after shutting down the Glitch game (45 people, $17.2M raised), the team's internal IRC-based communication, with added archiving, search and integrations, became the product.

Reflection questions: Which feature of what you've built has the most pull? What problem in your own startup do you wish someone would solve? What side project have you wanted to build?

chunks.heading: Summary checklist
chunks.text: Lenny's recap: look for ideas that are important, underserved, and exciting to you; choose one of the three routes; and you know you're onto something when you notice both pull and pain. The next step after the idea is validating it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Lenny studied how 50+ top consumer companies (Airbnb, Uber, Instagram, Coinbase and more) found their ideas. Nearly all came from paying attention: to your own problems, your curiosity, what's already working, paradigm shifts, or brainstorming with friends. He also lists traits of good ideas and what to do first once you have one.

chunks.heading: Most consumer startup ideas come from paying attention, not from sitting down to ideate
chunks.text:
Lenny studied how 50+ of the biggest consumer businesses (TikTok, Reddit, Uber, Airbnb and others) came up with their idea. He says "ideas don't matter" is wrong and quotes Sam Altman: "I myself used to believe ideas didn't matter that much, but I'm very sure that's wrong now."

- He finds five common strategies, all "rooted in paying attention":
  - Your own problems: ~30%
  - Your curiosity: ~20%
  - What's already working: ~18%
  - Paradigm shifts: ~15%
  - Brainstorming with friends: ~15%
- Fewer than 10 of the 50+ founders actively brainstormed ideas. Most ideas arrived organically.
- He says this doesn't mean you shouldn't spend time ideating. It just isn't where most of the biggest consumer ideas came from.

chunks.heading: Surprising facts about the founders behind big consumer businesses
chunks.text:
From the same dataset of ~50 companies, Lenny reports:

- Half of the founders were under 30 when they started, and 80% were under 35.
- Fewer than a third of the ideas came from founders solving their own problem. He expected the majority.
- Fewer than a third were actively ideating when the big idea hit.
- Only 18% of winning ideas came from pivots. He expected this to be much higher.
- Fewer than a third of founders had a unique or specific skill that enabled the build.
- Just over half of the ideas felt trivial at the time (Twitter, Snap, Pinterest, Coinbase, Tinder, Calm, Airbnb).
- Over 75% had 2+ founders, 68% had an engineering co-founder, 42% had previously started a company, and 11% had a co-founder with an MBA.
- Only one company, DoorDash, found its idea by actively talking to potential customers.

chunks.heading: Strategy 1: Solve your own problem (~30%)
chunks.text:
The largest group of companies began with founders fixing something that annoyed them, then realizing others wanted it too.

- Examples:
  - Dropbox: Drew Houston kept forgetting his thumb drive.
  - Airbnb: Gebbia and Chesky needed rent money and rented out an air bed during a design conference.
  - Uber: Garrett Camp couldn't reliably get a cab in San Francisco.
  - Hipcamp: Alyssa Ravasio found campsites hard to research and book.
  - GOAT: Daishin Sugano bought fake Air Jordans on eBay.
  - Warby Parker: the founders kept losing expensive glasses.
  - Calm: Michael Acton Smith used meditation to cope with his own pain.
- He quotes Paul Graham: "Pay particular attention to things that chafe you."
- His advice:
  - Build self-awareness about your day-to-day challenges.
  - Pay attention to problems that drive you to action.
  - Don't take your ideas for granted. If you find it valuable, others likely will too.

chunks.heading: Strategy 2: Follow your curiosity and tinker (~20%)
chunks.text:
About 20% of the businesses came from founders following their intuition and quickly building a prototype to see if there was a "there" there.

- Examples:
  - Coinbase: Brian Armstrong read the Bitcoin white paper and built a wallet.
  - Google: Page and Brin found the web interesting for its mathematical graph structure and built a crawler.
  - OpenSea: shipped a beta within a couple of months of the ERC721 standard.
  - Musical.ly: Alex Zhu saw teens combining video and music on a train and built a prototype.
  - Twitter: built a prototype in two weeks.
  - Tinder: prototyped at a hackathon.
  - Duolingo: began as an academic project.
- He quotes Paul Graham: working on projects that seem cool leads you to build things that are missing.
- His advice:
  - Give yourself time to tinker.
  - Build a prototype rather than just thinking.
  - Keep it simple and test as cheaply and quickly as you can. Your first idea is unlikely to be exactly right.

chunks.heading: Strategy 3: Double down on what's already working (aka pivot)
chunks.text:
Just over 15% of the companies launched something, noticed which element unexpectedly worked best, and focused on it.

- Examples:
  - Instagram: Burbn's users bounced off the check-in app but kept posting filtered square photos. Kevin Systrom's team cut everything but photos, and got 25,000 users on the first day of the new version.
  - YouTube: began as a video dating site.
  - Lyft: grew out of Zimride's long-distance ridesharing.
  - Pinterest: Tote users saved collections of items rather than buying.
  - Discord: the best part of a game was its voice and text chat.
  - PayPal: email payments started as an add-on "user acquisition engine".
  - Twitch: grew out of Justin.tv.
- Lenny says the best part of this path is that it should motivate you to launch whatever excites you most now, because even a failed idea may lead to the bigger one.
- He quotes Elon Musk on PayPal: when two paths aren't obviously different, "just pick a path and do it rather than just vacillate endlessly."
- His advice:
  - Kill your darlings. If not enough other people love your idea, it won't work.
  - Don't take for granted any part of your product people value, because that is a rare find.
  - Try lots of things. The more ideas you put out, the more likely one sticks.

chunks.heading: Strategies 4 and 5: Work backward from paradigm shifts, or brainstorm with friends
chunks.text:
**Paradigm shifts (~15%):** Founders noticed a shift in where the world was going and built for it. Lenny quotes Mike Maples Jr. ("Start from the future and work backwards") and Paul Graham ("Live in the future, then build what's missing").

- Examples:
  - Amazon: Bezos saw web usage growing 2,300% a year and chose books as the first product.
  - Spotify: Daniel Ek saw that only a better-than-piracy service would work.
  - 23andMe: genetic data had suddenly become cheap.
  - Instacart: on-demand rides and delivery were emerging.
  - Stitch Fix: retail was moving online.
- Elad Gil, quoted approvingly: the proof is in the growth rate or extrapolated technology curve, not "the number sitting in front of you."
- His prompts:
  - What will be very different in 5, 10 or 20 years?
  - What hasn't software eaten? Look for a big market with a bad customer experience.
  - What would be amazing if it were possible? Start from the ideal experience and work out what it would take.

**Brainstorming with friends (~15%):** 8 of the 50 companies found their idea this way.

- Examples:
  - Thumbtack: brainstormed weekly for a year. Its first idea, a financial aggregator, was beaten by Mint.
  - Netflix: Marc Randolph pitched ideas like personalized surfboards and custom dog food first.
  - Yelp, Reddit, Nextdoor (a standing 10 a.m. meeting for "billion-dollar ideas"), DoorDash, Bumble and Eventbrite.
- Lenny points to Michael Seibel's advice on this path.
- From Randolph's account: "for every good idea, there are a thousand bad ones."

chunks.heading: What makes a good idea
chunks.text:
Lenny says no one can truly know whether an idea will work, but the more of these elements an idea has, the likelier it is to succeed:

1. **You can't stop thinking about it.** Startups only really fail when the founder gives up, and passion makes that less likely. He quotes Sam Altman: founders often "wish they had waited to start a startup until they came up with an idea they really loved."
2. **You start building a prototype immediately and have the skills to do it.** Most companies came from a scrappy experiment within hours, days or weeks. This is likely why over 80% had an engineering co-founder (elsewhere in the piece he cites 68%).
3. **You have unique insight into the opportunity.** This usually comes from prior experience. It is why the best ideas often sound crazy, trivial or impossible to others. User research rarely drove early ideation; ideas came from experience, vision and gut instinct.
4. **The idea is easy to understand.** Every product he looked at can be explained in a sentence or two.

- The right founder (obsessed, with unique insight and the right skills) plus market timing creates the opportunity for massive consumer businesses.
- This is also why he says you shouldn't worry much about someone stealing your idea. The chance that someone else has that combination at the right time is very low.

chunks.heading: What to do once you have an idea
chunks.text:
Lenny's advice, quoting Walt Disney ("quit talking and begin doing"):

1. **Prototype cheaply and quickly to validate.**
   - Stitch Fix's Katrina Lake used SurveyMonkey and toted garments to customers' homes for a $20 styling fee.
   - Netflix mailed a used music CD to test DVD-by-mail overnight.
   - DoorDash built a static HTML page with a Google Voice number and PDF menus, offered $6 delivery, ran a small AdWords campaign, and got its first order within hours.
   - Rec Room built its first game in 90 days.
   - He points to Todd Jackson's post on validating startup ideas.
2. **Talk to potential customers to refine the idea.**
   - Rent the Runway's founders cold-emailed guesses of Diane von Furstenberg's address and got a meeting the next day.
   - Rec Room set up in its WeWork lobby for testers.
   - Discord's founders jumped into voice chat with anyone who showed up.
3. **Figure out who you're building for.** This is the focus of the next post in the series (Step 2: a "super-specific who").

The series he is launching has six steps: Insight, Audience, Hook, Reach, Retain, Scale.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Lenny reviewed the early growth of 100+ consumer companies and found only seven reliable ways to get the first 1,000 users: friends, targeted strangers, where your audience hangs out, influencers, press, viral content, and physical placement. Pick two or three, focus, and start with the easy inner circle before moving outward.

chunks.heading: Early adopters: the seven ways to find your first 1,000 users
chunks.text:
Lenny reviewed the early growth of more than 100 consumer companies and found only seven reliable ways to find the first 1,000 users. He treats them as a menu: pick two or three that look appetizing, try them, and double down on whatever works. Almost every startup got most of its early growth from one or two channels, and some from a single one (Udemy and PR, Etsy and communities, Twitter and influencers). His advice is to focus, not to order everything.

The seven strategies, with roughly how often each drove early growth:
- Reach out to friends and colleagues (about 20% of startups)
- Reach out to targeted strangers (about 30%)
- Go where your target audience hangs out, online or offline (over 50%, the most popular and highest-ROI)
- Enlist influencers, paid or organic
- Get press (over 20%)
- Create viral content (about 10%)
- Get physical placement such as flyers, stickers and signs (about 10%)

He says these seven account for 99% of early B2C growth. Rarely, a company wins "off menu."

chunks.heading: How to choose a tactic: three archetypes
chunks.text:
Lenny maps common startup types to a starting order:
- **Typical consumer startup:** friends and colleagues, then go where the audience hangs out, then influencers.
- **Marketplace or platform (DoorDash, Cameo, Substack):** reach out to targeted strangers (DM celebs, email owners), then physical placement, then get supply to drive demand.
- **Remarkable story (Airbnb, Spotify, Superhuman):** get press, then try to create viral content.

He frames the strategies as concentric circles with the founder at the center. The further out you go, the harder and less likely to succeed a strategy generally is. So start with the easy stuff and move outward only if nothing works.

chunks.heading: Strategy 1: Reach out to friends and colleagues
chunks.text:
- Easiest and fastest route, a large driver for about 20% of startups. Lenny cites Paul Graham: "you don't need to get the word out. You need to get the word *in*."
- Best for products most people find useful (Reddit, Facebook, Lyft). The key is that your friends resemble your super-specific "who."
- Takeaway question: "Have you asked your friends to try out your product yet?"
- Examples he cites: Yelp reached roughly 1K users two degrees out from ex-PayPal coworkers. Lyft sent personal email invites before its waitlist. Strava got about 100 users from direct friends and about 1,000 within 12 months by word of mouth. LinkedIn's founders invited their contacts on launch day (a couple thousand individuals), and most of the roughly 12,000 first-week signups were 1st or 2nd degree connections. Substack's Hamish McKenzie recruited Bill Bishop as the first publisher, then kept asking friends and each writer for more recommendations.
- Caveats: friends may not match your "who." WhatsApp's Jan Koum demoed to friends and none liked it. Patreon's founders emailed 40 creators they knew and all 40 said no.

chunks.heading: Strategy 2: Reach out to targeted strangers
chunks.text:
- Important for about 30% of consumer startups, used almost exclusively by marketplaces to bootstrap supply. He reasons that one unit of supply is worth enough to a new marketplace that manual cold outreach has high ROI.
- Best for marketplaces and platforms where each recruited user is very valuable (a Cameo celebrity).
- Takeaway question: "Would it be worth having someone on your team ping 100+ people directly?"
- Examples:
  - Cameo: "$10/month interns" DM'd talent on Instagram and Twitter.
  - YouTube: summer 2005 outreach to bloggers, video bloggers, photographers and pet communities.
  - DoorDash: the founder went door to door to restaurants.
  - Thumbtack: emailed local service pros and then sent them job leads once registered.
  - Uber Black: phoned limo companies, pitching a guaranteed minimum income if they kept the app on.
  - Airbnb: direct sales let local teams choose which supply (neighborhood, size, price) to acquire.
  - Udemy: after manually creating successful courses, returned to the same experts with proof and landed Zed Shaw and Bess Ho, then 5 to 10 more that summer.
  - Behance: contacted the 100 designers they admired most, offered an interview for a productivity blog, then built each a portfolio. Nobody declined; the result was a v1 with about five projects per top creative, which "solved our chicken-or-egg problem."
  - Nextdoor: picked the Lorelei neighborhood and approached homeowners association board members.
  - Shef: asked friends where they bought authentic dishes, got intros to those cooks, and joined their Facebook groups.

chunks.heading: Strategy 3: Go where your target audience hangs out
chunks.text:
- Lenny calls this the single most popular (over 50%), effective and highest-ROI strategy. It is why a very specific "who" matters: you need to know where they gather.
- Places include niche forums, events, transit hubs, Hacker News, Product Hunt, college campuses, malls, even an REI.
- Key: give real value instead of spamming your pitch. Takeaway question: "What are 1-2 places where your super-specific who already gather?"
- Online examples:
  - Netflix: an early hire joined DVD forums as an enthusiast and seeded mentions with moderators and top commenters months before launch.
  - Discord: a Final Fantasy subreddit member mentioned the app.
  - Etsy: reached Craftster.org's founder (about 100,000 members) and had thousands of sellers ready at launch, with fee-free listing for the first few months.
  - Behance: used StumbleUpon, Reddit, NotCot and Pinterest, and sent personal "I noticed your work on..." emails (more personal converted better). The practice was to bring in 10 amazing new members a day.
  - Dropbox: Hacker News in April 2007 (top for two days), Digg and Reddit in March 2008, public launch September 2008, a million signups by May 2009.
  - Robinhood: a waitlist accidentally hit #3 on Hacker News, with about 600 concurrent visitors on a Saturday.
  - Facebook: a message to a mailing list of 300 Harvard students.
- Offline examples:
  - Morning Brew: a hub-and-spoke model, pitching business professors and club presidents at Michigan (lectures of 75 to 500 people) for a couple thousand readers.
  - Etsy: a team at craft fairs nearly every weekend across the US and Canada, buying sellers lunch and dropping off "craft show kits."
  - Lyft: free Bi-Rite ice cream sundae drop-offs at startups, with Lyft credits.
  - Uber: street teams handing out referral codes at Caltrain.
  - Hipcamp: about 100 users from a fold-up table and stickers at REI.
  - Pinterest: the founder changed Apple Store demo computers to Pinterest.
  - Rent the Runway: trial trunk shows on college campuses.
  - Wealthfront: educational seminars at Facebook and LinkedIn aimed at engineers, with the pitch dropped entirely ("80% education and 20% selling" had to become all education).

chunks.heading: Tinder and Bumble: the campus playbook
chunks.text:
Lenny highlights Tinder's launch as a detailed offline recipe:
- A launch party of about 300 USC students where you had to download Tinder to get in.
- The next Monday, a pitch in every sorority and fraternity; then SMU, UCLA, UCSB and Boston.
- A "Tinder University Program": pick influential students per campus, send swag (T-shirts, stickers, cups), and make them brand ambassadors, measured by the percentage of people downloading in an area. About 15 universities at a time, adding another once an area saturated.
- Bumble reused the playbook: sororities pitched "from the heart," pizza boxes and cookies wrapped in Bumble stickers for fraternity members.
- Snap spread from a high schooler in Orange County: just over 2,000 users in December 2011, 20,000 in January, 100,000 by April.

chunks.heading: Strategy 4: Enlist influencers
chunks.text:
- Underutilized. Figure out who your super-specific who is influenced by and get them genuinely excited, paid or not (bloggers, newsletter writers, tweeters, Instagrammers, celebs).
- Takeaway question: the center of the Venn diagram of who your audience is influenced by and which of them you can get excited about what you're building.
- Examples:
  - Instagram: seeded the prototype with people with large followings inside the designer community, not necessarily large overall.
  - Tinder: prominent Instagrammers posted authentically.
  - Product Hunt: personal emails inviting influencers to contribute.
  - Spotify: seeded with journalists, musicians and tech CEOs to build pent-up demand.
  - Cameo: Ronnie Radke, found via famousbirthdays.com, got booked about 500 times in days; his poor seven-second videos still got positive reviews, showing the magic is the fan-talent relationship.
  - Pinterest: a blogger collaboration ("pin it forward") after the Alt Summit conference.
  - Twitter: Om Malik's post drove more than 250 signups the next day, when the service had under 600 users.
  - Reddit: Paul Graham's essay forced an unplanned launch and passed 1,000 users in a day.

chunks.heading: Strategies 5 to 7: press, viral content, physical placement
chunks.text:
**Press** (over 20%). Best for products or founders with a great story and a drumbeat of news. Takeaway question: what's the most interesting or surprising thing about your company to someone who doesn't care?
- Instacart's Max Mullen: "PR is an untapped growth channel for early-stage consumer startups."
- Airbnb's 2008 DNC bump lasted only a week, so the founders sold Obama O's and Cap'n McCain's cereal at $40 a box; they pitched the smallest bloggers first as social proof for bigger outlets.
- Udemy's first 10,000 registrants came directly from its press launch. Spotify relied on PR per country launch. Superhuman landed pieces in Wired, TechCrunch and Cheddar.
- Instagram contacted press directly instead of using a PR firm and got coverage including the New York Times.

**Viral content** (about 10%). Best for founders with an existing audience who can make something remarkable. Takeaway question: what story would get thousands of people to share it?
- Duolingo: the CEO's TED talk led to 300,000+ private beta signups, then no ad spend.
- Calm: donothingfortwominutes.com collected about 100K emails in two weeks.
- Patreon launched via a YouTube video to the founder's fans. Superhuman's longform essays drove early growth. Substack's founding essay was picked up by NiemanLab before the product existed.

**Physical placement** (about 10%). Best for local products (food delivery, dating); the key is hustle. Takeaway question: where would you put flyers, stickers or signs?
- DoorDash printed tens of thousands of flyers ("Dubar delivers, get hummus delivered!") and stuffed them in delivery bags, because customers cared about the restaurant, not DoorDash.
- Instacart delivered in logo-branded reusable grocery bags.
- Grubhub tried in-store signage (copied from Yelp's stickers), sandwich boards, menus and delivery bags.
- Tinder's Whitney Wolfe Herd printed about 1,000 "Find out who likes you on campus" flyers at FedEx and paid people $20 to place them.

chunks.heading: Off-menu tactics
chunks.text:
Lenny lists four rarer approaches:
- **Build an audience first:** Product Hunt began as an email list and reached 100 users in its first week; Stack Overflow seeded a private beta from its founders' existing communities; Patreon launched to a creator's fanbase.
- **Let supply drive demand:** DoorDash restaurants made their own placards and window stickers; Etsy sellers did grassroots marketing and were pushed to promote their shops; also Cameo, Behance, Product Hunt, Substack.
- **Be first on an emerging platform:** Noom was the fourth app in the Android store; TikTok (Musical.ly) used a very long App Store name to rank in search; WhatsApp's status pings turned it into messaging after Apple's push notifications launched in June 2009.
- **Host a launch party:** Hinge spent its last $25,000 on a 2,500-person party in D.C. where everyone had to download the app to get in.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Lenny shares research from interviews with founders and early employees at 17 major marketplaces. The first step to cracking the chicken-and-egg problem is to constrain the marketplace by geography or category, since the best way to get big is to start small. He also warns against over-relying on any single company's story.

chunks.heading: Constraining the marketplace: the "go small to get big" rule
chunks.text:
Lenny's research across 17 marketplaces found that, with one exception, every marketplace constrained its initial scope to reach critical mass faster. He frames this as counter-intuitive: "the best way to get big is by first going small."

- There are two ways to constrain: by **geography** and by **category**.
- If supply and demand must meet physically, the constraint is always geographic (a single market).
- Otherwise the constraint is category-based (for example, handmade goods).
- The sole exception was Thumbtack, which launched with all categories and all geographies.

chunks.heading: Marketplace definition and why it is a great business
chunks.text:
Lenny defines a marketplace as a business that:
1. Connects demand (people who want a thing) with supply (people who have it).
2. Leads to a financial transaction.
3. Generally owns no supply, provides no products or services directly, and eventually handles the money.

- **Marketplaces:** Airbnb, Uber, Lyft, Etsy, eBay, DoorDash, Rover, Thumbtack, TaskRabbit, Craigslist.
- **Not marketplaces:** Delta (owns inventory), YouTube (no transaction), Slack (no supply).

Why they are great businesses:
- **Network effects:** more users make the product more useful or cheaper.
- **Barrier to entry:** hard to replicate once the network effect is strong.
- **Efficiency:** no inventory means cheaper operation.
- **Scalability:** no inventory means easier scaling.
- **Flexibility:** easier to pivot (for example, Uber Black to UberX).

chunks.heading: The chicken-and-egg problem
chunks.text:
- A working marketplace has supply serving demand. At launch you have neither.
- You must convince one side to commit before the other. Without restaurants, a hungry customer has no reason to open your app; without customers, restaurants have little reason to onboard.
- Solving this is "one of the biggest barriers to launching a marketplace business."
- Lenny's phase 1 steps: constrain the marketplace, pick which side to focus on, drive initial supply, drive initial demand.

chunks.heading: Geographic constraint: examples from location-based marketplaces
chunks.text:
- **Rover:** started and stayed "hyper-focused" on Seattle: dog-friendly, early adopters, techy working professionals who travel (David Rosenthal's account). It helped them figure out the product quickly.
- **Airbnb:** focused first on New York. When it expanded internationally in 2011, it built critical mass in just a few markets where supply and demand could be unlocked quickly.
- **Uber:** the Launcher team had a playbook for new markets that started with supply. Goal: over 30 drivers, with an ETA under 15 minutes.
- **OpenTable:** density mattered because "dining is local." Rule of thumb: 50-100 concentrated restaurants in a city gave diners a meaningful consideration set.
- **Instacart:** picked markets with likely demand, such as Chicago in winter (high household income, fewer households with cars, bad weather).
- **Zillow mortgages:** started in a single market, because rates were entered manually by brokers responding to emails.

chunks.heading: Breather's lesson: duplicate exactly what works
chunks.text:
Julien Smith's account, which Lenny includes as a marketplace lesson:
- With short transactions (a 2-hour room booking), proximity was critical.
- Dense areas like the Flatiron District saw new units booked immediately, which was clear product/market fit.
- Their approach: "This cafe, at this location, at this time, is working. Duplicate this exactly." Don't launch a new city yet, don't change anything; look for ways to extend or double the transaction.
- The lesson: if you're in a decent-sized market, "just double down on what's working." Airbnb did the same, recreating New York "again and again."

chunks.heading: Category constraint: examples from non-location marketplaces
chunks.text:
- **TaskRabbit:** always a broad platform, but deliberately built liquidity in its most popular categories: handyman tasks (including IKEA assembly), house cleaning, and moving help.
- **Eventbrite:** found its core use case in tech mixers and conferences, based on where early traction appeared. Invites carrying the Eventbrite name made it "a thing."
- **Etsy:** began with only three categories: vintage items, craft supplies, and handmade items.

chunks.heading: The Thumbtack exception, and caveats on the research
chunks.text:
**Thumbtack** (Sander Daniels) deliberately did the opposite: all categories and all geographies from the start.
- It didn't get funding for many years in part because investors thought it was "boiling the ocean."
- Breadth in category raised usage frequency from once every couple of years (hiring a house painter) to 8-12 times a year (average American household services).
- Breadth in geography let them scale as fast as possible, giving the revenue, traffic, and experimentation velocity to bootstrap the product.
- Per Sander: "In our case we wouldn't have survived had we done it any other way."

Lenny's caveats:
- Many of these companies succeeded mainly through great product/market fit; growth levers accelerated and controlled growth, but they may have succeeded anyway.
- Past behavior is not predictive. Focus on ways of thinking, not specific tactics, since many past growth levers no longer work.
- The research is based on interviews about events many years ago, so memory may be faulty.
- He warns against leaning too heavily on a single company's experience (including his own Airbnb background).

chunks.heading: First-principles reminder from DoorDash
chunks.text:
The opening quote Lenny leads with, from Micah Moreau (DoorDash VP of Growth):
- Everyone looks for the growth hack or channel that unlocks something big.
- Every time DoorDash looked for why it wasn't growing, "it always came back to the basics: selection, delivery quality, pricing."
- "Always come back to first principles. Whenever we made a mistake, we forgot this."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Lenny distills seven years at Airbnb into lessons on culture, problem statements, wildly ambitious goals, working backward from the ideal experience, org design, a high bar, and team focus. Practical, with concrete Airbnb examples like Instant Book and Snow White.

chunks.heading: Culture as a competitive advantage
chunks.text:
Lenny credits Airbnb's strong culture, clear values and quirky rituals as a real competitive advantage. It helped the company hire top talent, move fast when opportunities arose, push through adversity, and let the team hold leaders to the long-term mission.

He names three ingredients:
- **Founders obsessed with culture.** This shapes who the first hires are (who co-create the culture) and which values get modeled, knowingly or not. It matters more as you scale.
- **A strong sense of self.** Airbnb codified core values through a small task force about three years in. They are used to measure success, hire (a core values interview group vets every candidate), evaluate performance (baked into peer review) and assess large deals. Everyone at the company could recite them verbatim.
- **Rituals.** Cookie time Tuesdays, new hire tea time, hosted bar, human tunnels, fun facts. They create space for bonding and joy. His advice: "Don't overthink your rituals; experiment and see what sticks."

Takeaway: be obsessed with company and team culture.

chunks.heading: Nail the problem statement
chunks.text:
Lenny calls crafting and aligning on a problem statement "the single most important step in solving any problem." He saw simple projects with vague problem statements circle for weeks or months, while complex projects with strong ones "sail smoothly."

Tools he uses:
- A one-pager template he refined over the years to crystallize the problem and opportunity for his team and stakeholders.
- The situation-complication-resolution framework, to tell the story to a wider audience.
- The jobs-to-be-done framework, to make sure real customer needs are being addressed.

Takeaway: crystallize the problem and align the whole team behind it.

chunks.heading: Setting wildly ambitious goals
chunks.text:
At the end of each year, Airbnb was often shocked at how close it came to "seemingly impossible" goals. CEO Brian Chesky was known for doubling proposed goals and often pushing teams to 10x.

Lenny's five ingredients:
- **Set uncomfortable goals.** Pick one that makes you uncomfortable while clearly understanding why hitting it would be incredible for the business. Ask: what would need to be true to hit it, and what could we accomplish without barriers (budget, people, dependencies)?
- **Make someone directly accountable.** "If a number doesn't have a person's name next to it, it's not going to happen."
- **Think long-term.** Airbnb looked five to 10 years ahead to set each year's goal, for both growth and mission.
- **Give a cross-functional team ownership of how to achieve it.** A leader's number-one job is assembling the right team, pointing it in the right direction, and unblocking it.
- **Celebrate success, don't punish failure.** Goals are meant to push you, not kill you. If a team gets close, congratulate them and move on to the next goal.

Takeaway: when setting goals, think bigger.

chunks.heading: Start with the ideal and work backward
chunks.text:
Lenny describes a variation of Amazon's working backward method that worked well at Airbnb: envision the perfect user experience first, then close the gap.

**Snow White example.** Inspired by how Disney developed the original film, the founders treated Airbnb as a story with a beginning, middle and end. The team storyboarded the ideal guest and host experience and identified key emotional moments. The storyboards exposed the biggest gaps and informed early company strategy.

**Instant Book example.** Booking had many steps, including a wait while the host reviewed the request. Rather than micro-optimizing parts of the funnel for months or years, the team defined the ideal: a guest instantly books any home with no waiting.
- Only about 5% of bookings were instant at the time, and getting every host to allow booking without approval seemed impossible.
- It was clear this was where the business had to go, so the team put all its resources behind the bet.
- Over a couple of years the marketplace shifted so the vast majority of bookings are now instant.

His process:
- **Write or draw the ideal experience.** The team sketched the ideal booking flow on paper and wrote a sample blog post announcing it as if it were real.
- **Create a framework to make the problem tractable.** The biggest gap was giving hosts control over who could book instantly. The team split it into "can" problems (am I able to use it?) and "want" problems (do I want to use it?) and worked through them in priority order.
- **When it feels uncomfortable, get more data.** Many people assumed instant bookings would hurt quality (less communication, more transactional). A quick data dive showed otherwise, which, with a few other data points, cleared the path for internal buy-in.

Takeaway: look for step-function change by imagining the ideal state and working backward.

chunks.heading: Treat org design as a product
chunks.text:
Lenny argues that as you move up in product leadership, "the most important product to get right is how you organize your people." Structure can multiply or hinder the mission.

- **Optimize for dedicated cross-functional teams with a clear mandate.** He calls this the single most impactful thing leaders can do when setting up a team. Teams should be self-contained and autonomous. A missing resource (designer, data scientist, budget), an extra cross-team dependency or a conflicting surface area cuts impact sharply, often invisibly until later. Minimize how often a team must meet with or wait on another team. Well-functioning teams "feel like a black box that outputs regular updates and amazing work."
- **Get the goals right.** Teams underestimate this. Good goals are:
  1. limited in number, ideally one or two
  2. quick to show impact
  3. directly tied to top-line business growth
  4. easy to understand
  5. uncomfortable
- **Accept there is no perfect org design.** He went through almost a dozen reorgs at Airbnb and never saw a plan that fixed every issue and pleased everyone. Address the biggest pain points, future-proof where you can, then move forward. Note the flaws (overlapping product ownership, two teams sharing a key metric, a team owning too much), build systems to work around them, and set the expectation that the org will change again.

Takeaway: build autonomous units with well-defined goals and get out of the way.

chunks.heading: Maintain a high bar for everything
chunks.text:
Coming from startups, Lenny was used to moving fast, settling for good enough and thinking short-term. An early Airbnb manager taught him the power of a high bar, which he says "profoundly impacted my career."

Practices:
- **Emails:** reread before sending; there is always something to cut or clarify.
- **Shared docs:** get feedback from at least one person before sharing widely, keep formatting clean and consistent, close out comments before sharing with execs, make it scannable.
- **Meetings:** put the goal and ideally an agenda in the invite, invite as few people as possible, call out unproductive meetings, leave with action items, and follow up by email with owners.
- **Presentations:** ask whether an email would do. State whether you want a decision, feedback or just to share information. Get feedback first, and keep it short: "no one has ever wished that presentation went longer."
- **Hiring:** "The people you bring in determine the company you become." Only hire people you feel "hell yes" about. "If it's a maybe, it's a no."

Questions to keep asking: how could we go a bit bolder, make this slightly better, make this meeting more productive, make this doc crisper, set the bar higher?

chunks.heading: Keep teams focused
chunks.text:
Lenny found a small supply growth team spread across a long funnel at Airbnb, seeing wins but unable to build momentum. He saw the same on a trip quality team. In both cases, narrowing the problem space and giving a focused mandate improved impact and morale.

- **Supply growth:** split into focused units (referrals, top-of-funnel organic growth, performance marketing, and so on), then grew each with resources matched to its problem.
- **Trip quality:** dedicated a quarter at a time to one aspect (host response rate, guest review rate, etc.). When a large opportunity appeared, the team doubled down the next quarter.

The same applies to product. Giving users fewer things to think about drove some of the biggest guest conversion gains he saw:
- opening listings in new tabs (avoids getting lost while exploring)
- extending session length (fewer logins)
- removing links within the payments flow (fewer distractions)

On the host side:
- always showing a "recommended" tag when presenting options
- defaulting settings by host persona
- adding inline tips so users don't bounce

Takeaway: "Focus. Focus. Focus."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Lenny maps content-driven growth on a 2x2 (SEO vs. virality, user- vs. employee-generated), giving five strategies, then zooms into editorially generated SEO content. He collects how HubSpot, Ahrefs, Intercom, Slidebean and Webflow started, staffed and operationalized content. Takeaways: start small, set a clear goal, be patient, dedicate a team.

chunks.heading: The five content-driven growth strategies, and Lenny's map of editorially generated SEO
chunks.text:
Lenny maps content-driven growth on a 2x2. One axis is what you optimize for (SEO vs. virality). The other is who generates the content (users vs. employees). That gives five strategies:

- **User-generated SEO-optimized (UGSO):** users create public content that Google surfaces. Examples: Quora, Glassdoor, Reddit.
- **Editorially generated SEO-optimized (EGSO):** employees or contractors create content to rank for keywords. Examples: Ahrefs, Slidebean, HubSpot.
- **Data-generated SEO-optimized (DGSO):** a company auto-generates thousands of pages from UGC and proprietary data. Examples: Thumbtack, Zapier, Tripadvisor, Yelp, Grubhub.
- **User-generated virality-optimized (UGVO):** UGC that users share with friends, pulling them into the product. TikTok (watermarked videos) is the ultimate example, along with the Reface app. Airbnb listings and Zillow's Zestimate sit at the edges.
- **Editorially generated virality-optimized (EGVO):** one-off viral content from founders or the company, a.k.a. thought leadership or brand building. Examples: Spotify Unwrapped, Mr. Beast, Stir's one-off drops, Superhuman's early blog posts.

He had already covered UGSO/DGSO and the viral strategies in earlier posts. This piece zooms in on EGSO. He asked Twitter which companies do it best, and Slidebean, Ahrefs, Intercom and HubSpot came up repeatedly. Webflow is a bonus case. Intercom and Webflow aren't primarily SEO-driven, but he included them because their perspectives are instructive.

chunks.heading: Seven high-level takeaways on editorial content growth
chunks.text:
Lenny distilled the lessons from the five companies into seven points:

1. **Start small.** Be scrappy and experiment with platform, topic and style until something works.
2. **Align on a clear goal.** Decide whether the goal is SEO traffic, virality, brand building or sales enablement.
3. **Hunt for opportunity.** Research topics where searchers are underserved, and deliver compelling, differentiated value to them.
4. **Give the reins to someone who cares.** The best content comes from people who care about the product, business and topic, usually founders or a passionate full-time employee.
5. **Think long-term.** Make sure there is a clear path to the investment making a significant dent in growth, and ask whether the upside is even worth it.
6. **Build a dedicated team.** Eventually you need at least five people dedicated to the effort, more if you do video.
7. **Be patient.** It took years for each company to see significant payoff.

chunks.heading: Scale benchmarks from the companies Lenny profiled
chunks.text:
Lenny shared these numbers from each company:

- **Ahrefs:** 300+ posts, 1.5M visits/month. Top posts: Top 100 Most Visited Websites by Search Traffic, Affiliate Marketing for Beginners, Top Google Searches.
- **Slidebean:** 250+ YouTube videos, 160K visits/month. Top videos are company stories (Boosted Boards, Zoom vs. Skype, Spotify vs. Apple).
- **Intercom:** 870 posts and 262 podcasts, 100K+ visits/month and 75K+ listeners/month. Top posts cover RICE prioritization, design workshops and what a product manager does.
- **HubSpot:** in its early days, 30% or more of customers came from demand generated by blog posts. Its web traffic (organic, direct, referral) exceeds that of many business publications such as TechCrunch, so it treats other media outlets, not other SaaS brands, as its competition for online attention.

chunks.heading: Why these companies started investing in content
chunks.text:
Lenny collected the origin stories:

- **Slidebean:** The "pitch deck" keyword on SEM was its best lead source. SEM was expensive and covered only about 5% of searches, so it moved to SEO. It published roughly 150 articles in a year and reached SERP positions 3-5 for most target keywords. That traffic drove growth for two years. It then judged that positions 1-2 were unlikely however many articles it published, so it moved to YouTube as "the next" search engine. It started with search-style videos, then moved to videos built for the YouTube algorithm (high CTR, high watch time, broad topics, sharing).
- **HubSpot:** It published before it had a product. Dharmesh Shah's OnStartups community showed that value-first content builds an audience. Inbound marketing means "create assets of value for your audience vs. pay money to interrupt them via traditional advertising." The media strategy has two parts: content to educate (blog posts found via search, with e-book, template or course upgrades) and content to influence (original stories on trends and case studies, via video and podcasts, aimed at a large audience).
- **Ahrefs:** There was no single decision. Tim Soulo inherited a small blog in 2015 and improved it gradually.
- **Intercom:** The founders came from the Web 2.0 blogging era, and Des Traynor wrote the first ~100 posts. Intercom deliberately chose high-quality editorial content to stand out from the SEO-driven norm. Customers who came through the blog and podcast spent more and stayed longer. Gated content must be a fair value exchange. More recently the focus has been enablement: making content usable by sales, account-based marketing and paid acquisition.

chunks.heading: Starting resources: cheap experiments and company-wide content incentives
chunks.text:
- **Intercom:** For the first year, John Collins was the whole content team ("team blog"), backed by the brand design team. Everyone was incentivized to create content (blog posts, talks, podcasts) by adding content creation to personal and team goals, so it counted toward career growth. Nobody was paid extra.
- **Slidebean:** The founder edited the first YouTube videos, and team members with video backgrounds carved out time. Because experiments were so cheap, the team could trial-and-error for over 18 months before finding a format that worked. For about the first year the videos "sucked" and got no traffic.
- **Ahrefs:** A budget to find talent for the blog, plus borrowed designer time. Small steps, no tipping point.
- **HubSpot:** Early marketing hires all focused on creating content (blogs, social posts, webinars).

chunks.heading: Team structures at scale
chunks.text:
- **Slidebean (YouTube):** a content/strategy manager, 1 lead animator and 2 junior animators (all full-time), 2 screenwriters (mostly research), and a community manager. Video production cost about $125K in 2020.
- **HubSpot:** a full media operation: blogs, content offers (e-books, templates, courses), HubSpot Stories, YouTube, Audio (podcasts, Clubhouse), the daily newsletter and Trends subscription (both run by The Hustle, which HubSpot acquired), and a Distribution team to plan promotion.
- **Intercom:** a team of 10 in Dublin, with three more roles opening. It has three pillars: Audiences (top-of-funnel content for support and success leaders, and where they get information), Enablement (reworking content for sales, such as turning commissioned research into slides, plus customer evidence), and Channels (SEO and the podcast).
- **Ahrefs:** a blog lead, two in-house marketers, one part-time technical writer who also sits on the product team, a video lead with three production helpers, and one graphic designer.

chunks.heading: How HubSpot operationalizes SEO content
chunks.text:
- Full-time analysts build quarterly editorial calendars across all blogs, mixing search-first posts and influence-focused posts.
- The team knows how much net-new search traffic is available for each calendar, like a quarterly TAM. That tells them how much traffic they can expect and when they are running out on a topic.
- A team is alerted to posts losing traffic and optimizes them to recover traffic and conversions.
- Slidebean uses a tool to decide which videos to make.

chunks.heading: Advice for starting content-driven growth
chunks.text:
Lenny's takeaways, using the founders' own words:

- **Choose SEO or viral deliberately.** Tim Soulo says SEO content is much easier than viral content because keyword research gives you topics. Viral content depends on creativity and unique ideas.
- **Master one channel before adding the next.** HubSpot started with a blog and focused on it for years. "There is always room to be better or different." Brands compete with every tweet, post and podcast, not just direct competitors. "Good no longer gets you results."
- **Set intentional goals and model them.** For demand generation, estimate available search traffic for your topics and apply rough conversion rates to size the demand TAM. A goal might be a blog worth 20% of needed demand, or a podcast that influences your audience.
- **Hold your nerve, then double down.** Intercom's John Collins says content "doesn't generate returns as quickly" as other marketing, and "content is a supertanker, not a speedboat." Once a format shows engagement, double down on it quickly rather than starting a second medium.
- **Video is expensive and long-term.** Slidebean says it takes months and dozens of videos to build an audience, and most startups need customers faster in a way they can control. When it works, the brand effect is strong. Slidebean says it wishes it had focused on brand sooner.

chunks.heading: Webflow: video education to lift activation, not just traffic
chunks.text:
Lenny's bonus case shows content used for new-user success rather than top-of-funnel traffic. He notes that, unlike SEO, any B2B company can use video to increase activation or conversion.

- Webflow built Webflow University, free courses that help designers of all skill levels learn a powerful platform with no watered-down interface.
- Video was a priority from launch, when a founder recorded a full-site build walkthrough. In 2016 a community member posted a much higher-quality tutorial video and the community reacted positively, so Webflow adopted that direction. It eventually hired him to lead education.
- The team started as one full-time power user, working with support on docs and guides. Since 2016 it has added a dedicated team (producers, editors, designers), modern equipment, a soundproof studio and custom music and animation. The content marketing team uses freelancers and agencies, and plans to double headcount.
- People who enroll in the courses are "much more likely" to become subscribers. New courses attract new people and introduce use cases and features.
- Webflow's non-tutorial content has inspirational examples and useful resources for designers, with a fun, friendly social tone.
- Advice from Mischa Vaughn: "you need a devoted team with a clear charter." Find a leader, build a distinct vision and voice, and give them plenty of support.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Lenny reflects on hitting 500,000 subscribers and distills ten lessons. Growth comes from consistently publishing high-quality, original, shareable work, not from design, branding, or growth strategy. He covers picking a topic by energy, spending more time per post, cutting words, and sustaining a cadence.

chunks.heading: Quality and consistency are the whole growth model
chunks.text:
- Lenny says the things that don't matter are design, title, strategy, growth plan and vision. What matters is quality and consistency.
- "There's no trick to making something like this grow." Growth comes from publishing something valuable, over and over, that people want to share with friends and colleagues.
- If a newsletter isn't growing, he says it is most likely a quality problem or a consistency problem.
- Quote: "people don't want more emails. They want better emails."
- His growth path to 500,000 subscribers (Sep 2023):
  - First 100: a Medium post about his time at Airbnb, which grew his Twitter audience, then a tweet announcing the newsletter.
  - Next 1,000: guest posts on First Round Review and Andrew Chen's blog.
  - Next 10,000: nine months of useful weekly writing, plus tweeting summaries and word of mouth.
  - Next 100,000: two more years of the same.
  - Next 200,000: more of the same, week after week.
  - Last 200,000: the same plus Substack's recommendations feature.

chunks.heading: Pick a job to be done and do it better than anyone
chunks.text:
- Lenny buckets every great newsletter by the job it does for readers: help me parent, cook, understand tech or the world, inspire me, entertain me.
- There is room for many winners in each category, so you needn't be the best in the world, but you should strive to be.
- His own job: help readers get better at work, specifically building and growing their product and career. Do it well and consistently and they keep reading.
- Two questions to start:
  1. Who exactly is your audience? Think of one specific person and what they'd find extremely useful.
  2. What concrete job are you doing for them (entertainment, making money, inspiration, understanding the world)?

chunks.heading: Choosing a topic: follow your energy
chunks.text:
- Writing consistently is a grind, and you may spend years thinking and writing about one topic. If you aren't genuinely curious you "will create a job for yourself that you will hate."
- Three filters, in order:
  1. Follow your energy: which topics give you energy and which sap it. Do more of the former.
  2. Base it on real-life experience. The best newsletters come from people with deep experience in the space. Look for the center of the Venn diagram of your skills and background.
  3. Pay attention to what people value. He puts this third on purpose, because many people start here and it's a trap. Look at what people ask you advice about and where you find pull.
- Find a niche (a "personal monopoly") but don't go too narrow, or you'll get bored.
- He deliberately stayed broad (building products, growth, career, startups) instead of just product management, because he doesn't care about PM that much. It made the newsletter harder to explain but kept him excited.
- Rule of thumb: first get 1,000 people to think your newsletter is the best in the world. At 1,000 paid subscribers he could make a real living from it.

chunks.heading: Spend more time on each piece, and nothing else
chunks.text:
- Lenny says 99% of content isn't very good, so there is always room for better. You have to rise above what exists, and that takes work.
- He spends a median of 10 hours per post. Some take hundreds of hours, like his B2B startups series. He sees a strong correlation between time spent and how well a post does.
- That's why it's hard to do well alongside a full-time job.
- Any newsletter time that isn't writing, or making the writing better, is wasted. Many writers optimize their site, build a brand or craft a big strategy, and their growth slows.
- He values Substack because he can focus exclusively on writing while they handle everything else.
- Substack's recommendations feature is, in his view, one of the most impactful growth features in history and changed his trajectory. Over 9,000 other newsletters recommend his, not from anything he did actively. It's the quality-spreads-itself point again.
- He says that because of recommendations there has never been a better time to start a newsletter.

chunks.heading: Writing craft: cut 30-50% and add something new
chunks.text:
- With no writing background, the biggest lesson he learned was "cut, cut, and cut some more." He credits On Writing Well, Nobody Wants to Read Your Sh*t and Several Short Sentences About Writing.
- Tactics:
  - Cut every word that isn't absolutely necessary.
  - Make the intro 50% shorter and get to the meat fast. He quotes Wes Kao: "Start your story right before you get eaten by the bear."
  - In nearly every guest post he edits, deleting the first paragraph of the first draft makes it stronger.
- Contribute something new. Most writing rehashes what's been said. Ask what new ideas, insights and concepts you add.
- Most of his top posts came from tens of hours of primary research that surfaced insights not shared before. He's doing a lot of work on the reader's behalf.
- That requires real experience. He keeps doing advisory work on the side so he doesn't lose touch with the real work.
- If you're considering going all-in on content, he advises doing the work for many years first (e.g. 10), which also builds career optionality. He endorses Elena Verna's point that a leadership title should be a step toward career optionality (for her, solopreneurship with her brain as the product), not the end goal.

chunks.heading: Cadence: pick one you can sustain for years
chunks.text:
- A deadline is an essential forcing function. He picked a cadence, shared it publicly and tried hard to stick to it.
- Weekly is a good starting point. People often publish too fast and burn out. He can sustainably write one great post a week.
- Daily, monthly, or even one incredible post a year can all work depending on goals. The key is a cadence you can keep up for years.

chunks.heading: Just start, and the real downsides
chunks.text:
- Quote he cites from Joan Didion: "I don't know what I think until I write it down." He writes to mold a rough idea, not to share a finished thought.
- Start with something you want to get out of your head, write it, share it, and don't overthink it. Post on Substack or similar so you start collecting email addresses in case it takes off.
- His first public piece was a write-up of what he learned at Airbnb, which people found valuable, so he wrote more.
- Downsides he is candid about: no PTO, benefits or 401(k) match, and nobody to write if he's sick. For parental leave he worked doubly hard for a couple of months to build a content backlog. In theory he must write an awesome newsletter every week for the rest of his life.
- Despite that, he calls it the most fulfilling work of his life and highly recommends it. His mission is to help people get better at work and increase net happiness in the world.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Lenny reflects on two years of podcasting (10M downloads, 3M YouTube views). He covers niching down to 100 superfans, interviewing craft, landing dream guests via cold outreach, his tool and hardware stack, outsourcing production, and why YouTube drives most discovery.

chunks.heading: Start with 100 people who love it, then widen
chunks.text:
Lenny's founding podcast principle: instead of making something many people like, make something 100 people love. He says it is the same advice as starting a company.
- 100 sounds tiny, but most podcasts can't reach it. A small focus lets you give those people exactly what they want.
- Once you have that foothold, fans tell friends, better guests say yes, and you improve at the craft.
- "Love" matters because you must displace another show in someone's rotation, and they only do that for a show they keep loving.
- For his own show, he knew at least 100 people would want a product management podcast, so he made it the best one for them. Then he expanded into sales, storytelling, design, fear and productivity, and the audience grew with him.

chunks.heading: Aim for B+ at the start, and don't pre-record too much
chunks.text:
Lenny says a podcast boils down to one job: create a great audio file, meaning A+ content and A+ audio quality. He does not think you need to start at A+.
- What got him over the hump was low pressure: basic equipment, audio only (YouTube came later), and telling early guests it was an experiment to scrap if it went poorly.
- His advice is to aim for B+ and work up. Many famous tech podcasts had weak first episodes.
- He pre-recorded about 10 episodes before launch and calls that a mistake: after launch you learn what resonates and spot audio, video and speaking issues, but the first batch can't be improved. He recommends recording only three to five ahead.

chunks.heading: Interviewing tactics
chunks.text:
Lenny's interview tips (he says he has much left to learn):
- **Be the listener's home base.** Mirror back what the guest says, ask the questions the listener has in mind, and reframe when the conversation gets complicated or tangential. Don't interrupt, because "some of the best stuff comes at the end."
- **Get to the gold quickly.** Spend little time on backgrounds and intros unless the guest is famous or wildly fascinating. Listeners want to learn something.
- **Look for "dropped facts."** Guests mention something interesting offhand and move on. Come back to it; they often want to talk about it. He learned this from a book on interviewing.
- **Prepare.** He spends one to two hours per guest (more for famous ones): reading their posts and social media, listening to past interviews, exploring LinkedIn.
- **Just ask the next question.** Skip "So interesting!" and "Thank you for sharing" unless you have something to add. He points to Tyler Cowen as maybe the best interviewer.
- **Go off-script.** Follow unexpected threads; guests don't mind, and you can cut it in post.
- **Keep your ego in check.** "Don't try to sound smart. Make your guests sound smart."
- **Be yourself.** Early on he imitated hosts he admired; things improved when he stopped.

He sends every guest these questions beforehand:
1. Are there 2-3 topics you'd especially love to talk about?
2. Any frameworks, methods or processes you've found especially useful that others may find useful too?
3. Anything you have a contrarian opinion about that would be fun to share?
4. Any fun, surprising or wild stories from your career or life?
5. Anything you haven't shared elsewhere that could make the conversation extra-special?
6. If this were the one episode you'd send anyone who wants to learn how you think and operate, what would you want in it?

chunks.heading: How he finds and books guests
chunks.text:
- **Work backward from a wishlist** of dream guests and slowly find a connection to each, the same way the best products are built from the ideal experience. Current wishlist names include Satya Nadella, Tony Fadell, Jony Ive, Gwynne Shotwell and Nikita Bier.
- **Mix famous and under-the-radar guests.** People won't listen to names they don't recognize, but known people are already everywhere. The mix brings listeners in while surfacing wisdom-rich unknowns. He also makes an effort to include a more diverse mix of guests than the typical tech podcast.
- **Most people say yes**, often to a simple cold DM or email, though not the most high-profile on day one.
- **Use your unfair advantage.** His is seven years at Airbnb plus newsletter collaborators.
- **Say no to most inbound requests.** He gets one to three a day, many from PR people. Some became great episodes, but it is the least useful channel.
- **Keep trying.** Brian Chesky took a year to agree and is now the most listened-to episode.

How his most popular guests came on:
- Brian Chesky: knew him from Airbnb, floated it around big launches, agreed a year later.
- Shreyas Doshi and Marty Cagan: wishlist from day one, approached before the podcast was live (Shreyas pitched as first guest alongside Julie Zhuo; Marty by cold email).
- Elizabeth Stone: a friend's introduction, before she became CTO of Netflix.
- Gustaf Alströmer: former Airbnb colleague, then YC Partner, via email.
- Nikhyl Singhal: suggested by past guests; introduction from one of them.
- Matt Mochary: cold DM.
- Ethan Smith: several founders credited his SEO work; asked for an intro.
- Ethan Evans and Geoff Charles: collaborated on popular newsletter posts first.
- Marily Nika: Maven reached out to pitch her.
- Claire Hughes Johnson: replied "Come on the podcast?" to her tweet about her book; her people followed up. He says "This method works really well."

chunks.heading: Tech stack and studio setup
chunks.text:
Software:
- Recording: Riverside (what most podcasters use); Podcastle as backup; Descript for solo portions like ads and intros.
- Editing: Descript (his editor uses it too).
- Hosting: Substack, which makes sense if you run a significant Substack newsletter. Alternatives: Spotify for Podcasters (free, limited analytics), Transistor, Simplecast.
- Analytics: Podstatus for charts, Chartable for general analytics, plus the host's built-in data. He says podcast analytics "stinks."
- Website: Podpage (behind LennysPodcast.com).

Starter hardware: Shure MV7 USB mic, Sony MDR7506 headphones, Opal camera (he is an investor), Lume Cube Edge light, and a portable tripod as mic holder (he suggests trying a few options).

Six months in, he took the Dream Studio course and upgraded: Canon EOS M50 Mark II with a 22mm f2 lens, a three-light setup (key light with soft box, hair light, side light), a teleprompter rig so he looks into the camera, quiet Logitech keyboard and mouse, and an Elgato deck for muting and DND. His favorite lesson: the more work your studio seems to have taken, the more professional it looks. For the room, he cites Descript's advice: pick a smaller room with soft surfaces (carpet, curtains, upholstery) and avoid large empty spaces and hard surfaces that echo.

chunks.heading: Outsourced help and per-episode workflow
chunks.text:
His team:
- Pen Name for core production (editing, titles, thumbnails, show notes).
- Supermix for Instagram, TikTok and Shorts clips and trailers.
- An EA from Double for guest scheduling.
- A newer researcher for famous guests.
- Earlier, an audio engineer, Tommy Harron, when it was audio-only.

What the help saves:
- Editing used to take hours; now 10 to 30 minutes to review the producer's work.
- Titles, thumbnails and show notes used to take 1-2 hours; now 10 to 20 minutes to approve, often after many title and thumbnail iterations.
- Guest prep: a week before, guests get detailed instructions (no AirPods, avoid bright windows, turn on DND), an offer of a free mic to keep, and an optional audio/video setup call.
- Guests review the final audio, video, title, description, show notes, thumbnail and shareable assets before publishing.
- Organization: Notion production calendar, Coda for questions, Slack, Google Calendar.

Time per episode is about 4 to 5 hours total:
- Schedule with guest: 30 minutes.
- Prep questions: 1-2 hours, with a draft agenda sent to the guest 3-7 days ahead.
- Record interview: 1.5-2 hours in Riverside.
- Record guest intro: 15 minutes. Record ads: 15 minutes each.
- Ship and promote (including X and LinkedIn posts): 10-30 minutes.

chunks.heading: YouTube as the discovery channel
chunks.text:
Lenny says YouTube is a must eventually: "There's no better way for new people to discover your podcast than through YouTube's algorithms."
- Over half of his views come from YouTube sending new people his way; he cites 39.5% + 15.1% + 7.8% = 62% from YouTube's discovery features.
- He started about six months in, at his producer's urging, and wishes he'd started earlier, though he says not to let that stop you from starting; video can be added later.
- Video means more work, especially editing, but it enables TikTok, Instagram and Shorts clips (he mentions Opus.pro for automating clips) and posts on X and LinkedIn, plus diversification across platforms.
- Results at the time: over 10M downloads, 3M YouTube views, a top 10 global technology podcast, and a 5.0 average rating across nearly 4,000 reviews.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Lenny's framing intro to Jackie Bavaro's guest post on becoming a senior PM. He lays out the three career milestones (senior IC, manager of PMs, director) and argues the first takes longest, so speeding it up matters most. The detailed strategy, autonomy and nuance framework is Jackie's, not Lenny's.

chunks.heading: Senior PM: three differentiators (strategy, autonomy, nuance)
chunks.text: Lenny shares Jackie Bavaro's framing, "the best framing I've come across" for leveling up to Senior PM. Senior PMs aren't much better at the regular PM's craft. The biggest differences are behind the scenes: teammates who only see specs and product choices may not understand why someone got promoted. The three differentiators are strategy, autonomy and nuance.

chunks.heading: PM career ladder and how long each step takes
chunks.text:
Lenny says the PM career is "unnecessarily shrouded in mystery". The path has three milestones after starting as an IC:
1. Become a "senior" IC PM.
2. Become a manager of PMs (Group PM or Product Lead).
3. Become a manager of PM managers (Director).

His estimate of time per step:
- Entry-level PM to Senior PM: median about 3 years. This is the longest step.
- Senior PM to manager of PMs: 1-2 years.
- Manager of PMs to Director: 2-3 years.

His conclusion: accelerating the move to Senior PM has the most impact on the overall PM career.

chunks.heading: Strategy: the senior PM develops and evangelizes it
chunks.text:
Senior PMs are responsible for a strategy that leads to meaningful customer and business success. They paint an inspiring future, find the best path to it, make sure people understand and agree, and convince executives to spin up the teams they need.

- Newer PMs prioritize by how much incremental value work adds to the product.
- Senior PMs prioritize by how much work moves the product toward the long-term vision.
- Example: the top-requested feature may delight current customers, but features that expand the customer base can be more strategic.

How to start:
- You don't need a promotion to create a strategy. Propose what the team should work on next.
- Make space for it. Block off half a day (Jackie jokes: pretend you're attending a Zoom wedding).
- If the engineering team needs you too much to find time, first level up core PM skills so day-to-day work goes faster.
- The strategy doesn't have to be perfect. It will change as you learn, but having one improves your moves now.

chunks.heading: Three parts of a strategy: vision, framework, roadmap
chunks.text:
A strategy has (1) a vision, (2) a strategic framework and (3) a roadmap. Start with whichever appeals most.

- **Vision:** Storyboard future customers using the future product and show how much better their lives are than the status quo. Model it on an infomercial, spending time on how painful things are today. Include a few strategic insights or bets so it feels believable. Example: "Ouch! I stepped on a lego brick... Imagine a future where cleaning up toys is a game and your kids race to be the fastest!"
- **Strategic framework:** Write down the target market, their pain points, and the bets or differentiators you believe will win. Write alternative approaches and why yours is better. Example: enter the positive-parenting market with a fun game that solves a top pain point (putting away toys, picky eating, staying in bed), then expand into other pain points. A game rather than a tool or book expands the market beyond parents to anyone buying the child a gift.
- **Roadmap:** Write a rough plan for the next few years, grouped into strategic themes. Then imagine someone asking "why?" about each part; the answers become the start of your framework. Example: this quarter launch the cleaning game, next quarter the picky-food game, next half two more games, next year license new games to expand faster.

chunks.heading: Autonomy and the template for sharing work with your manager
