chunks.text:
Senior PMs can run a team independently: keep it running, work with stakeholders, resolve conflicts and ship successful products without their manager guiding them. They ask for lots of input, and they know when to question a direction they were handed instead of treating it as fixed.

- Autonomy is also about earning the trust to be allowed to work independently, through proactive communication and a track record of successful launches.
- The irony: high autonomy can make trust harder to earn, because your manager doesn't see your good decisions and hard challenges. You must share them intentionally.
- Sharing can backfire: you sound self-promotional, your manager thinks you're stuck, or they're frustrated you're not asking for advice.

The template that avoids these problems:
1. "Hi manager, let me tell you about a challenge I ran into ___"
2. "Here's how I'm thinking of handling it (or did handle it) ___"
3. "Any thoughts?"

It shows the challenge and how you handled it while opening the door to feedback. If the solution was good, the manager says "Great work!". If not, proactively asking shows you can be trusted to seek input when needed. Use it in your next one-on-one.

chunks.heading: Nuance: structured reasoning when "it depends"
chunks.text:
The more senior you get, the more decisions have "it depends" as the right answer. Senior PMs:
- Recognize these decisions and reason through them in a structured way, without falling back on rigid frameworks.
- Understand goals and constraints of departments across the company and don't assume their own team's goals outrank others'.
- Decide quickly, laying out their thought process in minutes thanks to product expertise and rich mental models.
- Rapidly pick the most important problems in an ambiguous area and drive them to tangible impact.
- Have constructive discussions with leaders, explaining tradeoffs and defending a recommendation without becoming defensive.

chunks.heading: Practicing nuance: example and exercise
chunks.text:
Teammates and stakeholders are the best guides. Take their concerns seriously and look for hidden complexity: when would they be right, and what information might they have?

Example: launching a feature, the head of customer support complains it can't be controlled by her team's operational scripts. Instead of brushing her off with "I'll update the scripts after launch", keep asking until you understand why. You might learn that without scripts, reps take longer on tickets, which lowers customer satisfaction, which correlates with cancellations. You might then delay the launch until the scripts are updated.

Exercise: when you make a decision, write "It depends. If X, then A is the best choice. If Y, then B is the best choice. I think this situation is X, so A." Share the longer answer only when it's useful, so you don't annoy teammates.

chunks.heading: Three things to start today
chunks.text:
1. Block time on your calendar for strategy.
2. Use the autonomy template in your next meeting with your manager.
3. Look for the "it depends" answer to practice on.

Jackie and Gayle go deeper in their book *Cracking the PM Career*.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Lenny explains how to tell if PM is right for you, the four common routes into a first PM role, and the seven skills to build, in order of importance. Advice is drawn from his Airbnb transition from engineering to product and from helping others make the move.

chunks.heading: Deciding if product management is the right role
chunks.text:
- Lenny calls PM "often a thankless, nerve-racking, and all-consuming" role, but says that when it works, "you feel like you were born to do it." He started as an engineer, moved into product seven years before this 2019 post (one of Airbnb's first few PMs), and says he couldn't imagine another role now.
- Become a PM if you are fulfilled by:
  - solving problems for users and for your team
  - driving business growth
  - working closely with many kinds of people
  - developing a strategy
  - getting things done
  - leading through influence, not authority
  - communicating often and broadly
  - making decisions
  - creating great experiences
  - being organized, detail oriented and prepared
- Do not become a PM if you are primarily fulfilled by:
  - appreciation
  - having your way
  - being left alone
  - always being right
  - designing or building things yourself
  - everyone liking you
  - flow states
  - avoiding meetings, email or people
- You don't need to match every item on either list, but the gist should feel right.

chunks.heading: Four common paths into product management
chunks.text:
Lenny has helped people move into product from Operations, Data Science and Finance. He says every PM working today made this transition in some form.

1. **Internal transition at a large company.** Usually the easiest and fastest. It needs three things: an internal transfer process, a chance to demonstrate the PM skills, and an internal PM champion (generally your new manager). If two of the three exist, find a way to make the third happen. Otherwise pursue another path.
2. **Junior PM role at a large company.** Probably the most common route, but limited to companies with APM or internship programs. It is increasingly common for MBA graduates, though he says an MBA is not necessary. Without an MBA, he suggests programs like Product School and General Assembly, communities like PMHQ, and practicing the core skills in your current job. The key is clearly showing you are smart, driven and have raw strengths in a handful of the core skills.
3. **Joining a startup with a burning need.** Needs connections with founders, a lot of hustle, and delivering when given the chance. Look for jobs on HN and AngelList, find ways to meet founders, and build the core skills. A strong growth mindset matters because you learn the job on the fly. You can start as a founding PM or transition into it later; Airbnb's original head of product got in this way.
4. **Starting your own company.** The most work-intensive path and rarely planned, but it is how Lenny got into product. CEOs often become PMs after an acquisition, and founders can take the PM role as the company grows. He wouldn't recommend prioritizing this route.

chunks.heading: The seven core PM skills, in order of importance
chunks.text:
Lenny says the role varies by company and team, but these seven are the most crucial to build early. Don't try to be incredible at all of them: "double down on your strengths and fill in the gaps."

1. Strategy: take any problem and develop a strategy to resolve it
2. Execution: getting things done
3. Communication
4. Leadership through influence
5. Decision-making informed by data
6. Building great products and having taste
7. Always being prepared

His bonus skills to build over time:
- **Vision:** set your team's north star, articulate it, and get buy-in.
- **Business sense:** understand what drives the business and build the right things in the right order.
- **An obsession with impact:** connect everything you do to its effect on the business and customers.
- **A growth mindset:** see yourself and others as capable of improving.

chunks.heading: Strategy and execution
chunks.text:
**Strategy.**
- A PM's job is to marshal the team's resources to drive business value. The team is handed problems (grow adoption, reduce churn, increase conversion) and the PM guides the team to make the problem smaller.
- A strategy paired with a clear vision is the route from problem to solution.
- He endorses Richard Rumelt's definition: "A good strategy is a set of actions that is credible, coherent, and focused on overcoming the biggest hurdle(s) in achieving a particular objective."
- Ways to build it:
  - Ask the best PMs you know to walk you through the vision and strategy of a recent initiative.
  - Take a problem at your company (or a friend's) and break it into solvable chunks with a framework such as an opportunity-solution tree.
  - Learn the difference between vision, mission and strategy.
  - Practice Amazon's working-backwards approach.
  - Read *Good Strategy, Bad Strategy* by Rumelt.

**Execution.**
- A PM who is good at nothing else but execution is valuable; a team with a PM who can't execute is better off without that PM.
- Tactically this means a roadmap everyone is aligned behind, setting and hitting deadlines, and "ruthlessly unblocking blockers."
- His advice for new PMs is to start practicing immediately, because you only learn it by doing.
  - Ask a friendly PM to take the project-management duties on one of their projects. Never call a product manager a project manager.
  - Study people who are good at shipping: how they run meetings, handle issues as they arise, and keep the team aligned.
  - Learn OKRs and goal setting (*Measure What Matters* by John Doerr).
  - Regularly ask, "how am I going to move my product forward today?"

chunks.heading: Communication and leadership through influence
chunks.text:
**Communication.**
- "Engineers code, designers produce designs, and product managers … communicate." Everything a PM does happens through writing, speaking and meetings. Quoting Boz: "communication is the job." You can never be too good at it, and it is very hard to over-communicate.
- Emails: look at it at least once before sending; there is always something to cut or clarify.
- Docs:
  - Get feedback from at least one person before sharing widely.
  - Keep formatting clean and consistent.
  - Close out comments before sharing with execs.
  - Make it easy to scan.
- Meetings:
  - Put the primary goal in the invite, ideally with an agenda.
  - Invite as few people as possible.
  - Point it out if a meeting isn't productive.
  - Leave with clear action items, and follow up by email with action items and owners.
- Presentations:
  - Check you need a presentation rather than an email.
  - Make clear whether you want a decision, feedback, or to share information.
  - Get feedback first and keep it short: "no one ever wished that presentation went longer."
- Storytelling is a meta-skill that improves all of the above. He recommends the situation-complication-resolution framework for laying out a pitch.

**Leadership through influence.**
- PMs generally have all the responsibility without actual authority. To succeed you must build trust, make decisions while giving everyone a voice, and keep morale up regardless of circumstances.
- The best PMs become the de-facto team leaders, "not because of any actual authority, but because they help everyone on the team do the best work of their lives."
- Ways to build it:
  - Watch how PMs get things done without managing anyone.
  - Lead a small project, ideally with a PM mentor.
  - Build team culture with fun rituals, outings and a lasting team identity.

chunks.heading: Decisions, product taste and being prepared
chunks.text:
**Decisions informed by data.**
- Teams look to the PM to reach decisions; expect dozens of them daily.
- Two aids: a clear set of principles the team aligned on beforehand, and hard data, both quantitative and qualitative. "The less opinions you have to rely on, and the more facts you have at your disposal, the easier your life gets."
- Ways to build it:
  - Study how Airbnb, Uber, Netflix and Pinterest decide through experimentation, and launch an experiment or two where you work.
  - Watch how fast successful leaders decide, what they ask first, and how they explain their reasoning.
  - Always have your own point of view, but be ready to change your mind on new information.
  - Learn Type-1 versus Type-2 decisions.

**Building great products and taste.**
- This means building an instinct for what makes a product great, balancing art and science, and working well with other disciplines.
- He endorses Merci Victoria Grace's line: "Product intuition is a skill: it is the observation of human behavior, trained by data, and applied to software."
- Ways to build it:
  - Build and ship a product yourself or with friends, solving a small problem for someone (or yourself). "There's absolutely no better way to learn than to do it yourself."
  - Notice what makes you like or dislike a product and keep notes.
  - Learn design thinking.

**Always being prepared.**
- He calls this one of the most underrated and valuable PM traits, the "I got this" aura: everyone should feel that if you take something on, it will get done and done exceptionally well.
- It comes from being detail oriented, being more prepared than anyone else, and keeping a higher bar than those around you. He started off very bad at it and saw a lot of career growth once he prioritized it.
- Tactics:
  - Never come to a meeting without spending a few minutes preparing.
  - Keep a high bar for everything, including the communication practices above.
  - Build "spidey sense": look around corners, ask what could go wrong, and plan contingencies.
  - Learn from very well-organized people by asking what they concretely do to stay on top of things.

chunks.heading: How to move forward
chunks.text:
- Lenny boils the PM job into four words: "Figure out what's next."
- His advice: start developing and demonstrating the seven skills, then push forward on one or two of the four paths. Read, process and put learnings into action, since creativity is part of being a PM.
- Be as prepared as possible for when an opportunity arises. The transition may take a year, two or three. If you're not getting anywhere, try another route.
- Meet PMs, listen to their feedback and act on it. "If you truly believe this is the right role for you, find a way."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Lenny lays out seven ways people become aware of a new product, from friend referrals to outbound sales, with examples and the conditions under which each channel works. He closes with a five-step process for picking where to invest based on your early adopters.

chunks.heading: Seven channels people use to discover new products
chunks.text:
Lenny posits that people become aware of new products in exactly seven ways:

1. Friends or colleagues (e.g., an invite)
2. Browsing online, organically (e.g., SEO)
3. Browsing online and seeing a promotion (e.g., Facebook ads)
4. Out and about, organically (e.g., a store shelf)
5. Out and about and seeing a promotion (e.g., a billboard)
6. At home, seeing a promotion (e.g., direct mail)
7. Someone reaching out to you (e.g., sales)

He frames the list as a way to develop a growth strategy beyond the obvious channels like Facebook ads and SEO.

chunks.heading: Word of mouth from friends and colleagues
chunks.text:
- Lenny calls this "the oldest growth channel in the book." It can be free and organic ("I LOVE my new spatula, check it out!") or incentivized through a referral program or even an MLM program.
- He says it is "by far the cheapest and best way to grow if you can pull it off."
- Invest in it if the product is innately better with friends or colleagues (Snapchat, Slack), is innately fun to share (travel photos, homes for sale, crime nearby), or is remarkable, meaning "something worth remarking about."
- He warns that most products do not grow this way and that it is "nearly impossible to layer on" if the product isn't naturally suited to it, so founders shouldn't be sad if it doesn't work.

chunks.heading: Organic discovery while browsing online
chunks.text:
- The next cheapest way to be discovered: people on the internet talking about the product organically. This includes social posts, press, influencers sharing unprompted, forum comments, Wirecutter articles and organic search results.
- Products that grew primarily this way: Clubhouse (people on Twitter), e.l.f. Cosmetics (TikTok influencers raving about it), Zillow (press articles), Animal Crossing (people posting on Facebook).
- Bet on organic traffic if:
  - The product is remarkable and people are naturally excited to share it (e.g., Instapot).
  - People are already searching for the product category, such as Googling "best CRM" or "best credit card."
  - The product or company makes a good story that reporters would want to cover.

chunks.heading: Paid promotion while browsing online
chunks.text:
- Covers ads (Facebook, Google, Twitter, YouTube, Instagram), paid influencers, affiliate programs and channel partners.
- Companies that grew primarily through this channel: Wish, Casper, Calm, Blue Apron, Hims.
- Most effective when:
  - Customers aren't naturally looking for the product (e.g., Impact Gum), so you have to go to them.
  - The product generates revenue directly from new users (a purchase or subscription), which can fund more ads (e.g., jeans).

chunks.heading: Offline discovery: shelves, products in the wild, and out-of-home ads
chunks.text:
**Organic, out and about**
- People stumble on products in the world: a new cereal on the shelf, a Tesla driving by, a Peloton in a friend's home.
- Most CPG products grow this way via shelf placement, as do retailers (foot traffic) and some consumer electronics (the white iPod headphones).
- Works for physical products that look great, are prevalent, and are impulse purchases.

**Paid out-of-home (OOH)**
- Billboards, bus ads, taxi ads, backs of trucks, flyers: you pay to reach people who spend time around a location.
- ROI is traditionally hard to measure, but done well it can "build a massive brand moat" (Nike, Apple, Coke).
- It is also a way to target a specific audience in a specific place. Example: Brex used billboards and bus stops in SF to reach founders.
- Best for companies that need to build strong brands, sell to a broad mainstream audience, or want to make a splash.

chunks.heading: In-home promotions: TV, mail, podcasts and newsletters
chunks.text:
- Goes well beyond TV: direct mail, ads on packaging, flyers inside packaging, radio, podcast ads, newspaper and magazine ads.
- Direct mail has become a staple of DTC growth strategies, and podcast and newsletter ads are an increasingly popular way to reach new customers.
- Best suited to:
  - Subscription companies or high average order value (AOV) products that can sustain the cost of this advertising.
  - Companies that get a lot of value from geo-targeting.
  - Companies that can be creative with the platforms (e.g., Geico).
  - DTC brands.

chunks.heading: Outbound sales
chunks.text:
- Someone comes to you to pitch a product, by phone, email, DM, LinkedIn message or door-to-door.
- Large enterprises grow mainly this way (Oracle, Workday and ADP each have outbound teams reaching out daily), as do telemarketing- and door-to-door-driven businesses like Cutco and many insurance companies.
- Best suited to products that:
  - Have high AOV and high LTV, to support the cost of a sales team.
  - Require hand-holding to be successful.
  - Are just getting started and looking for initial customers.
  - Began with a bottom-up sales motion and are ready to layer on sales.
- For founders doing sales, he highly recommends the book Founding Sales.

chunks.heading: Five-step process for choosing where to invest
chunks.text:
Lenny suggests working through these steps to pick a channel:

1. **Who are your early adopters?** e.g., middle-aged men in the Midwest, new dog owners in cities, HR leaders at growth-stage companies.
2. **Where do they spend time?** A community, newsletter, event or physical location.
3. **What's the quickest way to get in front of them?** e.g., a mailer, a LinkedIn DM, a billboard, Facebook ads.
4. **What's the cheapest way to get in front of them?** e.g., shelf placement, encouraging existing users to send invites, micro-influencers.
5. **How can you stand out?** What's remarkable about the product, story or vision? What big problem do you solve? What's most surprising about the offering?

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Lenny surveyed about two dozen top investors on what counts as good and great growth by stage. Early on, investors ignore small-base MoM percentages and watch time to $1M ARR, retention, and efficiency. For consumer, engagement and retention beat revenue. Most of the quotes are from the investors, not Lenny.

chunks.heading: Early-stage B2B: ramp to $1m ARR matters more than month-over-month growth
chunks.text:
- Lenny asked about two dozen investors what counts as GOOD and GREAT growth by business stage. Across all of them, early-stage month-over-month (MoM) growth was not the headline metric.
- Reason given: percentages on a tiny base mean little. In Kimberly Tan's words (a16z), "10% vs. 20% growth at $100K ARR isn't substantial."
- Investors would rather see accelerating MoM growth (for example 10% to 12% to 15%) as a sign of momentum.
- If a MoM benchmark is needed below $1m ARR, answers typically fell in the 15%-25% range.
- What early-stage B2B investors focus on instead is how fast the company ramps to $1m ARR after going live.

chunks.heading: Benchmarks: 0 to $1m ARR after launch
chunks.text:
- Lenny's summary: getting to $1m ARR within a year of launch is GOOD; getting there in three quarters (9 months) is GREAT.
- John Luttig (Founders Fund): "If you grew to $500k ARR in 3mo post-launch, that's more impressive than $1m in 24mo post-launch." He treats 0 to $1m ARR in 12 months or less as great. Exceptions exist, since not every company's success is measured in ARR since launch (Figma, open source).
- Sandhya Hegde (Unusual Ventures): "You start the growth clock the month you go GA."
- Grace Ge (Menlo): "Velocity is everything post-launch." As a company matures, it is less about convincing investors to dream the dream and more about proving it is real, executable and monetizable.

chunks.heading: Timing your launch strategically
chunks.text:
- Once you have numbers, investors scrutinize them. Caitlin Bolnick Rellas (CRV): "The great irony is that once you start having numbers, investors start to really care what those numbers are."
- Luttig: launching with very little traction is worse than being pre-launch, because it shows the market or value prop is already demonstrably weak. "No data is better than bad/small data."
- Takeaway Lenny draws: be deliberate about when you launch, because the growth clock and the scrutiny start then.

chunks.heading: Slow starts can be forgiven if takeoff is strong
chunks.text:
- Some investors don't care how long it took to get going, only how fast it grows once it does. One example: a business that grew revenue from $500k to $5m this year is attractive whether it launched 1 or 5 years ago. That investor noted some of their biggest winners took several years to find product-market fit.
- Kanyi Maqubela (Kindred): speed from $500K to $5M ARR has been less predictive-of-nothing than 0 to $1M; rather, it is more predictive than 0 to $1M. It indicates "minimum viable durability" of revenue that compounds over a longer period.
- During the 0 to $1M phase, companies are often still optimizing retention, experimenting with efficiency and segmenting customers.

chunks.heading: Without fast ARR growth, show retention and efficiency
chunks.text:
- Rebecca Kaden (USV): revenue growth is an output of customer love and acquisition efficiency. The most important health factors are cohorted revenue retention and/or purchase behavior (ideally U-shaped cohorts where net revenue retention rises over a year) and marketing spend/revenue.
- Another investor looks for a leading indicator of ARR that compounds at a high rate: very productive salespeople, oddly short sales cycles, customers who rave and tell friends (typically giving oddly low CAC).
- Ellen Chisa (Boldstart): "It's a huge mistake to focus on the growth number before getting retention." Early numbers are small enough to hit "great" by brute force, which won't translate to continued growth and can leave you worse off than building fundamentals first.
- Quality of ARR matters as much as rate. Arra Malekzadeh (Craft) looks at the components (new, retained, expansion, resurrection, contraction, churn), customer concentration, sales efficiency, CAC payback, and new ARR versus sales and marketing spend.

chunks.heading: Early-stage consumer: engagement and retention before revenue
chunks.text:
- For B2C, early investors look at intensity of use, sharing and retention rather than revenue growth.
- Mike Vernal (Sequoia): "For consumer, I focus on engagement and retention first and foremost. >50% DAU/MAU or >50% D30 retention is excellent. If you have both of those, only then do I worry about whether you can grow it."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Lenny explains how he stumbled into full-time writing after leaving Airbnb by tracking what energized him, and how he runs his newsletter: topic selection, a dense-advice writing style, Substack's discovery value, and niche opportunities. He also covers his angel investing and personal finance approach.

chunks.heading: Lenny's path from Airbnb to writing full-time
chunks.text:
- After leaving Airbnb in 2019, Lenny gave himself 6 months to tinker. His rule: "do more of what gave me energy, and do less of what sapped me of energy." After every call, project and meeting he noted whether he felt more or less energized.
- His plans were A) start a company, B) advise full-time, C) join a startup, D) return to a big company as a PM. "Not even Plan Z was to write full-time."
- He ran two-week sprints: write three work goals and three personal goals, email them to three friends, then circle back at the end. The goals kept pulling him toward writing.
- Two wise friends pointed this out, so he leaned into writing and paused the rest. He called the path "Project: Avoid getting a real job," aiming for low stress and good-enough income.
- It became the most he has ever earned. He says he makes more than he did as an Airbnb product lead, stock included.
- He describes himself by what he does (newsletter, podcast, job board, angel investing) rather than calling himself a "writer."

chunks.heading: How Lenny chooses topics and writes each post
chunks.text:
- He keeps a list of about 50 topics and a rough plan for the next 2-3 posts. Each week he picks the one he's most excited about: "I optimize for my own curiosity vs. what people want, because that always leads to the best stuff."
- Every post is framed as a question, since it's an advice column. It opens with a concrete, direct reader question, such as "what is a good retention rate" or "how did the biggest consumer apps get their first 1,000 users."
- Each topic gets a Coda page where he dumps bullets, quotes and stats.
- For expert quotes, he lists the people he wants and emails each individually. This needs 2-3 weeks of lead time.
- For his own research, he throws findings in messy and keeps adding.
- Then he looks for patterns, frameworks and simple ways to share conclusions, drafts the post, and adds charts, tables and visuals.
- He rereads dozens of times, emails himself a copy to see it with fresh eyes, and has a copyeditor review it. A designer sometimes makes a graphic. It's ready around the 50th read.
- Median time is 10 hours per post, ranging from 3 hours to 100+.

chunks.heading: Writing principle: density over "writing"
chunks.text:
- He didn't set out to be a writer. He focused on "a density of high-quality, easy to understand, advice."
- He says people fill writing with long intros, useless context and pontification. His rule: get to the point, synthesize clearly, and get out of your own way.
- Books he credits: "On Writing Well" (cut, cut, cut some more) and Steven Pressfield's "Nobody Wants to Read Your Sh*t."

chunks.heading: What performs best
chunks.text:
- Time invested correlates strongly with performance. All the 100+ hour posts are in his top 10.
- Exceptions: two of the top five (Favorite Templates, and Mission → Vision → Strategy → Goals → Roadmap → Task) took under five hours.
- Many top-20 posts are guest posts. They take much less time (mostly editing and refining with the author) and are among the most popular, which he calls a win-win.
- He calls a paid newsletter "the ultimate meritocracy": people subscribe, pay and tell friends if it's useful, and unsubscribe when it isn't.

chunks.heading: Why he stays on Substack despite the fees
chunks.text:
- Substack's discovery features, especially recommendations, drive 12% of his new paid subscribers and 78% of his free subscribers.
- Their fee is 10%, so "they now pay for themselves."
- He has seen people leave to avoid fees and then see growth slow. He prefers optimizing for long-term growth over "eeking out every last %."
- Time on anything other than great content is wasted, and time spent drives quality, so he values not handling administration.
- If starting again, he'd change little: maybe charge sooner, and pick a better name than Substack's default.
- Surprises: nobody was doing this well and there's still lots of open space; how long he's kept going; how fulfilling it is (at least one message a day from someone whose career benefited); and how lucrative it is.

chunks.heading: Newsletter niches and the math
chunks.text:
- Four jobs to be done in newsletters: entertain people, help people make money, help people be better at work or life (his bucket), and inform people (news).
- His advice: "Pick a niche and pick a JTBD and there's an opportunity there."
- The math: 1,000 paid subscribers at $10/month is over $100k/year. "How many niches have 1,000 people willing to pay something for great content?"
- Engineering newsletters (Gergely Orosz, Alex Xu) are now covered. He sees open opportunities in B2B sales, negotiation and angel investing, and has a "random feeling" about gardening.

chunks.heading: Angel investing and personal investing
chunks.text:
- He started about five years ago by investing in friends leaving Airbnb to found companies, then other friends' companies.
- As the newsletter grew, he became helpful to more founders and saw better deals, and he followed that pull.
- He aims for about 10% of net worth in angel investing, which he calls "a very expensive hobby." It's too soon to know if it will pay off, though he's optimistic.
- His three buckets are index funds, individual stocks and angel investing. After the market came back to earth, he's "increasingly convinced index funds are the way to go."
- He read The Bogleheads' Guide to Investing in high school and put most money in index funds early. In hindsight he'd put more in index funds.
- He eventually hired a professional financial advisor because he lacks time to optimize.
- Best spending since liquidity: trips and being generous with family and friends. Beyond that, only a great laptop and phone noticeably improved his happiness.

Moats! Does anyone have one anymore?

Yes. Yes, they do.

But only a small subset of what people call moats create real long-term value and defensibility.

Not actually a moat:
1. Distribution: This does matter more than ever. Building products has gotten easier, but getting them to customers has not. Distribution, however, does not create durable defensibility. It helps create the raw ingredients for one, but it is not itself a moat.

2. Execution: Yes, speed is critical for startups. But a company that has to sprint forever is not a good business. Ultimately, it will misstep, slow down, and competition will catch up. Speed gives a company more shots on goal as it tries to build a great product and a great business, but it must eventually find something more durable.

3. Brand: The idea is that when everyone is building the same thing, the most resonant brand will win. But for startups, brand works more like customer acquisition spend: Put money in, get growth out. It’s not something that will effectively keep others from competing long-term. Brand can become a true moat over time (as with Coke or Nike or Apple), but it just takes too long to really matter for most startups.

What you're looking for is compounding advantages: a self-reinforcing flywheel that gets stronger and stronger over time, ultimately making a company very hard to compete with long-term.

There are only four compounding advantages that really matter. Every major tech company has at least one:

1. Switching costs: The more deeply embedded a product is in the way a customer works, the harder it is for that customer to switch. This increases retention and revenue per customer, which can be reinvested into the product.

2. Network effects: The more users a product has, the better it gets for everyone. This increases engagement and attracts more users.

3. Scale economies: The more volume a company has, the larger and more efficient its operations can be. This lowers unit costs, funding lower prices or a better product at the same price, further driving up volume.

4. Data effects: The more usage a product has, the more data it generates. This data can be used to improve the product and increase usage.

If you can’t see the potential for any in the startup you’re considering joining, that’s a red flag.

In today’s incredible post, @danhockenmaier shares a simple framework you can run in about an hour after getting an offer:
1. Identify a startup’s compounding advantage
2. Gauge how strong it could get
3. Measure whether it’s working

We surveyed my readers about how they're using AI today, and more importantly, how they want to be using AI.

For PMs, the biggest opportunity is research. User research shows the largest demand gap of any task. Only 4.7% say it’s their primary AI use case today, but nearly a third want it to be. PMs have figured out how to use AI for output tasks like writing PRDs and drafting communications, but they’re hungry to apply it upstream, to the messy work of understanding what to build.

Prototyping is a breakout category across functions, both today and in the future. For PMs, “creating mockups/prototypes” jumps from 19.8% (currently using) to 44.4% (want to use next), a +24.6pp swing that makes it the single most-wanted future use case. 

For designers, prototyping and interaction design show similar momentum (+27.8pp). This tracks with the rise of tools like Lovable, v0, Replit, and Figma Make.

Engineers are shifting their use of AI to handle work after writing the code. Writing code is by far their most popular use case (51% current), but it has a demand gap of only +5.6pp. However, documentation (+25.8pp), code review (+24.5pp), and writing tests (+23.5pp) all show massive opportunities for growth in engineering AI tooling.

Founders are doubling down on AI as a thinking partner. Product ideation shows massive demand, jumping from 19.6% (currently using) to 48.6% (want to use next), a +29.0pp gap. Growth strategy and GTM planning (+24.7pp) and market analysis (+24.0pp) follow close behind.

Founders already use AI heavily for personal productivity (32.9% currently), but they want to move upstream. They’re looking for pressure-test ideas, explore markets, and think through go-to-market. AI as a co-founder, not just an assistant.

Raising a seed round 101

1. How much should you raise?
A simple formula is to aim for a 24- to 36-month runway, building in a 25% buffer.

Why 24 to 36 months? Generally, this is the right amount of time because it tends to be about how long it takes to hit product-market fit (and ideally become default alive) and/or raise a series A. As one data point, Carta has the median time from seed to Series A as 23 months.

You also probably want a 25% buffer because unexpected things always happen.

Here’s a simple spreadsheet illustrating how to model this out: https://t.co/4isR3KF19J

2. What do I need to prove to investors before I raise?
Generally speaking, before you raise, you should have taken the following steps:

- Proof of commitment: You have left your old job and are fully committed to being a founder. You can’t expect to raise capital if you aren’t yet fully committed yourself.
- Proof of work: You have done enough customer development and research on the problem to give yourself total conviction in the opportunity. Tomer London from Gusto puts it this way: “Validate the customer’s needs and your unique product insight. Speak with buyers (100+ in the consumer space, 30+ in SMB, 10+ in enterprise) to deeply understand their pain point, and offer them your solution in the most realistic way possible (a prototype is better than a pitch deck) and name a price. You’re looking for at least 40% of ‘wow!’ and ‘when can I get this?.’ Anything less is just people being nice to you.”
- Proof of insight: You have some expression of your thesis. At the most, you have built a simple product and have some paying customers. At the least, you have a clear written memo and/or deck that outlines what you plan to build (more on this below). According to Ivan at Notion, “Notion was like a better mousetrap but built differently. (We wanted to decompose SaaS into software Lego blocks—text editor, databases, charts—and allow end users to create their own tools with our Legos. The value prop is to reduce their tool fragmentations and give them new power.) We knew, or at least we had the conviction, that if we build it, people will come. That first-principle conviction turned out to be true. It is also why we started the company in the first place.”

3. How do I maximize the odds of raising a great seed round?

To maximize the odds of a successful raise, you need to choreograph your approach to maximize the number of potential options. Raising a seed round comes down to activating emotional triggers in prospective investors, including the fear of missing an incredible opportunity. The most surefire to get a yes from many investors is to get a yes from other investors.

In short, you have to create FOMO among investors. Here’s how to do that:

1. Plan your raise
You probably double the odds of success if you spend some time planning your raise. Carve out a two- to three-week window on your calendar to run your fundraise and speak to investors. Ideally, you want to speak to as many investors as possible in the shortest period of time. This compression of time creates the conditions for desire and scarcity, which can help prompt an investor to a yes. 

Here is a link to a sample timeline you can use to plan your raise: https://t.co/9WYn8X0ptu

2. Do your research on investors
Assemble your target list and research each investor before your pitch window. Have they invested in similar companies? (Check Crunchbase and their LinkedIn.) What’s their check size and investment philosophy, and do they lead? (Check their fund and personal website.) What do other founders think of them? (Ask for references from other founders.) 

Here is a spreadsheet to help organize your outreach: https://t.co/zfmGN7qZcF

3. Prepare (well-crafted) materials
A minimal deck and/or memo with a simple budget is all that you’ll need at this stage. You need to show there’s a real problem to solve, in a big enough market, and that you’re the one to solve it. That’s it.

However, the quality of this content matters a lot. The better crafted the materials, the more persuasive they will be, and the more likely they will result in capital. You should have all your materials polished and ready to go before your pitch window, and you should be ready to tailor your pitch to each prospective investor.

- Sequoia has a great template for a deck: https://t.co/m4sAxaZqIo
- As does YC: https://t.co/rbqh0b4WJB
- Rippling wrote the gold standard for a memo: https://t.co/IsiLeEUvO9

4. Get powerful, warm intros
Who introduces you to prospective investors matters a lot more than you might think. Take the time to consider your most powerful connection to each investor before you ask for introductions. High-influence intros for prospective investors include:
- Successful founders in the investors’ portfolios (regardless of investment)
- Other successful founders or influential operators
- Investors (angels, seed, or multi-stage) who are investing in your startup

Naturally, the stronger the relationship, the more powerful the intro will be.

There are also low-influence intros, such as investors who are not investing in your company (politely decline these, as they are a negative signal), and lawyers or other service providers (these are typically harmless but usually not very helpful).

If you can’t find a warm intro, craft a good cold email. These don’t convert as well, but there is almost zero downside to sending one.

5. Practice and prep your pitch
Your presence in a meeting matters even more than your materials. Showing up as the best version of your authentic, relaxed, and confident self is key. And that’s not something you can wing. Here’s what to do and know before you start speaking to investors:
- Prepare your pitch by writing a memo. Even if you don’t share it with investors, writing a memo is a great start to sharpening your ideas and communication.
- Practice your pitch a bunch of times before actually getting in front of an investor. Start real pitches with less important investors so you can iterate.
- Investors tend to overweight answers to their questions when evaluating your pitch, so answer their questions calmly and succinctly. If you don’t know, simply say, “I don’t know, but I’ll get that answer for you.” Preparing an FAQ can help.
- Acknowledge competitors factually, including their strengths. Then promptly move on to your strengths and your vision. Avoid disparaging competitors or spending too much time on them.

6. Start small to build social proof
You don’t need a lead investor to start taking on capital in a seed round. In fact, it is often better to open a SAFE (simple agreement for future equity) at reasonable valuation and start collecting the checks of smaller angels while you are having conversations with larger funds. Not only will you be taking on capital, but you’ll build social proof for the larger investors.

7. Follow up sparingly with investors, and never chase or “back-channel” them without strength
Interested investors will typically drive the process (more on this below). If you do have to follow up over email, do it sparingly, and don’t chase investors in a needy way. In such follow-ups, always pepper in some positive development, whether in revenue, a new hire or feature release, or additional angels closed (see above). Related, having an angel or existing investor check in, chase, or pressure lead checks often backfires. Savvy VCs and lead investors will take this pressure as a sign of weakness. If there is any sort of “back channel” that works, it’s having angel or existing investors saying they “vouched” for the lead check, as a type of reference. With this, you flip the power dynamic.

8. For bigger checks, never reveal who else you are talking to
Mystery is always more seductive than the truth. Never reveal the actual names of who gave you a term sheet. Just accurately describe them in the abstract (and never lie).

9. You don’t have a term sheet until you have an actual term sheet
Verbal commits are not term sheets. In seed, a term sheet is commonly a SAFE with a post-money cap. You don’t actually have a commitment from an investor until you have a term sheet or a SAFE. This carries through to every round you raise.

10. Your round is not closed until it’s closed
While less common at seed, rounds are actually not closed until the funds wire. Set reasonable but quick dates for closes (wires). Keep everyone moving toward those dates. This carries through to every round you raise.

For much more, including how to talk terms, how to choose investors, how to know if your raise is going well, and whether you should raise at all—don't miss the full post by @tmrohan and @jaltma: https://t.co/2Y79EcxHr5

The tech workforce is splitting in two

A year ago, we ran the first large-scale survey of how tech workers feel about their jobs and careers. What emerged we summarized in four words: burned out, but optimistic. Today, we're back with the results from our 2026 survey, and it's a tale of two workforces.

Half of tech right now feels amplified by AI—more capable, more confident, more excited than they've been in their entire career.

The other half feels shaken by it—less sure of their value and whether there’s still a place for them.

Which side of that line you fall on predicts how you feel about your career more than anything else, including your role, seniority, company size, or any other measure we collected. 

The workforce is bifurcating into two realities.

A few other takeaways that surprised us:
+ Significant burnout jumped from 44.7% to 55.7% in one year, while career optimism fell from 54.8% to 48.7%. A worrisome trend.
+ 53% of tech workers would steer a newcomer away from a career in their own role, even when they're optimistic about their own future.
+ The biggest AI fear is of being squeezed to do more work. Only 22% worry about “losing my job to AI.” Far more worry about being expected to do more for the same pay, getting trapped in an unsustainable pace, and the quality of their work declining.

The question that best predicts how a tech worker feels about their work, in 2026, is no longer "What do you do?" or "Where do you work?" It’s "What has AI done to your sense of who you are?"

🚨 Hot-off-the-presses data about the state of the product job market, in collaboration with @GotLiveData.

1. Growth is the #1 fastest-growing roles right now
I didn't see this coming. I’ve always thought of growth roles as a niche, and not one that was significantly expanding. I was wrong, but I can also understand why. With the market starting to return, companies are increasingly leaning into growth. You can see this in the chart with the upward inflection in sales and marketing roles as well.

It’s also interesting though to see that growth roles are growing much faster than sales and marketing roles. This might mean an increasing focus on product-led growth, potentially driven by a need for capital efficiency—something investors and public markets are increasingly prioritizing.

2. User research is resurgent
Another unexpected insight from this data is that user research is the second-fastest-growing role right now.

I believe what’s happening is that the UXR function went through a huge overhiring phase (see the large bump in late 2022) and then a reckoning as the market tanked last year. Companies realized their UXR teams were not adding enough value, and thus those saw some of the most significant layoffs in the tech industry. Now that the market is returning, companies are starting to rehire these roles after realizing they went too far.

I’ll note, though, that the absolute number of UXR people is relatively small compared with other roles. There are only around 14,000 active UXR roles in the U.S., according to the data, and about 200 are being hired each month.

3. Product management is doing fine
The story the data tells me is that there was a hiring acceleration through 2022 and then a steady state (i.e. the number of PMs being hired and fired each month staying relatively even) over the past 1.5 years. That feels healthy to me.

Numbers-wise, there are about 450,000 active PMs in the U.S. right now, and 2,500 to 4,500 are being hired each month.

4. Product owners are owning it
Another surprising result is that product owners are the third-fastest-growing role in tech. And there are around 65,000 of them.

Also, the growth of this role has been very steady. No big spikes, no slowdown. I don’t have a great explanation for this role’s growth other than that non-tech companies (e.g. banks, telecom) are expanding their product investments as they grow.

If anyone has any insights on this role and its continued growth, please let me know.

5. Scrum masters are masters no more
The only role that’s shrinking (i.e. more people being let go than hired each month) is the scrum master. Sorry, folks.

I’m guessing this in part explains the growth in product owners—people who used to be called scrum masters are now called product owners. There are still about 40,000 active scrum masters in the U.S., so we’ll see if this trend continues.

My biggest surprises and takeaways:
1. The top two companies are based in Europe! One in London, one in Berlin. Go Europe!

2. Fintech is dominant—5 out of the top 10 companies! Did not expect that. It’s probably no coincidence that the PayPal mafia has been so successful. One explanation, shared by my buddy Dennis Yang (PM at Chime), is that fintech nurtures strong product leaders because fintech work is on hard mode—lots of risk/fraud vectors, difficult stakeholders (e.g. compliance, regulations), and endless complicated tradeoffs. Another explanation could be that fintech PMs leave to join other fintech companies or start fintech startups, and since they know that space well, they’re more likely to thrive.

3. We have a new set of startup mafias: Palantir, Plaid, N26, Ramp, Intercom, Revolut, Duolingo, Uber, Notion, and Coinbase. The standout company is Palantir, where almost a quarter of Palantir PMs went on to start their own company. Almost a fifth of Plaid PM alumni went on to start a company, which is also incredible. Of older and larger companies, LinkedIn, Google, Intuit, and eBay made it into the top 15. Impressive! Props to LinkedIn for being the most founder-friendly big company.

4. FAANG companies lag behind. eBay, Intuit, and LinkedIn are far ahead of companies like Microsoft, Google, Apple, Meta, and Amazon in these lists. One explanation is that PMs at FAANG companies learn how to operate well within that specific company and are less successful elsewhere. Another explanation is that the best PMs at FAANG companies are happy and don’t leave, and so we don’t see their trajectories in the data.

5. There are an equal number of B2B and B2C in the top 10. You can do great no matter which direction your career goes.

Now that the Lenny & Friends Summit is a few weeks behind us, I’ve had a chance to reflect on the day. Here are the themes and takeaways that have stuck with me most:

1. There’s a huge need for (curated) IRL events right now
I’ve rarely felt this much PMF for anything I’ve done. It’s wild. My sense is that the more time we spend working with agents, the lonelier the work becomes, and the more we need to find a place to connect with other humans. I heard this theme more than anything else from attendees:

- “Things are certainly different now, but underneath all this technology, we’re still just ancient humans looking for connection.” —Charlie Koch

- “I left filled with gratitude for the experience, the conversations, and the reminder that even in a role that can sometimes feel lonely, we don’t have to figure everything out alone.” —Hemanth Babu Shekar

- “I left feeling genuinely sparked by what’s possible, and also a little less alone in figuring out what comes next.” —Attendee

- “I left this conference having fallen in love with product all over again.” —Jenny Zhao

2. Nobody has it figured out
Should we be building software factories? Are roadmaps over? Should PMs be shipping to production? We had speakers take both sides of these debates throughout the day. But what everyone agreed on is that there’s no one way to do it. My takeaway is we’re all still figuring it out, and the best way to do that is together. We heard this theme from both speakers and attendees:

- “The answer that we have come to is: it depends. It depends what type of product it is. It depends on what phase in the product it is.” — @TYehoshua, Atlassian

- “We don’t know the answer. We don’t think anyone knows the answer. We’re all going to discover it. And we’re all fundamentally on the same team.” —Ami Vora, Anthropic

- “This is just one way. There’s so many ways to build products. You probably heard 10 other ones today that were just as valid as this one. You should decide on what makes sense for you.” — @rmstein, Google Search

- “The best practices have not been written yet. We get to do that.” — @lil_dill, Stripe

3. It’s never been easier to build something nobody wants
As building gets easier, choosing the right thing to build, knowing what good looks like, and caring enough to fix it are becoming increasingly important for successful product teams. Almost every speaker touched on this theme:

- “And now we can ship all our bad ideas, like congratulations to us.” — @clairevo, How I AI

-“If almost anything you can think of can get built, it’s more clear to me than ever that the actual true value of PM is around judging. It’s around taste. It’s around doing something extremely well.” — @rmstein, Google Search

- “They’re not impressed if we animated something with Three.js and Blender in 30 minutes. They are impressed by us solving their problems and clever touches in the details that show we anticipated their needs.” — @lil_dill, Stripe

- “The output is not the product. Customers are not buying the lines of code.” — @karrisaarinen, Linear

- “Is this useful or is it just new? It’s a big thing you need to differentiate.” — @danshipper, Every

4. The PM job is expanding, not disappearing
Instead of the PM, eng, and design circles of the Venn diagram collapsing into one “builder,” each role is instead evolving and expanding.

- “Roles are overlapping, but they are also expanding. . . . Everyone can do so much more than they could do before.” — @TYehoshua, Atlassian

- “PMs will absolutely evolve and expand their role to not just the product organization but the marketing organization, the sales organization, the growth organizations, the operational organizations. PMs will become GMs, and they will own the actual business outcome and lead the entire function.” — @geoffintech, Ramp

- “I build and change the pricing page. I build prototypes, I deploy to production myself. I do the user research, I do the analysis, I do all of the optimizations.” — @ElenaVerna, Lovable

5. It’s important to be reminded of what’s possible—and to raise our ambitions
One of the most inspiring parts of the experience for me, and for a lot of people at the Summit, was to be surrounded by people at the top of their craft, demonstrating what great looks like. This is especially important now that AI allows us (and forces us) to be a lot more ambitious.

- “If we only use AI to make the things that we already make just faster, then we are definitely missing out on the most interesting part. AI can help us raise the ceiling, not just the floor.” — @lil_dill, Stripe

- “The biggest constraint is honestly people’s understanding and ability to absorb what you’re giving them.” — @thenanyu, OpenAI

- “I think next year is the ambition game. . . . What experiments can I run in two weeks, three weeks, that would have taken us a year last time?” — @clairevo, How I AI

- “Other conferences collect a bunch of people seeking validation that what they were doing in product wasn’t too off the mark. Whereas this group set the bar for what’s possible.” —Attendee
